title: ci: lint.yml's curl retry hardening covers the installer script but NOT the release-zip download that actually fails
description:
FOUND BY THE FIX-WORKER DISPATCHED TO PR #7881, which was red on the clj-kondo job. The job HAD NOT FAILED A LINT — it never ran clj-kondo at all.

THE EVIDENCE, quoted from the job log (gh run view 31456796279 --job 93672540971 --log). The entire content of the "Install clj-kondo" step was:

  Downloading https://github.com/clj-kondo/clj-kondo/releases/download/v2026.04.15/clj-kondo-2026.04.15-linux-static-amd64.zip to /tmp
  ##[error]Process completed with exit code 35.

Exit 35 is curl's SSL-connect error, thrown 0.24 seconds after the step started. There is NO lint output anywhere in the log — no file, no line, no finding.

THE REAL GAP, and it is a near-miss rather than an absence. lint.yml ALREADY carries `--retry 5 --retry-all-errors --retry-delay 3` on that step's FIRST curl, added by rf2-cq0s2j after an identical class of red. Those flags cover fetching the `install-clj-kondo` SCRIPT from raw.githubusercontent.com. They do NOT reach the SECOND download — the release-zip fetch that the fetched script performs itself — which is exactly where this one died. So the hardening was correct in intent and one hop short in reach.

WHY THIS IS WORTH FIXING RATHER THAN RE-RUNNING. A transient install failure presents as a RED LINT GATE on somebody's PR. That is the worst possible disguise: the natural response is to hunt the diff for a lint error that does not exist, and this instance consumed a whole fix-worker doing exactly that before it read the log. It will recur, it will land on a PR whose author has no reason to suspect the installer, and the cost each time is one worker plus a mayor tick.

REMEDY OPTIONS, for the worker to choose and justify — do not implement all of them:
  - Pre-fetch the release zip with the same `--retry 5 --retry-all-errors --retry-delay 3` flags before invoking the installer, so both hops are covered by one policy.
  - Or pin the binary through a cached action, removing the second download entirely.
The first is the smaller change and matches the precedent rf2-cq0s2j set. The second removes the class rather than the instance. Argue the choice.

HOT ZONE: .github/workflows/lint.yml is a hot-zone file — SEQUENTIAL, never parallel. Confirm no other in-flight PR touches .github/workflows/** before dispatching this, and remember that a merge changing the workflow matrix invalidates the check sets of PRs behind it.

VERIFY BEFORE EDITING: read the current lint.yml install step at source. The flags and their placement are quoted from a worker's report and were accurate against the tree it read; confirm which curl carries them now.
close_reason: Fixed in PR #7888 (branch worker/kondoinstall-rkl9). Remedy: fetch the pinned clj-kondo release archive directly under --retry 5 --retry-all-errors --retry-delay 3, dropping the install-clj-kondo script hop entirely (two network hops become one, and the remaining one is retried). NOTE FOR THE RECORD: the bead's first remedy option as worded CANNOT work — script/install-clj-kondo does 'rm -rf $filename' immediately before its own un-retried 'curl -o $filename -sL', so a pre-fetched archive is discarded unread; any remedy keeping the installer keeps the bug. Cached-action option rejected: reverses a documented decision, adds a third-party action to a required gate, and does not remove the download on cold-tool-cache ephemeral runners. SECOND FILE REQUIRED: scripts/check_fast_pr_gap.py reads the kondo pin off this exact step and knew only the 'install-clj-kondo --version <pin>' shape — dropping the installer broke that required gate (--check exited 1) and misreported the install step as an unrun gate; pin now anchored on the release URL. Check-NAME set verified UNCHANGED by parsing both sides (jobs, names, ifs, needs, triggers, path filters, step names all identical), so PRs behind it need no recompute.

title: mayor-method: workers share ONE scratchpad directory, so a generic filename is silently overwritten by a peer
description:
FOUND IN THE FIELD, 2026-08-11, by the clockfix-4mvd worker while it was finishing rf2-4mvd/rf2-w2e6. It reported this out of its own lane, correctly, rather than just working around it.

WHAT HAPPENED. It drafted its PR body to the session scratchpad at the generic path `scratchpad/pr-body.md`. The doctruth-dsnq worker, running concurrently, wrote the same path. The first worker's file was GONE. It recovered only because it noticed and rewrote to `pr-body-clockfix-4mvd.md`, which then survived even the worktree wipe later that hour.

WHY THIS IS NOT A NUISANCE. It is the same defect class the method already records for gate logs — "concurrent workers share the machine's temp directory; two workers writing the same /tmp/gate.log overwrite each other, and the loser reads a green belonging to someone else's run". The recorded remedy is worktree-local log paths. But the SCRATCHPAD is a second shared surface with the same property and it is NOT covered by that rule: the harness hands every worker in a session the same scratchpad directory, and a worker following its brief exactly will still collide there.

THE FAILURE IS SILENT AND IT CUTS BOTH WAYS. A worker that loses its draft may not notice — nothing errors, the write succeeds, the file simply holds someone else's content. Worse, the losing worker can READ the survivor and believe it is its own: a PR body describing another bead's work, with plausible structure and the wrong subject. That is exactly the shape of the gate-log case, where the loser reads a green with plausible numbers and the wrong code.

THE FIX IS ONE LINE IN THE BRIEF, and it should go in the canonical worker preamble in docs/the-mayor-method/dispatch-prompt-template.md, next to the existing shared-temp-directory rule rather than as a new section: EVERY scratch file a worker writes carries its worktree name — `pr-body-<worktree>.md`, not `pr-body.md`. And a worker must confirm a scratch file is its OWN before believing it, exactly as the gate-log rule already requires for logs.

DO NOT over-engineer this. No lock, no per-worker subdirectory scheme imposed by the mayor, no script. The naming convention plus the confirm-before-believing rule is the whole remedy, and it is the same remedy the sibling rule already uses.

SECOND, SMALLER FINDING FROM THE SAME REPORT, worth recording beside it because it strengthens an existing rule rather than adding one: the HARNESS reported that worker's revert-gate run as "completed (exit code 0)" while the gate's own captured status was 1. The method already says the exit code is the verdict and the summary is decoration, and already names the harness as one of the shapes that lies. This is a fresh, dated instance of exactly that, and it is why the one-line redirect-and-echo convention is not belt-and-braces but the only reliable verdict. If dispatch-prompt-template.md's wording on that point can be sharpened by citing this, do so; otherwise leave it alone — the rule is already there.
close_reason: Fixed in PR #7880 (https://github.com/day8/re-frame2/pull/7880). One rule added to the paste-verbatim worktree-boundary block in docs/the-mayor-method/dispatch-prompt-template.md, beside the no-stash rule: every scratch file written outside the worktree carries that worktree's name (pr-body-<worktree>.md, never pr-body.md), and a worker confirms a scratch file is its own before believing it. Plus one entry in the Failure-modes index. No lock, no subdirectory scheme, no script. CORRECTION TO THE BEAD: it says to place this 'next to the existing shared-temp-directory rule' in dispatch-prompt-template.md, but that rule lives in bootstrap.md (lines 260-264), not in the template — the template has no shared-temp rule at all. Placed in the paste-verbatim boundary block instead, because the bead's own finding is that a worker following its brief exactly still collides, so the rule must reach the WORKER. Second item: the harness-vs-captured exit-code instance is ALREADY recorded in bootstrap.md (lines 231-241), so no new rule was added; the template's exit-code bullet was sharpened by one clause instead — the number you quote is the one you captured, never the harness's — since that bullet covered pipes and fresh shells but never named the harness.

title: hic: a runtime tap makes its namespace's whole require graph reachable — record the rule the erasure gate proved
description:
A GENERAL RULE, ESTABLISHED BY A GATE THAT ACTUALLY FAILED during the rf2-hic-081 spike. It is not written down anywhere, and the next person to add a runtime-tapped instrument will rediscover it the same way.

WHAT HAPPENED. The spike's first cut put the receipt envelope in impl/receipt, which required re-frame.hicasso.evidence. `npm run build:hicasso-release` then FAILED with:
  DEV SURFACE LEAKED: evidence projection — sentinel "re-frame.hicasso.evidence"

WHY. re-frame.hicasso.evidence is dev-only BY REACHABILITY, not by any marker on it. A collector tap is reachable from the PUBLIC door, so ANYTHING THE TAP'S NAMESPACE REQUIRES BECOMES REACHABLE TOO. The leak was not in what the tap did; it was in what the tap's namespace imported.

THE RULE, which governs any future runtime-tapped evidence: RAW COUNTERS WHERE THE TAP IS; ENVELOPE IN A DEV-ONLY CONSUMER. Splitting that way, the same gate reads OK — 5 sentinels absent, 3 positive controls present (verified).

WHY THIS IS WORTH A RECORD RATHER THAN VIGILANCE. The gate caught it, so nothing shipped — that is the gate working. But the failure mode is invisible at the edit site: the diff that breaks it adds no dev surface and touches no dev namespace, it only adds a :require. A reviewer reading such a diff has nothing to notice. The rule is cheap to state and impossible to infer from the gate's own message, which names the leaked sentinel rather than the mechanism.

WHERE IT GOES: beside the ERASURE GATE'S OWN DOCUMENTATION, not in specification.md section 11. The spike explicitly flagged this — the rule is general to the erasure gate and not specific to capability receipts, so filing it under the receipts design would bury it where nobody hunting an erasure failure will look. Locate the gate's documentation from the sentinel string and the release-build script; if the gate has no prose record at all, that absence is itself the finding and this bead should say so and put the rule wherever the gate's behaviour IS described.

SCOPE: a documentation record of a rule already enforced by a shipped gate. Do NOT add a checker, do NOT change the gate, do NOT re-run the spike. If you find the rule already recorded somewhere, close as verified-duplicate citing where.
close_reason:
RECORDED. PR #7878 (branch worker/erasrule2-nkr3).

WHERE IT WENT: the header block of
implementation/hicasso/scripts/check_production_erasure.cjs, as a new section
"## A tap drags its namespace's requires onto the shipped path", placed
immediately above "## What this gate does NOT cover, and why".

THE GATE HAS NO PROSE RECORD ANYWHERE ELSE — that absence was checked, and it
is what decided the location. Nothing under docs/ describes this gate's
behaviour: docs/design/hicasso/product/invariants.md carries a one-line I12
invariant row, not the mechanism, and TESTING.md documents the
build:hicasso-release BUILD and its CI scheduling rather than the erasure
mechanism. The sibling live-half test
(implementation/hicasso/test/re_frame/hicasso/erasure_sentinels_cljs_test.cljs)
explicitly DEFERS to the gate's docstring — "The scan's docstring says why in
full" — rather than restating it. So this bead's primary instruction ("beside
the erasure gate's own documentation") and its fallback clause ("put the rule
wherever the gate's behaviour IS described") resolve to the same file.

NOT A DUPLICATE, but adjacent to something already there. The evidence
sentinel's own `why` field already says re-frame.hicasso.evidence is "dev-only
by REACHABILITY", and its `remedy` already says "find the :require". What was
NOT recorded, and is now, is the design consequence for an AUTHOR rather than a
diagnosis for a debugger: that a tap on the shipped path drags its namespace's
whole require graph with it, and therefore RAW COUNTERS WHERE THE TAP IS,
ENVELOPE IN A DEV-ONLY CONSUMER.

NOT filed under rf2-eoo9 (capability receipts), per this bead: the rule is
general to the erasure gate and burying it under one feature is how nobody
hunting an erasure failure finds it.

CONSIDERED AND REJECTED: amending the evidence row's `remedy` string so the
printed failure names the mechanism rather than only the sentinel. It is
tempting precisely because the rule's justification is that the message cannot
teach it — but it would change what the gate EMITS, which both this bead and
the dispatch brief fence. The header addition leaves roster, sentinels,
controls, premises and every emitted string byte-identical.

The new text also cross-references check_optional_module_reachability.py as the
source-side counterpart, which decides the same reachability property over
:require forms rather than over a bundle.

GATES: check_production_erasure.cjs --self-test exit 0 ("5 sentinels, 3
positive controls" — which independently confirms the counts the new prose
quotes); check_retired_spellings.py self-test + full exit 0;
check_thrown_error_messages.py self-test + full exit 0; check_gate_scheduling.py
self-test + full exit 0; check_fast_pr_gap.py --list exit 0. The bundle half of
the gate (npm run build:hicasso-release) and the Hicasso CLJS suite were NOT run
locally — both need implementation/node_modules, which a fresh worktree lacks
and which can only be supplied by junctioning into the mayor checkout, the
operation that has twice emptied the mayor's real node_modules; an external
process emptied six worktrees during this session, so that junction was
unusually unsafe. Neither reads the edited bytes (a block comment cannot change
a bundle), and CI runs build:hicasso-release in the required cljs job.

title: docs+hic: chapter 20 teaches a defhost :slots option that does not exist, and ch09/ch10 call an absent h/as-element
description:
TWO TAUGHT-BUT-ABSENT SURFACES, both found by the rf2-hic-032 worker (PR #7874) and both left alone because docs/** was outside its fence.

1. `defhost`'s `:slots` OPTION DOES NOT EXIST. `codec/host-options` is `#{:callbacks :ssr}` and an unknown key REFUSES AT MINT. So chapter 20's taught Suspense-host recipe — `(h/defhost suspense react/Suspense {:slots #{:fallback}})` — cannot be written today; a reader copying it gets a mint-time refusal. The rf2-hic-032 lazy DOM row hosts Suspense NATIVELY instead, which is the shape that works and is the obvious candidate for the corrected recipe.

2. `h/as-element` DOES NOT EXIST, while chapter 09 calls it and `h/as-component` "the two halves of one seam" and chapter 10 prescribes it as a recovery. `impl/intent`'s docstring already records that FOUR DESIGN DOCS copied the spelling before anyone checked it resolved (rf2-2rtt6.120). PR #7874 shipped `h/as-component` — the outward half — so the seam now has one real half and one imagined one.

WHY BOTH MATTER MORE THAN A WORDING NIT: each is a COPYABLE RECIPE that fails at the first attempt. That is the ergonomics half of the pre-alpha stance — a guide that teaches a verb the compiler refuses is worse than a guide that omits it, because the reader spends their first minutes debugging our documentation.

SCOPE: correct the two recipes to what the code actually supports. Do NOT add `:slots` or mint `h/as-element` to make the prose true — that is a design decision nobody has taken, and the inward bridge was deliberately NOT built (h/defhost and [:>] already hand a native component a raw JS props object; making a marked component a first-class hiccup head would put native-tier knowledge in the codec and break clause 6). If the seam genuinely needs an inward half, that is a separate ruling.

Chapter 10's troubleshooting and chapter 20's Suspense recipe are also the two places that promised `n/memo` and `n/lazy` before they existed; those two verbs landed in #7874, so re-read those sections as a whole rather than patching one line.
notes:
CROSS-REFERENCE from rf2-hic-035 (its worker, before opening its PR). READ rf2-hic-035's VERDICTS note before writing a line of this bead.

BOTH of this bead's 'taught-but-absent' surfaces are NO LONGER ABSENT. rf2-hic-035 makes them real rather than making the doc wrong, and the design record — specification.md:119-120/:172/:174, lanes/design-laws.md law 5, lanes/ergonomics-api.md:13-14/:109 — is where the decision this bead says 'nobody has taken' was in fact taken and published.

- defhost :slots exists. Chapter 20's Suspense recipe mints and renders as written; chapter 09's ReactNode-slots section is true as written.
- h/as-element is exported from re-frame.hicasso. ch09's :render recipe, ch09's undeclared-prop recovery row and ch10's native-child conversion are all true as written.

SO THE SCOPE OF THIS BEAD SHRINKS TO THE DRIFTS THAT ARE ACTUALLY DRIFTS, and one of them belongs to another bead: ch09:58's 'four options: :callbacks, :slots, :server, :fallback' and the {:server :render} rows are the :ssr -> :server two-policy rename, which rf2-hic-035's own description assigns to rf2-hic-028. Do not correct those to today's :ssr spelling only for hic-028 to correct them back — sequence after hic-028. The h/event vs h/fn spelling is a naming-ledger item and is neither bead's.
MAYOR — THE PREMISE HAS INVERTED. Verified on main at f7bf8a665c, 2026-08-11, after PR #7876 merged.

BOTH ABSENT SURFACES NOW EXIST. This bead was filed because chapter 20 taught a `defhost` `:slots` option that did not exist, and ch09/ch10 called an absent `h/as-element` — which made a taught Suspense recipe unwritable. PR #7876 (rf2-hic-035) made both real:
  - `:slots` is now an accepted `defhost` declaration key. codec.cljs's declared-key set reads #{:callbacks :slots :ssr}, up from #{:callbacks :ssr}.
  - `h/as-element` ships in implementation/hicasso/src/re_frame/hicasso.cljc, documented as "the one explicit hiccup→ReactNode crossing", and delegates to re-frame.hicasso.impl.codec/as-element.

title: docs: two more carriers of the 'reference-stable for the same resolved frame' sentence the rf2-40kv defect hid behind
description:
TWO MORE CARRIERS of the sentence rf2-ow4e corrected, both verified on main after that bead's PR (#7873) was written.

SITE 1 — `implementation/adapters/uix/README.md:14`, the strong form, verbatim:
"The returned map is reference-stable across re-renders for the same resolved frame (safe in effect deps)."
This is the SAME sentence rf2-ow4e corrected in spec/006 and spec/API.md, and it was NOT in PR #7868's file list — so the code fix landed while this reader-facing document kept describing the defect as the contract.

SITE 2 — `docs/design/hicasso/draft-guide/10-native-tier.md:169`, and it is WEAKER STILL:
"the map is reference-stable across re-renders. It is therefore safe to pull `:dispatch` off it and close over it in callbacks."
No frame qualifier at all. A reader takes "reference-stable across re-renders" unconditionally, which is broader than even the uncorrected spec sentence claimed.

THE CORRECTION, from rf2-ow4e's landed wording — do not invent a third phrasing: reference stability holds for the same resolved frame INCARNATION, because a frame keyword is an ADDRESS, not an identity. `capture-frame` pins the exact incarnation live when it ran and every op on the bundle refuses a superseded target, so a bundle surviving a same-id reincarnation would not be merely stale — IT WOULD BE SILENTLY INERT. Read PR #7873's diff and match it; the guide's register is lighter than the spec's, so compress rather than paste.

WHY THIS IS NOT A NIT: rf2-40kv was exactly this sentence made executable — `use-frame` memoised on the frame KEYWORD by `=`, and a keyword is `=` across a same-id reincarnation, so the hook served the dead incarnation's pinned bundle for the rest of the mount with every op silently recovering. THE SENTENCE IS WHERE THE DEFECT HID. Leaving two copies standing leaves two places for it to hide again, and the README is the first thing a UIx consumer reads.

SCOPE: two sentences, two files. Do not re-derive either document, do not touch `implementation/adapters/uix/**` beyond that one line, and do not change behaviour — the code is correct as of PR #7868 (merged).

PROVENANCE: the fourth copy was found and REPORTED rather than taken by the rf2-ow4e worker (PR #7873), correctly — `implementation/**` was outside its fence. The guide line was spotted in the same sweep and left because that tree was in flight.

title: spec: 'reference-stable for the same resolved frame' describes the rf2-40kv defect as the contract — it is per-incarnation
description:
`spec/006-ReactiveSubstrate.md` (around lines 2620 and 2651) and `spec/API.md` (around line 579) all say the ops bundle is "reference-stable across re-renders for the same resolved frame".

THAT SENTENCE IS THE ONE THE DEFECT HID BEHIND, which is why it is worth correcting rather than leaving as a wording nit. rf2-40kv was exactly this: `use-frame` memoised on the resolved frame KEYWORD compared by `=`, and a keyword is `=` across a same-id reincarnation — so after a destroy-and-recreate the hook kept serving the DEAD incarnation's pinned bundle for the rest of the mount. A keyword-keyed memo SATISFIES the spec sentence perfectly. The spec described the buggy behaviour as the contract.

WHAT MAKES IT A BUG RATHER THAN A SMELL, and what the corrected sentence must convey: `make-capture-frame` PINS the incarnation live at capture (rf2-9pyles), and both `capture-dispatch!` and `capture-subscribe!` REFUSE a superseded target (rf2-tdjv7p). So the stale bundle is not merely old — every operation through it silently recovers. "Surviving a reincarnation" means "silently dead".

THE CORRECTION, in substance: reference stability holds for the same resolved frame INCARNATION, not merely the same frame id. The shipped fix keys on the frame plus `frame/frame-incarnation-token` (the `:drain-lock` identity) by `identical?`, with a `nil` token as a legitimate key pairing with the unpinned, address-directed capture. A frame keyword is an ADDRESS, not an IDENTITY — the same distinction `native.cljc` draws about component names, and the third time this session that distinction has been the root of a defect.

SCOPE: three sentences across two files. Do NOT re-derive either document, and do not change the API — the code is already correct as of PR #7868; this is the spec catching up to it.

description:

WHY IT MATTERS: an absent-state assertion passes whether the populated rendering is correct, broken, or absent entirely. It is the "what single narrowing would let this row pass while the law is broken?" question with an uncomfortable answer — nearly any narrowing of the populated path.

BEFORE BUILDING ANYTHING, ESTABLISH THE COST-BENEFIT HONESTLY. The repo's standing position is that browser coverage is expensive and deliberately thin: one adapter-level smoke per shipped adapter, real regressions caught by substrate contract tests and feature-matrix gates. So the question is not "should every arm have a browser row" — it is whether the POPULATED tab has a failure mode the Node-lane test structurally cannot see. If the answer is no, THE HONEST OUTCOME IS A RECORDED NO, citing what the Node lane does cover; that is a complete deliverable and cheaper than a browser row nobody needed.

title: pair: retire the 33-line tool catalogue from the instructions blob in favour of routing rules — operator call
description:

THE PROPOSAL: retire the 33-line per-tool enumeration in get-re-frame2-pair-instructions' `## Tool catalogue`, and replace it with roughly half a dozen ROUTING RULES of the form "to read one sub, use read-sub, not eval-cljs".

THE CASE FOR IT, measured rather than asserted:
- The catalogue is 7188 of the blob's 9548 characters — 75.3%, about 3594 tokens. Every OTHER section is a convention, constant in size as the tool count grows. So the catalogue IS the growth.
- It DUPLICATES what tools/list already ships: 33 :description paragraphs totalling 79,127 characters, roughly 19,781 tokens, delivered before any tool is called. The agent already has this.
- A routing rule says the one thing a per-tool descriptor structurally CANNOT: which tool to prefer over which, and why. That is the part a consuming agent actually cannot derive.
- It would free real headroom. Today the tool sits at 4888/5000 with 112 tokens of margin, and the prose rides the wire TWICE (pr-str EDN and structuredContent JSON), so a character costs ~0.5 tokens and the effective prose budget is ~2500. Deleting 75% of the artefact is the only move that buys room without deferring the problem.

That is a product/ergonomics judgement about what a consuming agent needs on first contact — trust-the-programmer applies to the AI here too — and it is not the mayor's to make.

A CONSEQUENCE WORTH KNOWING BEFORE DECIDING: until this is settled, the authoring-time budget guard landed by rf2-3dmj must sit AT the cap rather than below it with a reserve. At 97.8% consumed any reserve is red on arrival, and trimming prose to create one is the exact deferral rf2-3dmj forbade. So "leave it as is" has a standing cost: no early warning, only a hard stop.

NOT URGENT. Nothing is broken today and the guard now catches a breach at authoring time rather than in an unrelated PR's CI run.

title: gate: a retired :where coordinate can survive as a string in a test assertion, which no symbol-shaped check sees
description:
A retired coordinate can survive as a STRING in a test assertion, where no symbol-shaped check can see it. rf2-hic-007 demonstrated this the hard way: after the sweep moved 42 `:where` symbols off `front.*`, CI went red on `test_kit_runtime_parity_cljs_test.cljs`, whose predicate used `(str/starts-with? (str (:where …)) "front.codec/")`. A green test was ASSERTING that a shipped refusal still named the benchmark tree — and it was a string, invisible to every `'front.` scan, including the two greps the mayor used to "verify" the close.

WHY THIS WANTS A STANDING CHECK RATHER THAN VIGILANCE: the failure surfaced only in CI, from an assertion, in a file the sweep's own author had already edited. The next rename of an impl namespace re-opens exactly this path, and the cost is a red build in someone else's PR whose diff has nothing to do with the cause.

THE CHEAP ANSWER IS AN EXISTING CHECKER, NOT A NEW ONE. `scripts/check_retired_spellings.py` already exists for precisely this category — a spelling that has been retired and must not reappear — and `front.*`/`arm1.*` are retired spellings by any reading. Adding a rule there costs one rule plus its self-test corpus. Do NOT write a new checker: the rf2-hic-007 worker measured that both check_retired_spellings.py and check_freeze.py require substantial prose plus a self-test corpus per rule, and a second checker would duplicate that machinery for one pattern.

THE RULE MUST COVER BOTH SHAPES, which is the whole point: the quoted symbol (`'front.codec/thing`) AND the bare string (`"front.codec/"`), across `implementation/hicasso/src/**`, `implementation/hicasso/test/**`, `implementation/hicasso/test_kit/**` and `spec/009-Instrumentation.md`. A rule that only knows the symbol shape reproduces the exact blind spot this bead exists to close.

DELIBERATE EXCLUSION, verify before writing the rule: `implementation/hicasso/src/re_frame/hicasso/impl/state.cljc:104` carries `;; Errors — the lane's shape (front.presence/fail!)` — a section-header comment, prose provenance into the frozen bench tree, kept verbatim by the freeze manifest and carried by no refusal. The rule must not red on it. Decide whether that means excluding comments or allowlisting that line, and say which and why.

PROVE IT BITES: plant both shapes, quote both exit-1 messages, restore and verify BY HASH (on Windows `sed -i` rewrites CRLF→LF, so `git diff` reads clean while the bytes differ — use `git checkout --`).

PROVENANCE: raised by the rf2-hic-007 worker, which correctly did NOT add the gate — the audit's fence said add no new machinery — and flagged it for a ruling instead. The mayor's ruling is that a rule in an existing checker is not "new machinery" in the sense the fence meant, and that the demonstrated regression path earns it.
notes:
MERGED-PR AUDIT #7867: reopen. Two executable shapes escape or mis-trigger rule (d). (1) In .clj* a syntax-quoted coordinate such as `(def x `front.codec/realize-deep)` is live Clojure but returns zero findings because the shared token-start regex denies a preceding backtick; that exclusion belongs only to Markdown provenance. (2) The string arm treats escaped quotes as literal boundaries, so `(def msg "the old assertion used \"front.codec/\" here")` is falsely reported although the retired spelling is quoted prose inside a larger string. BOUNDED REPAIR: make the symbol boundary source-kind aware, recognize real unescaped string delimiters, and add one positive syntax-quote fixture plus one escaped-quote negative fixture. Preserve comment masking and the existing whole-literal rule; no parser or new checker.
MERGED-PR AUDIT #7875 (merged 2026-08-11T03:20:09Z as 63644094fd23c0bd0c54203b1b7bdb094df65a56) — REOPEN THIS EXACT RULE OWNER; do not create another checker bead. The new source-kind split correctly finds `(def x `front.codec/realize-deep)` in a .clj* file, but denies the backtick everywhere in .md. A direct call to _scan_coordinates on ```clojure / (def x `front.codec/realize-deep) / ``` returns 0 findings. That contradicts the existing positive spec_code_block.md fixture rationale that a fenced example carries the same weight as a test assertion: a reader copies it. BOUNDED REPAIR: keep ordinary Markdown inline provenance such as `front.codec/realize-deep` green, but recognize syntax-quoted retired coordinates inside fenced Clojure examples and add the missing positive fixture. Preserve comment masking, whole-literal string matching, and the single existing checker.
close_reason:
RE-CLOSED after a silent tracker revert (2026-08-11). This bead was closed by its worker, verified CLOSED by the mayor, and read OPEN again on a later tick — the documented rollback-or-reimport failure. Re-closing on landed evidence rather than on the earlier close.

EVIDENCE: PR #7875 is MERGED. It merged on all five clauses at 91/91 (73 SKIPPED + 18 SUCCESS, zero nonterminal, five runs at head sha 7d4c526540 all COMPLETED, check-name set identical to merged #7874), and its changes are on main — including the two new fixture files scripts/_test_fixtures/check_retired_spellings/coord/positive/syntax_quoted_symbol.cljc and .../negative/escaped_quote_in_prose_string.cljc, which are the red-and-green halves of the proof.

title: docs(hicasso): the HMR inversion fixed in chapter 10 survives in 20-code-splitting and the glossary
description:
The HMR inversion corrected in guide chapter 10 by PR #7856 (rf2-hic-092) PROPAGATED to two other files, which still teach the false contract. The rf2-hic-092 worker found them, reported them, and correctly did not follow them out of its fence — these are corrections, not trivially-additive edits.

THE SHIPPED CONTRACT, from `implementation/hicasso/src/re_frame/hicasso/native.cljc` (~281-287 and ~452-455): minting a component is ALLOCATION, NEVER A LOOKUP BY NAME. A reload re-evaluates the module, a fresh element type is allocated, and A CLEAN REMOUNT ACROSS A SAVE IS THE DESIGNED CONDUCT — not a fault. A component's name is an ADDRESS, not an identity.

THE THREE SITES STILL WRONG:
- docs/design/hicasso/draft-guide/20-code-splitting.md:99 — "and HMR still replaces the implementation without remounting it", the same false claim, made about `n/lazy`.
- docs/design/hicasso/draft-guide/20-code-splitting.md:192 — the same healthy-symptom troubleshooting row, near-verbatim: it treats remounting as evidence of a fault.
- docs/design/hicasso/draft-guide/glossary.md:428-429 — "erase identity metadata that Xray AND HMR need".

WHY THIS IS WORTH A BEAD RATHER THAN A SHRUG: the ch20 troubleshooting row has the same defect chapter 10's did, and it is the worse half — it sends a programmer to hunt an erased marker when nothing is broken. A reader who lands on ch20 gets exactly the debugging goose chase we just removed from ch10.

TAKE CHAPTER 10's REPAIR AS THE MODEL, because it solved the harder problem well: it did NOT simply delete the bad troubleshooting row. An anonymous Xray boundary IS a genuine erased-marker symptom, so the row kept that half and dropped the healthy half — and a NEW row was added so the reader who arrives with "my state resets on save" has somewhere to land: that is designed conduct, and state that must outlive a save belongs in app-db. title: hic: a port is not reliably a move — six ports deleted their originals, the two :ssr ports left duplicates
description:
A PORT IS NOT RELIABLY A MOVE, and the triage tree is now inconsistent about it.

FOUND BY the rf2-b6ja worker (PR #7850) while recording the sequencing decisions; flagged in the document, deliberately NOT settled, because picking a convention is a ruling rather than a repair.

THE STATE: the six front/* ports DELETED their bench originals. The two :ssr ports DID NOT — so host_ssr_dom_cljs_test and fallback_contents_cljs_test now live in BOTH trees, the bench tree and implementation/hicasso/test/. That is precisely the "a second copy doubles the maintenance" case the triage document's own reasoning names as the thing to avoid.

WHY IT MATTERS BEYOND TIDINESS: a duplicated suite drifts silently. The two copies compile in different lanes against different hosts, so a fix applied to one and not the other produces a green build with a stale witness still asserting the old behaviour — and the stale one keeps passing, which is the worst shape of test rot because nothing goes red to announce it.

THE RULING NEEDED — one of:
(a) A PORT IS A MOVE: the original is deleted as part of the port, always. Simple, and it matches what six of eight ports already did. The cost is that the bench tree loses coverage the moment a port lands, and if the port later proves inadequate there is nothing to fall back to.
(b) A PORT MAY LEAVE THE ORIGINAL, but only with a recorded reason on the row and a named condition for deleting it later. Honest about the cases where the donor suite is still earning its place (a different host, a lane the package cannot reach), at the cost of a standing obligation somebody must discharge.
My recommendation is (a) with (b) as a NAMED EXCEPTION requiring the reason in the row — the default should be the one that cannot rot, and the exception should have to justify itself in writing.

WHATEVER IS RULED, the two :ssr rows are then either deleted from the bench tree or given their recorded reason. Do not resolve this by deleting the bench copies before the ruling: rf2-b6ja established that implementation/hicasso/* does NOT arm implementation_jvm, so a bench original can be carrying a host the package copy does not have, and that is exactly the case (b) exists for.

CONTEXT: the census has also drifted — 63 of 69 files remain (25,268 lines). The document's header now says once that its counts are census-time values; renumbering it was deliberately fenced out of rf2-b6ja and is not part of this bead either.
notes:
MAYOR RULING: (a) with (b) as a NAMED EXCEPTION requiring its reason in writing.

THE DEFAULT IS (a) — A PORT IS A MOVE. The original is deleted as part of the port. Six of the eight ports already did this, so the default matches the practice rather than fighting it, and it is the option that CANNOT ROT: there is only ever one copy, so there is nothing to drift out of step.

THE EXCEPTION IS (b), AND IT MUST JUSTIFY ITSELF IN THE ROW. A port may leave the original standing ONLY with a recorded reason on the triage row and a NAMED CONDITION for deleting it later. "We might still want it" is not a reason. A reason is a capability the package copy does not have — and rf2-b6ja established that exactly such a case exists: implementation/hicasso/* does NOT arm implementation_jvm, so a bench original can be carrying a JVM host the package copy simply cannot reach. That is what (b) is for, and it is why (a) alone would be wrong.

WHY THE DEFAULT GOES THIS WAY RATHER THAN THE OTHER: a duplicated suite drifts SILENTLY. The two copies compile in different lanes against different hosts, so a fix applied to one and not the other leaves a green build with a stale witness still asserting the old behaviour — and the stale one keeps PASSING. Nothing goes red to announce it, which makes it the worst shape of test rot. An exception that has to be written down is cheap; a silent duplicate is not.

APPLIED TO THE TWO OPEN CASES: host_ssr_dom_cljs_test and fallback_contents_cljs_test currently live in both trees with no recorded reason. Under this ruling each is either deleted from the bench tree, or given a written reason plus its deletion condition. DO NOT DELETE THEM BLIND — first check whether either is carrying a host the package copy cannot reach (the implementation_jvm case above is the live precedent). If it is, that is case (b) and it gets the note; if it is not, it goes.

SCOPE NOTE: renumbering the drifted census (63 of 69 files remain, 25,268 lines) is NOT part of this. rf2-b6ja deliberately fenced it out and so does this bead; the document's header already says once that its counts are census-time values.
CORRECTION: the close reason names rf2-oc9j for the dangling codec.cljs citations; that id was written before the bead was filed and is wrong. The real id is the one created immediately after this close — see the bead titled 'hic: two codec.cljs prose citations name a bench suite the c78g port deleted'.

title: gate: check_doc_slugs skips fenced doc links outside one tree, so bootstrap.md's links are green-but-unchecked
description:
check_doc_slugs.py checks markdown doc links inside fenced blocks ONLY for trees listed in FENCED_DOC_LINK_TREES, which is `("docs/design/hicasso",)` — scripts/check_doc_slugs.py:1648. Everywhere else, a doc link inside a fence is skipped.

WHY THAT IS A FAIL-OPEN AND NOT MERELY A LIMITATION: docs/the-mayor-method/bootstrap.md is ALMOST ENTIRELY ONE FENCED `text` BLOCK, because the file IS a pasteable prompt — the fence is the deliverable, not decoration. So the gate reports green on that file, the file is genuinely in the corpus, and its out-of-fence prose IS checked — and none of that says anything about the block that contains essentially the whole document. A future edit adding a doc link inside that block gets a green that verified nothing, and the green is more misleading than a skip would be, because the file is demonstrably covered.

THIS IS THE SAME SHAPE THE REPO HUNTS IN ITS OWN INSTRUMENTS: a gate that verifies the absence of bad news rather than the presence of good news. It is also the same shape as the two witnesses PR #7846 repaired — rows that ran in three engines and could not fail.

PROVENANCE, and it is a measurement rather than a reading: the rf2-fbi4 worker (PR #7849) planted TWO bogus anchors while proving gate coverage — one outside the fence, one inside it. The gate reported exactly the first, `BROKEN ANCHOR: docs\the-mayor-method\bootstrap.md:1 -> README.md#rf2-fbi4-bogus-anchor`, exit 1, and was silent on the second. Nothing was riding on it in that PR (the added text carries no markdown links), which is why it is filed rather than fixed in flight.

THE DECISION TO MAKE — this is deliberately not pre-judged, because the cheap answer may be the wrong one:
- Simply adding "docs/the-mayor-method" to the tuple would close this instance. But the tuple existing at all implies fenced links are skipped BY DESIGN somewhere, presumably because a fence can legitimately hold illustrative or non-resolving links (sample code, a template with placeholders). Establish what that design reason actually was before widening the list — the answer determines whether the right fix is a wider tuple, an inverted default, or a per-file opt-in.
- Consider whether the gate should SAY it skipped a block, rather than being silent. A gate that announces "this file has N fenced blocks I did not check" turns an invisible hole into a visible one, which is the cheaper half of the fix and may be the whole of it.

DO NOT invert the default across the whole corpus as a first move without checking what breaks — sample blocks under docs/core/ are digest-pinned, and a sweep that reds every illustrative link would be worse than the hole.

RELATED, from the same worker and NOT a defect: scripts/check_readme_links.py DOES cover .claude/commands/*.md path references via _check_command_file_refs, and the bare mayor-dispatch.md reference added in #7849 resolves against the tracked-basename set. That half is sound.
notes: MAYOR: PR #7857 open, and MY FRAMING IN THIS BEAD WAS WRONG in a way worth recording before it closes. I described FENCED_DOC_LINK_TREES as a roster of trees where fenced links get validated, and worried that widening it to a prompt full of placeholder paths might therefore be wrong — that worry is what made me push the announce-the-skip option. The worker established from the block comment at scripts/check_doc_slugs.py:1626-1648 and from 68a9173592, the only commit that has ever touched the constant, that it is the OPPOSITE: a roster of trees where a markdown doc link inside a fence IS ITSELF A FINDING, because a fenced block is verbatim and a link inside one renders literally. Widening therefore means BAN, not RESOLVE — which is exactly right for a text fence whose idiom is already backticked bare paths, and my objection evaporates. The announce option I argued for was then defeated on measurement rather than dismissed: 538 of 721 corpus files carry a fence, so it fires on three quarters of the corpus, and its text is IDENTICAL before and after a doc link appears inside a fence — a signal that cannot change when the defect appears is not a signal. The chosen fix widens the roster to docs/the-mayor-method, which measures 0 fenced doc links and lands green; docs/design/freehand/ stays out for want of an incident, which is the roster's own evidence-scoped discipline. bootstrap.md is 334 of 335 non-blank lines fenced (99.7%), and only two other corpus files exceed 80%, so the measured class is essentially this one file.

title: hic: the test kit has no clock control, so a presence bridge under test cannot advance time deterministically
description:
rf2-5gka (migrate Story's presence bridge off Freehand, census cluster S2-S6) names a target-side `advance-clock!` as its prerequisite. IT DOES NOT EXIST, and 5gka cannot build it.

VERIFIED ABSENT, not assumed. Searched implementation/hicasso/test_kit/src/ and implementation/hicasso/src/ for any `defn` matching clock, tick, advance, flush-timers or run-timers: zero hits. The only "clock" matches anywhere near this surface are prose in tools/story/src/re_frame/story/budgets.cljc and determinism.cljc about wall-clock time NOT being asserted by the gate — unrelated to a test-time clock control.

WHY THIS BLOCKS RATHER THAN MERELY SLOWS 5gka: that bead's own fence says "Do not touch implementation/**". So the bead is gated on a capability it is explicitly forbidden from creating. Dispatching it as written produces a worker that reads its fence, discovers the gap, and stops — which is a wasted worker and, worse, a plausible-looking partial migration if the worker decides to route around the fence instead.

WHAT IS NEEDED: a test-time clock control on the Hicasso side, so a presence bridge under test can advance time deterministically rather than waiting on wall-clock. The natural home is the L3 mounted facade in implementation/hicasso/test_kit/src/re_frame/hicasso/test/mounted.cljs, which already publishes mount!, hydrate!, render!, dispatch-and-settle!, settle!, unmount! and assert-clean! — settle! in particular is the neighbouring concept and the new control should compose with it rather than duplicate it.

DESIGN QUESTIONS TO SETTLE FIRST, because getting this wrong makes every downstream witness flaky:
- What exactly advances: setTimeout/setInterval, requestAnimationFrame, microtasks, or a Hicasso-internal scheduler? These are not the same, and a control that advances only some of them produces witnesses that pass for the wrong reason.
- Does it compose with settle!, or replace it for timed work?
- Is it a test-kit-only facility (almost certainly yes — it must not appear on the public facade; see rf2-31xm, which is a live bug about exactly that mistake)?

NOTE THE ADJACENT LIVE WORK: a concurrent worker is renaming the kit's L2 entry points (rf2-0ckh, render/:reads to possibly tree/:subs), so land this AFTER that merges and use whatever vocabulary it settles on.

BLOCKS: rf2-5gka.
notes:
MAYOR: RATIFYING A DELIBERATE FENCE CROSSING, reported transparently by the worker after the fact.

WHAT IT DID: the witness is a BRAND-NEW file at implementation/hicasso/test/re_frame/hicasso/test_kit_clock_dom_cljs_test.cljs — a tree I had fenced out because the rf2-hic-007 :where sweep held it. The worker judged that stopping would ship a clock control with NO WITNESS, which the same brief also forbids, and took it.

RATIFIED, and the reasoning is sound: it touched NO EXISTING FILE in that tree, so there was no textual overlap with a sweep operating on existing files; the witness asserts no :where key, so it could not collide with the sweep's subject; shadow-cljs.edn's own comment says kit witnesses live under hicasso/test, so the location was not a choice it invented; and check_test_lane_bijection.py passed at 1880 files / 49 lanes with every file selected. Both PRs (#7858 and #7861) merged without conflict, so the judgement is confirmed by outcome as well as by argument.

THE GENERAL RULE THIS SETTLES: a fence over a DIRECTORY held by another worker does not, by itself, forbid ADDING A NEW FILE there — the hazard a fence guards against is two workers editing the same text, and a new file has none. What still requires stopping is editing an existing file in the held tree. A worker taking this route must say so prominently, as this one did.

THE DESIGN ANSWERS ARE BETTER THAN THE BEAD ASKED FOR, and the key one is that the trio moves in lockstep: setTimeout, setInterval AND Date.now. That is the whole design rather than a convenience — impl.presence-react arms the retirement timer, but the callback runs impl.presence/expire, which takes `now` and compares it against a stored deadline. A FAKE TIMER ALONE FIRES ON TIME AND THEN DECIDES NOTHING HAS EXPIRED: green for the wrong reason. The instant moves to each timer's own due time BEFORE that timer runs, and cascading timers armed inside the window fire in turn.

DELIBERATELY NOT ADVANCED, each with a reason in the docstring rather than by omission: requestAnimationFrame (a frame is a paint, not a duration — left on the platform schedule where it still fires); microtasks and promises (a microtask queue cannot be drained from inside a task, so no control could honestly claim it); performance.now (React's scheduler reads it for frame budget); the Date constructor; and any setTimeout captured before the window opened — React's own scheduler being the deliberate exception, keeping its module-load reference so flushes still work. That list is more useful than the coverage itself, because it tells the next author exactly where a witness would pass for the wrong reason.

RELEASE RE-ARMS OUTSTANDING TIMERS on the real scheduler with the time they had left; without that the runtime's own reapers would be stranded and assert-clean! would report residue the runtime was about to release. Released by unmount! AFTER React's teardown so component cleanups can still clear their timers, and by residue as a backstop, because a virtual clock still installed there would freeze quiesced!'s wait and hang the async test.

THE SABOTAGE WAS HONEST ABOUT ITS OWN LIMITS: disabling both advance-clock! calls in W1 reds the two DEADLINE assertions, and the one-millisecond-short assertions stay green — deliberately, because they are the half proving the retirement belongs to the deadline rather than to "any advance". Saying so is better than claiming the whole row discriminates.
MERGED-PR AUDIT #7877: hydrate! honors {:clock true} and returns a handle accepted by advance-clock! (mounted.cljs:653-660,700,724-738), but the runtime docstring at 791 and missing-clock error at 849 still describe mount! as the only producer. Correct both to name mount! or hydrate!; no behavior change.
MAYOR — THIS AUDIT FINDING IS ALREADY OWNED AND IN FLIGHT. DO NOT DISPATCH IT FROM HERE.

The MERGED-PR AUDIT #7877 note above asks to correct advance-clock!'s runtime docstring (~791) and its missing-clock error (~849) so both name mount! OR hydrate!. MAYOR VERIFICATION, 2026-08-11 — THIS BEAD IS NOT SATISFIED, AND THE OBVIOUS READING SAYS IT IS.

The description's premise reads as though it has expired: it says advance-clock! does not exist, and today three of them do. Grepped at source on main:
  implementation/hicasso/test_kit/src/re_frame/hicasso/test/mounted.cljs:843
  implementation/freehand/src/re_frame/freehand/presence_runtime.cljc:207
  implementation/ui/src/re_frame/ui/presence_runtime.cljc:189

NONE OF THEM IS THE ONE rf2-5gka NEEDS. That bead requires a TARGET-SIDE advance-clock! — one shipping in Story's own src, reachable by a presence bridge under test. The hicasso one is a TEST-KIT facility; the other two belong to freehand and ui. A test kit cannot supply the target side by definition: it is the harness, not the thing under test.

I AM RECORDING THIS BECAUSE THE MISTAKE HAS ALREADY BEEN MADE ONCE ON THIS EXACT BEAD. title: pair: the instructions tool is within tens of tokens of its 5000-token cap, and the next tool added will breach it
description:
`get-re-frame2-pair-instructions` is within a few tens of tokens of its 5000-token cap. The rf2-n3mb worker's first draft overflowed it at 5088 and reddened three tests before being trimmed.

CURRENT STATE, and why this is a warning rather than a bug: the prose that shipped in PR #7848 is SHORTER than what it replaced, so there is more headroom now than before. Nothing is broken. But the margin is small enough that the NEXT tool added to that list will hit the cap, and it will hit it as three red tests in someone else's PR, whose diff will have nothing to do with the cause.

WHAT TO DECIDE, not what to do — this is a design question and the answer is not obviously "raise the cap":
- Is a single instructions blob the right shape once the tool list keeps growing, or should it be paginated / split by surface?
- Should the cap be enforced at authoring time with a message that names the budget and the current usage, so the failure surfaces where the prose is written rather than in an unrelated PR's test run?
- Is 5000 tokens the right budget at all, given what a consuming agent actually needs on first contact?

DO NOT simply raise the constant to buy room. That converts a hard limit into a soft one and defers the same failure to a later, larger blob. Whatever is chosen should keep the failure loud and keep it close to the author.

PROVENANCE: flagged by the rf2-n3mb worker (PR #7848) as a possible follow-up after it hit the ceiling and backed off. It did not act on it, correctly — the cap is not that bead's surface.
close_reason:
Landed via PR #7863 (merged d2dc4ceb55, rebased onto main). Green on all five merge clauses at 91/91, five runs completed/success. Clean reap on the worker's report; canary held.

THE MEASUREMENT: 4888 tokens against a 5000 cap — 112 tokens of margin, about 226 characters, two or three catalogue lines. Taken through the PRODUCTION gate (cap/sum-payload-tokens over the real handler result), and independently reproduced by an emulation that predicted a planted overflow to the exact token.

THE NON-OBVIOUS FINDING, and it explains the earlier 5088 overflow: wire/ok-text writes the payload into BOTH :content[0].text (pr-str EDN, 9776 chars) AND :structuredContent (JSON, 9777 chars), and the cap counts both — correctly, since both ride the wire. THE PROSE IS MEASURED TWICE. One character of prose costs about 0.5 tokens, so the effective prose budget is roughly 2500 tokens, not 5000. Sizing a draft from the raw character count is wrong by a factor of two, which is exactly how the earlier draft landed at 5088.

AND THE REAL COST OF A BREACH IS WORSE THAN THREE RED TESTS: at egress the WHOLE payload is replaced by the overflow marker, so an agent's first-contact call returns no onboarding text at all — and the marker's hint, "re-call with narrower args", cannot help a tool that takes no args.

THE THREE QUESTIONS, answered: SHAPE — one blob, do not paginate or split, because splitting adds round-trips to first contact and does not stop the growth; the growth is one section (## Tool catalogue is 7188 of 9548 chars, 75.3%), every other section being a convention that is constant in the tool count. AUTHORING-TIME ENFORCEMENT — yes, landed. IS 5000 RIGHT — right for the wire and must not move, since it is mcp-base's cross-MCP constant shared with story-mcp and envelope/marker-text? uses it as the sub-cap test; but it is the wrong number to reason about here, because it buys ~2500 tokens of prose. The budget does not need to change; the content does.

LANDED: instructions_budget_test.cljs runs the production cap/apply-cap over the real result against cap/default-max-tokens — no duplicated arithmetic, no hard-coded 5000 — plus a (pos? tokens) self-check so it cannot go vacuously green. Proven to bite: ~300 chars of realistic catalogue prose planted, exit 1 with four failures at 5112 tokens, restored and verified by sha256. The failure message names the budget, the usage, the margin, the exchange rate, WHERE to shorten, and explicitly that raising default-max-tokens is NOT the fix.

ONE HONEST LIMITATION, itself evidence for the recommendation below: the authoring budget could not be set BELOW the cap with a reserve. At 97.8% consumed, any reserve is red on arrival, and trimming prose to make room is the deferral this bead forbids. The guard therefore sits AT the cap; a reserve becomes available once the structural question is settled.

THE STRUCTURAL RECOMMENDATION WAS NOT TAKEN, correctly — it is the operator's call and is filed as its own owner (see the follow-up bead). In short: retire the 33-line per-tool enumeration, which duplicates tools/list (already shipping 33 :description paragraphs totalling ~19,781 tokens before any tool is called), and replace it with half a dozen routing rules of the form "to read one sub, read-sub, not eval-cljs" — the one thing a descriptor structurally cannot say.

title: mayor-method: routing a finding to a live worker needs a note on the owning bead
description:
A PRACTICE THE METHOD DOES NOT DESCRIBE, developed under load tonight and then CORRECTED BY AN AUDIT — which is why it is worth writing down rather than leaving as folklore.

THE SITUATION IT ANSWERS. Running six concurrent workers, findings constantly land on files a live worker already holds — from a merged-PR audit, from another worker's report, or from the mayor's own reading. Filing a bead for such a finding creates a second worker contending for the same file; waiting until the holder finishes loses the context in which the finding was found.

WHAT I DO: route the finding to the worker that already holds the file, by message, so it lands inside the existing PR. It works — six routed findings landed tonight, none conflicted, and several were fixed within minutes of being found.

THE DEFECT THE AUDIT CAUGHT (AUDIT #7825 on rf2-hic-021): "identified this exact stale deferral but ROUTED IT ONLY TO A TRANSIENT WORKER, LEAVING NO DURABLE BEAD OWNER." A SendMessage lives in an agent's transcript. If that agent dies, times out, or reasonably declines the extra item, the finding evaporates — nothing in the tracker re-surfaces it, and the audit that found it has already run. I had recorded one routing in a CLOSE REASON on a different bead, which is a record on the wrong object: nobody reads a closed bead looking for open work.

THE CORRECTED PRACTICE, which is what belongs in the method:
  1. Route the finding to the worker holding the file. (Keeps the efficiency; avoids two workers contending.)
  2. ALSO put one note on the OWNING bead saying WHAT was routed, TO WHICH worker, and WHAT HAPPENS IF IT DOES NOT LAND. The tracker then carries the obligation either way.
  3. On that worker's PR merging, VERIFY the routed item actually landed — do not assume. A routed item is exactly the kind a worker may reasonably decline, and declining is often correct.
  4. Then close the owning bead. Do NOT file a duplicate; the audit's own instruction was "if the routed worker lands the correction first, verify it and close this owner; do not create another issue."

WHERE IT BELONGS: .claude/commands/mayor-dispatch.md is the natural home (it owns what happens when work is assigned), with at most a pointer from mayor-merge.md's verify-the-bead step. docs/the-mayor-method/bootstrap.md's dispatch-discipline paragraph may want one clause.

WHAT NOT TO DO: do not turn this into a mechanism. There is no routing registry, no tracking field, no script. It is one message plus one note, and the note is the whole safeguard.

FENCE: this is a documentation addition of a few sentences. Do not restructure the dispatch loop, and do not add a seventh anything.

title: mayor-method: reap-before-merge fixes the orphaned-branch trap but contradicts the never-pair rule
description:
A TENSION BETWEEN A RULE AND A PRACTICE I ADOPTED TONIGHT. Flagging rather than resolving, because I am the one running against the written rule and the resolution is a judgement call.

THE RULE (.claude/commands/mayor-hygiene.md, the paragraph after the reaping rule): "**Never pair a merge with a reap in the same breath, and never put the reap in the merge loop.** The merge loop is the natural home for cleanup, because a merged PR is the moment a tree *looks* finished; that pull is exactly the failure... Reaping is a separate, deliberate step, run from a list of names for which you can point at the completion notification you received."

THE PRACTICE I ADOPTED, four times tonight and recorded as bd memory reap-before-merge-avoids-the-orphaned-branch: reap the worktree FIRST, then merge. Measured benefit — `gh pr merge --rebase --delete-branch` then deletes BOTH the local and the remote branch, cleanly, 4 for 4. Before I noticed the ordering, roughly twenty merges each left an orphaned origin branch needing a manual `git push origin --delete`. The worktree is what pins the branch; nothing else does.

WHY THIS IS A GENUINE TENSION AND NOT A LOOPHOLE. My sequence preserves the AUTHORISATION unchanged — I reap because the agent reported it finished, and I check that I can quote the sentence. But the rule forbids the PAIRING ITSELF, not merely the inference, and it does so for a reason I proved correct tonight: putting the reap next to the merge is exactly how the authorisation got corrupted. I reaped catalogrows-vkle mid-gate during a merge pass, holding its message reading "Holding for the spine — not done yet". So my new practice is efficient AND it re-creates the structural condition of my worst mistake this session.

THE TWO HONEST OPTIONS:
  (a) KEEP reap-then-merge, and make the rule's exception explicit: the reap may precede the merge PROVIDED the quotable-completion test is applied first, in its own step, with the sentence actually quoted. The method's newly landed clause supplies that test, so the guard exists; the change is to permit the ordering rather than forbid the adjacency.
  (b) KEEP the rule as written, accept the manual `git push origin --delete` after every merge, and record WHY the cheaper ordering is refused — because proximity to a merge is what erodes the discipline, and one manual command per merge is a small price for that.

MY RECOMMENDATION IS (a), but weakly, and I would not act on it without Mike. The argument for (a) is that the orphaned-branch cleanup is not free either: it is a step I forgot or skipped on several merges tonight before the pattern became visible, and every orphan is a name that a later cleanup might match. The argument for (b) is stronger than it looks: the rule was written after six proxies each killed a live gate run, and I have just demonstrated that I am not immune.

WHAT IS NOT IN QUESTION: the reaping authorisation itself. Only the agent's own report that it has FINISHED authorises a reap, and the quotable-sentence test stays whichever option wins.

SURFACE: .claude/commands/mayor-hygiene.md, and docs/the-mayor-method/bootstrap.md if the two need to agree. Whichever way it goes, the merge-trap paragraph in bootstrap.md and README.md currently prescribes the manual `git push origin --delete` as the remedy — under (a) that paragraph would need to say the ordering is the root-cause fix and the manual delete is the fallback.
notes:
SESSION EVIDENCE, 2026-08-11 — the contradiction this bead records now has a clean natural experiment behind it, seven merges, no ambiguity.

REAPED FIRST, then merged (a quotable completion report in hand each time): #7842 ports-a15c, #7843 areduce-ka4d, #7845 xrayviews-jkdy, #7848 pairwire-n3mb. FOUR OF FOUR: `gh pr merge --rebase --delete-branch` returned exit 0 and the remote branch was gone.

MERGED WITHOUT REAPING (no completion report yet, so the worktree correctly stayed): #7839 native-hic030, #7844 wirescan-hic024, #7846 ctrl-hic016. THREE OF THREE: exit 1 with "cannot delete branch ... used by worktree at ...", the merge itself succeeding and reading MERGED, and the REMOTE branch left behind — gh abandons the remote deletion along with the local one. Two were cleaned by hand afterwards; the third is still orphaned pending its worker's report.

SO THE MECHANISM IS NOT IN DOUBT: a worktree pins its branch, and a pinned branch defeats --delete-branch on both sides.

THE PRECISE SHAPE OF THE CONFLICT, because it is narrower than "the rule is wrong". mayor-hygiene.md forbids pairing a merge with a reap, and its stated reason is that a merged PR is the moment a tree LOOKS finished — the rule exists to stop the merge event from AUTHORISING the reap. Every reap above was authorised by the agent's own completion report and keyed on identity (worktree HEAD == PR head), never by the merge. What I am violating is the rule's mechanical clause (do not pair them) while fully honouring its protective clause (do not infer doneness from a merge).

EVIDENCE THAT THE PROTECTION HELD, not just an assertion: three times this session I DECLINED to reap for want of a report — ctrl-hic016, wirescan-hic024, and native-hic030 — and accepted the orphaned branch instead. The cost of the rule as written is a branch-cleanup chore; the cost of misreading it would be a destroyed gate run, which is what it is really guarding.

THE RULING NEEDED FROM MIKE — one of:
(a) Amend mayor-hygiene.md to permit reap-immediately-before-merge WHEN a quotable completion report exists, keeping the ban on merge-authorised reaps. My recommendation: this is what the evidence supports, and it makes the authorising signal explicit rather than relying on the two steps being separated in time.
(b) Keep the ban as written and accept branch cleanup as a separate hygiene pass — defensible, since the orphaned branch is cheap and the rule stays maximally simple.

Not urgent, and nothing is blocked on it. Recorded so the decision rests on measurements rather than on my preference.
DELEGATED DECISION (operator-directed dossier review, 2026-08-11, operator-overturnable):

RULING: Neither (a) nor (b). Take the dossier's appended Codex route: DECOUPLE remote-branch deletion from reaping. Enable GitHub's server-side head-branch deletion; merge WITHOUT --delete-branch; the never-pair rule stands verbatim; reaping stays report-authorised in the hygiene pass.

WHY: It dominates both framed options. (a) still orphans every merge whose worker has not reported (the experiment's own 3/3 arm) and makes merge-adjacent reaping the sanctioned norm — the exact structural condition of the catalogrows-vkle violation, guarded only by caller discipline broken once this same session. (b) keeps a per-merge manual delete demonstrably skipped ~20 times, and its orphan queue feeds the 2026-07-19 name-collision hazard. Server-side deletion yields zero orphans by construction, needs no quoted-sentence ritual in the merge path, and moves no reap anywhere. Verified live: gh 2.89.0 mergeRun abandons the remote delete when the local delete fails (pinned branch); day8/re-frame2 has delete_branch_on_merge: false; no stacked PRs in the last 500 merged; bd memory reap-before-merge-avoids-the-orphaned-branch currently teaches reap-first while mayor-hygiene.md bans the pairing — a live contradiction this ruling resolves by making the ordering MOOT.

IMPLEMENTATION GUIDANCE (one docs worker, ~30 min, not hot-zone, parallel-safe):
1. Enable the setting: gh api -X PATCH repos/day8/re-frame2 -f delete_branch_on_merge=true (verify with --jq .delete_branch_on_merge).
2. .claude/commands/mayor-merge.md L28: merge command becomes `gh pr merge --rebase` (drop --delete-branch). Replace the clause "--delete-branch does not survive a worker worktree ... git push origin --delete <branch> afterwards is on you (see the hygiene loop)" with: the server deletes the head branch on merge; `git push origin --delete <branch>` is ONLY the post-MERGED fallback when a remote ref survives (branch protection / cross-repo PR). Keep "NEVER git push origin --delete before the merge succeeds" and all five green-criterion clauses untouched.
3. docs/the-mayor-method/README.md L188-201 (merge-trap paragraph): root-cause fix is server-side deletion + merge without --delete-branch; manual remote delete demotes to the post-MERGED fallback; the "leave local cleanup until the worker has REPORTED done" sentences stay word-for-word.
4. CLAUDE.md L93 (pull-after-merge bullet): update the quoted command string to `gh pr merge --rebase`; the rule's content is unchanged.
5. .claude/commands/mayor-hygiene.md: NO CHANGE to the never-pair paragraph or the reap rule. Hygiene keeps owning: reap on quoted report, delete merged LOCAL branches, git remote prune origin.
6. bd memory reap-before-merge-avoids-the-orphaned-branch: rewrite to record supersession — the trap mechanism is eliminated at the server layer, so reap-first ordering is moot; never-pair stands; reap only on a quotable completion report.
7. Corrected surface (per dossier, verified by grep): the prescription lives in README.md + mayor-merge.md + CLAUDE.md:93, NOT bootstrap.md — bootstrap.md needs no reap-rule change; the six-proxies history stands.
8. Verify with one live same-repo merge: exit 0, PR reads MERGED, remote head ref absent, the worker's worktree and local branch still intact until its quoted report authorises the guarded reap.

FENCES: The authorisation clause is UNTOUCHABLE — only the agent's own completion report ("can I quote the sentence where this agent says it is done?") authorises a reap; PR/merge state never authorises anything about a worktree; no reap without a quotable report. The never-pair paragraph survives verbatim. For the rare surviving remote ref, verify MERGED and delete the remote ref only — never reap early to clean a branch. No wrapper scripts, no CI gate, no ledger.

DISPATCHABLE.

Took the ruled Codex route: decoupled remote-branch deletion from reaping. delete_branch_on_merge verified true on day8/re-frame2 (twice). mayor-merge.md now merges with 'gh pr merge --rebase' (no --delete-branch) and demotes the manual remote delete to the post-MERGED fallback; docs/the-mayor-method/README.md names server-side deletion as the root-cause fix and records that reap-first is MOOT rather than adopted; CLAUDE.md's pull-after-merge bullet quotes the new command. mayor-hygiene.md deliberately unchanged per ruling item 5 - the never-pair paragraph and reap rule survive verbatim, and its existing merged-branch/prune line remains correct. bd memory reap-before-merge-avoids-the-orphaned-branch rewritten in place as SUPERSEDED, keeping the original measurement and adding that the orphan is solved server-side and only the agent's own completion report authorises a reap. title: hic: the bad-reads recovery keyword still tells the programmer to use a retired option
description:

Both are rowed verbatim in `spec/009-Instrumentation.md` (hard fence for that worker), and `docs/design/hicasso/product/complaints.md:133` carries the row too.

THE TWO ARE NOT THE SAME QUESTION, and the distinction is the content of this bead:

  - THE RECOVERY KEYWORD GIVES WRONG ADVICE NOW. It tells a programmer to add the query to `:reads`, an option that no longer exists. That is a live defect: the refusal fires, the recovery instruction is unfollowable, and the reader has no way to know the word changed. Fix it.

  - THE ID SHOULD PROBABLY NOT MOVE. rf2-hic-021's law is that ids are a stable public contract; a spelling that is merely unfashionable is not grounds to break it, and renaming an id has a cost the recovery keyword does not — every consumer matching on it breaks. Weigh it, state the reasoning, and be willing to conclude the id STAYS while the recovery text changes. A documented "the id keeps a historical spelling, and here is why" is a good outcome.

The #7828 worker already updated the refusal MESSAGE text to say `:subs`, so the message and the recovery keyword currently disagree with each other — that inconsistency is the sharpest reason this cannot just be left.

HOT ZONE AND SEQUENCING: `spec/009-Instrumentation.md` is sequential-access. `complaints.md` was held by `worker/smallmisc-miw1` (PR #7827) — check it has merged before dispatching, and read what it landed, since it retired a reserved id in the same file.

GATE WITH TEETH: `implementation/hicasso/scripts/check_complaint_catalogue.py` runs unconditionally on every PR and reads BOTH the register and spec/009, so a half-done change reds. Run it and quote the exit code. Read its eight rules before editing either file — CHECK C in particular governs which ids may have a spec/009 row.

STANCE: no back-compat shim, no alias, no deprecation path. And do not widen this into a sweep of other recovery keywords unless you find they are wrong too — if you check them, say what you checked.

1. THE TWO ARTEFACTS ARE ON DIFFERENT ROWS. :add-the-query-to-reads is the recovery for :rf.error/hicasso-test-missing-read-fixture (spec/009:2613). :rf.error/hicasso-test-bad-reads (line 2617) carries :pass-a-map-of-query-to-value — which names a SHAPE, not a key, and needs no change at all.

3. NO MESSAGE/RECOVERY CONTRADICTION EXISTS ON MAIN. #7828's updated bad-reads message sits beside :pass-a-map-of-query-to-value — consistent.

THE ID STAYS, decided on merits rather than on the fence. Rule 1 does not fire: an id names the REFUSAL, not the option, and the refusal means what it always meant — only the option's spelling moved. Rule 2 prices the alternative: a tombstone kept forever, a new live row, a struck plus fresh spec/009 row, and a spelling every consumer re-learns, for one better word. A recovery keyword is read once by a human and branched on by nothing; an id is matched on by stored errors, monitor grouping and test assertions. The register already set this precedent with :rf.error/no-frame-prop.

THE KEYWORD FIX WAS CORRECTLY DECLINED. It has THREE sites — spec/009:2613, test_kit/.../test.cljs:1117 (PR #7828's), test/.../test_kit_cljs_test.cljs:558 (another worker's) — and the change is ATOMIC across them, because spec/009's recovery column states what the runtime raises and consumers may branch on it. NO GATE CATCHES A MISMATCH: check_complaint_catalogue.py tracks ids only, and the drift gate reconciles :rf.error/* ids. Taking the spec half alone would trade a stale-but-consistent word for silent untracked drift. The emit line is also a context line inside a #7828 hunk, so editing it guarantees a conflict.

WHAT IT SHIPPED INSTEAD: two rulings under 'Rulings this catalogue owns' — 'An id is frozen; the :recovery beside it is not' (settling the class, since the stability rule governed the id and said nothing about the rest of the row) and 'bad-reads keeps its spelling'. Both framed on naming-ledger row 23's recommendation ALREADY ON MAIN, so they are true today and after #7828 either way.

IT ENUMERATED ALL 56 hicasso recovery keywords and checked the ten naming a literal API spelling against implementation/hicasso/src — :callbacks, :ssr, :server, :timeout-ms, :prefetch, :on-mouse-enter, :event, :handler, :render all live. :add-the-query-to-reads is THE ONLY ONE pointing at a key being renamed. No sweep performed.

FOLLOW-UP: re-dispatch the keyword fix after #7828 merges, holding spec/009 + test_kit/** + test/** together — three lines plus wording in two Trigger cells and two register row descriptions. Filed as rf2-1t3f.
