CRASH RECOVERY RECIPE — PROVEN 2026-07-23 when the Claude Code host process exited with 6 workers mid-run. Follow in this order; the order is the whole point.

THE ONE FACT THAT DECIDES EVERYTHING: workers have died two entirely different ways in one session — a stream watchdog killing them after a long silent stretch, and the host process exiting. In BOTH cases the line between "fully recovered" and "lost" was exactly: WAS IT PUSHED? Commits on a worker branch survive anything. Uncommitted files survive only as long as nobody reaps the worktree.

STEP 1 — GROUND TRUTH, before touching anything. For each worktree, git-only (never a filesystem walk):
  git -C <wt> rev-list --count origin/main..HEAD     # unpushed commits
  git -C <wt> status --porcelain | grep -v .beads    # uncommitted WIP
  git ls-remote --heads origin <branch> | wc -l      # is the branch on origin at all
Classify: branch-on-origin = safe. Commits-but-no-remote = AT RISK. Zero-commits-plus-dirty-plus-no-remote = MOST at risk.

STEP 2 — MERGE ANY GREEN PR FIRST. A PR that was green when the process died is free progress and it unblocks whatever was sequenced behind it.

STEP 3 — PUSH THE COMMITTED-BUT-UNPUSHED WORK YOURSELF. This is pure durability and carries no judgement risk: the commits already exist, you are only making them survivable. Do NOT open a PR from them.

⚠️ STEP 4 — DO NOT COMMIT A WORKER UNCOMMITTED WIP YOURSELF. Tell the worker to do it. There is a recorded incident in this project where a mayor committed a worker partial work as a recovery PR and merged an incomplete state that broke main. Uncommitted files are mid-edit by definition; only the worker knows whether they form a coherent commit. The mayor pushes COMMITS, never creates them from someone else WIP.

STEP 5 — RESUME EVERY WORKER, with a message tailored to ITS state, leading with durability:
  - Say plainly it was not stopped for cause and its work is safe — a worker that thinks it failed behaves worse.
  - For the most-at-risk one, make the FIRST instruction "commit what you have (even as a WIP commit) and push, BEFORE rebasing, BEFORE gates, BEFORE anything."
  - Tell it exactly what landed on main while it was gone, and whether its rebase is EXPECTED (sequenced deliberately) rather than a surprise to investigate.
  - Re-state only the must-survive laws and traps specific to that worker — not the whole original brief.
THIS WORKED, MEASURED: the worst-off worker went from 0 commits / 12 uncommitted files / no remote branch to 3 commits pushed on its first resumed turn.

STEP 6 — clear any stale .git/index.lock left by the abrupt exit, then re-export beads FROM DOLT (never git checkout over them) and checkpoint.

PREVENTION, now standard in every dispatch brief and worth more than the recipe: "COMMIT AND PUSH AS YOU GO — not at the end", stated WITH the reason (two mechanisms have killed workers; incremental pushing is the only defence against both). Also: a bigger in-flight bubble is a proportionally bigger crash surface — saturation is right, but keep it within what one recovery pass can handle.

AFTER A CRASH, CHECK LANDED-NESS WITH A 600-COMMIT WINDOW BEFORE SALVAGING ANYTHING (2026-08-03).

Recovering from a host crash that killed ~18 workers, I found 14 worker worktrees with commits and NO remote branch — the classic 'stranded work' shape. I pushed 13 of them for durability, which the method explicitly sanctions.

Then I compared their commit SUBJECTS against main. Against 'git log --oneline -60 origin/main' only 2 of 13 looked landed. Against -600, ALL 13 had landed. The branches were pure residue: workers that had already shipped via PRs that already merged, leaving behind unreaped worktrees whose local branch ref simply predated the squash-merge onto main.

THE COST OF THE NARROW WINDOW: I nearly dispatched ~11 salvage workers to 'finalise' work that was already on main, and I did push+delete 13 redundant branches. On a repo merging this fast, 60 commits is a few HOURS of main. A 2-day-old worker branch needs hundreds.

THE RULE: before treating an unpushed worker branch as stranded, diff its commit subjects against at least 600 commits of origin/main (use 'git log --format=%s -600 origin/main' + 'grep -Fxq' per subject). A worktree with commits and no remote is USUALLY residue, not loss. Real loss looks different: UNCOMMITTED modified files (that worktree genuinely died mid-edit), or commits whose subjects appear nowhere on main.

ALSO: 'gh pr list --state open' returning 0 is a strong corroborating signal — if no PRs are open, no worker is mid-flight, so every branch is either landed or abandoned.

THIS CHECKOUT IS CRLF, SO A MULTI-LINE PATCH ANCHOR SILENTLY MATCHES NOTHING (2026-08-11, rf2-czlb / rf2-3f11).

WHAT HAPPENED. A worker planting a sabotage edit found its first multi-line patch attempt matched nothing and reported no error — the edit simply did not apply. Cause: the working tree carries CRLF line endings, so any anchor spanning a newline fails to match a pattern written with LF. It found it only because it verified the restore by SHA-256 rather than by reading `git diff`.

TWO PRACTICES THAT FOLLOW, both cheap:
  - USE SINGLE-LINE ANCHORS when patching by string match. A pattern that crosses a line boundary is a coin flip on this checkout.
  - VERIFY EVERY RESTORE BY HASHING THE BYTES, never by `git diff`. This is already the standing rule for sabotage restores, and here is the reason it exists: a CRLF-flipping rewrite reads CLEAN in `git diff` while having changed every line, and the inverse — an edit that never applied — also reads clean. `git diff` cannot distinguish "unchanged" from "not attempted".

WHY THIS MATTERS BEYOND SABOTAGE. The plant-and-restore discipline is how this project proves a guard is exact rather than merely present. If the plant silently does not apply, the sabotage run comes back GREEN and the worker concludes the guard fired when nothing was ever broken — a false proof of a real guard, which is worse than no proof at all. The same failure would make a "restored" tree quietly different from the committed one.

Brief it as: "verify the restore by hashing the bytes, not by reading `git diff` — this checkout is CRLF, and both a failed patch and a line-ending rewrite read clean there."

ON WINDOWS, `git diff` CANNOT VERIFY A BYTE-IDENTICAL RESTORE - VERIFY BY HASH (2026-08-11, found by the rf2-dly1 worker, PR #7859).

Every dispatch brief I write demands the same coverage drill for silent-on-success gates: plant a bogus anchor, quote the exit 1, RESTORE BYTE-IDENTICALLY, confirm green. A worker doing exactly that used `sed -i` to plant and restore, and `git diff` came back EMPTY while the sha256 DIFFERED. `sed -i` had rewritten the working copy CRLF -> LF. The content was identical; the bytes were not.

WHY git diff LIES HERE: with autocrlf normalisation, git compares the normalised form, so a pure line-ending change is invisible to `git diff` and to `git status`. Both report clean. The file on disk has changed for every tool that reads bytes rather than lines - and on this repo that includes the digest-pinned sample blocks under docs/core/, which hash exact block text.

THE FIX, two parts:
1. VERIFY BY HASH, not by `git diff`: record sha256 before planting and compare after restoring. The worker caught it precisely because it hashed.
2. RESTORE WITH `git checkout -- <path>`, which writes the exact checked-out bytes, rather than a second `sed -i` that re-applies the same normalisation.

PUT THIS IN THE DISPATCH BRIEF. I ask for this drill in nearly every dispatch, and until now the brief said "restore byte-identically" and let the worker choose how to check - which on Windows means most of them check with `git diff` and get a false pass. The claim "restored byte-identically, git status clean" is NOT evidence on this platform.

GENERAL SHAPE, and it is the same one that keeps recurring: an instrument answering from a NORMALISED view rather than the raw artefact is confidently wrong exactly about the difference you are checking for. Same family as `git branch -r` being a cache, `gh run list` returning lowercase status, and the beads export lagging the database.

A MULTI-LINE PATCH ANCHOR SILENTLY NO-OPS ON THIS REPO CRLF CHECKOUTS, AND THE SABOTAGE RUN THEN COMES BACK GREEN (2026-08-18).

Measured by rf2-0yp7w.9 slice 2 (PR #8502): "Two plants silently no-opped first and both runs came back green — a multi-line anchor does not match a CRLF working tree, and unchanged and not-attempted are the same diff. Only the hash caught it."

WHY IT IS DANGEROUS RATHER THAN ANNOYING. The planted-fault route exists to prove a gate READ YOUR WORKTREE. The worker plants a fault, expects red, and reads green. The green does not say "the plant failed to apply" — it says, to a tired reader, "this gate does not cover my surface" or worse "the control does not bite". Both conclusions are false and both are actionable in the wrong direction: one abandons a gate that works, the other reports a hollow control that is not hollow. The evidence in the report is internally consistent either way.

THE DIFF CANNOT CATCH IT. "Unchanged" and "not attempted" produce the identical diff, so a worker verifying its restore by reading a diff sees exactly what a correct plant-and-restore looks like.

TWO RULES, AND BOTH ARE NEEDED:
1. ANCHOR A PLANT TO A SINGLE LINE WITH NO NEWLINE IN IT. Multi-line anchors are the failure; on a checkout whose line endings are translated they match nothing, with no error.
2. HASH BEFORE THE PLANT AND AFTER THE RESTORE, using version control content hashing against the COMMITTED OBJECT (git hash-object), never a plain byte digest of the working file — a checkout during a rebase rewrites the working file after you hashed it, so a plain digest reports a CORRECT restore as failed. Three hashes tell the whole story: pre-plant, planted, post-restore. If pre-plant equals planted, the patch never applied and the green means nothing.

This is the Windows/CRLF half of a rule the dispatch template already carries in general terms. It is worth its own record because the general rule reads as a caution while this is a reproducible property of every checkout in this repository, and it has now bitten twice in one run.

MY CRLF REMEDY IN BRIEFS IS THE WRONG REFLEX FOR MOST TRACKED FILES (2026-08-06).

WHAT I HAVE BEEN WRITING: "spec/** files are stored CRLF here; if the diff explodes, rebuild byte-exactly from the base blob and `git -c core.autocrlf=false add`."

WHAT THE rf2-ix9tk WORKER MEASURED on spec/004-Views.md: the override staged 2906 changed lines out of 2906 - it forced CRLF INTO AN LF INDEX. The plain `git add` gave 2/2, exactly the intended change.

THE REASON, and it is the discriminator to use: the file is `i/lf w/crlf` - LF in the INDEX, CRLF in the WORKING TREE, which is what `core.autocrlf=true` is FOR. The normalisation on add is CORRECT and is what keeps the index clean. Disabling it makes the working-tree CRLF the thing that gets stored, which is a whole-file diff.

THE CORRECTED RULE: use PLAIN `git add`. Then check `git diff --numstat`. Only if a plain add blows the diff up does the override become a candidate - and check `git ls-files --eol <path>` first to see which way the file is actually stored. The numstat check is the load-bearing half and always was; the remedy I attached to it was cargo.

WHY IT SURVIVED SO LONG: it came from a real incident (a worker DID produce a ~4,200-line diff on spec/011-SSR.md for a +45-line change) and I generalised the CURE from one file to a whole tree without re-testing. Same shape as the git-grep-ref hazard I propagated for a session and the node_modules canary I quoted for weeks: BOILERPLATE IS THE LEAST-AUDITED TEXT I PRODUCE, because it is copied rather than composed. Re-test one boilerplate claim per retrospective.

ALSO CORRECTED IN THE SAME REPORT: my `.beads` hygiene check told workers to run `git diff --numstat origin/main..HEAD`. That is TWO-DOT, so it shows my own checkpoint commits as though they were the worker`s, and three workers in a row reported a false `.beads` positive. Use the MERGE BASE (or `sh scripts/check-beads-pr-boundary.sh origin/main`, remembering it exits 0 with no base ref so the ref must always be passed).

EDITING A CRLF-STORED FILE UNDER core.autocrlf=true SILENTLY NORMALISES THE WHOLE FILE TO LF — a multi-thousand-line whitespace diff that reads as real content. Found 2026-07-24 by the rf2-drpa3.103 worker, which caught it before committing.

THE CASE: spec/011-SSR.md is stored on main with CRLF. A normal edit produced a ~4,200-line diff on a HOT-ZONE file for a change that should have been +45 lines. Nothing warned; the diff simply looked enormous.

THE CURE the worker used: rebuild the file BYTE-EXACTLY from its base blob plus the intended change, then re-add with `git -c core.autocrlf=false add <file>`. Committed diff came out at +45 insertions and nothing else.

THE CHECK, and it is cheap: after ANY edit to a tracked file, run `git diff --numstat` and confirm the line counts match what you intended. A diff far larger than your change is a line-ending normalisation, not your edit.

⚠️ THIS COMPOUNDS WITH THE HOT-ZONE RULE. spec/ files are sequential-never-parallel precisely because they collide; a whole-file normalisation guarantees a conflict with every other branch touching that file, and buries the real change so a reviewer cannot see it. On a hot-zone file the damage is not cosmetic.

RELATED, ALREADY RECORDED: `sed -i` on a tracked file does the same thing for the same reason on this Windows checkout — which is why briefs forbid it and require the Edit tool. This is the SAME hazard reached through an ordinary edit rather than through sed, so the sed ban alone does not cover it. Put the numstat check in briefs that touch spec/ files, not just the sed ban.

MAYOR NOTE: my briefs already say "no sed -i" and "check git diff --numstat shows only the lines you intended" — the second half turned out to be the load-bearing one, and I had been treating it as a footnote to the first.

DELETING A DECORATIVE ROW LEAVES THE CLAIM UNWITNESSED — the discriminating-row rule has a second half (2026-08-11, AUDIT #7835 on rf2-wjag).

WHAT I HAD BEEN TEACHING: for every negative row, ask what single narrowing of the implementation would let it pass while the property is broken. If such a narrowing exists, the row is decorative. That is right, and it has caught real defects all session.

WHAT I PRAISED, AND WHY IT WAS ONLY HALF RIGHT: a worker wrote a cold-probe row, found its mutation red nothing, DELETED the row and recorded the finding in the namespace docstring. Its words: "Claim real, witness not." I called that the rule applied by a worker to its own work, unprompted — and it was, as far as it went.

THE AUDIT COMPLETED IT: the row was decorative AS WRITTEN because the frame it used (a make-frame frame) had no stale projection to flush. The CLAIM was real and became UNWITNESSED by the deletion. The only thing still exercising it was a prototype-tree row — exercising the prototype runtime, not the package implementation, which is exactly the dependence the bead existed to end.

THE COMPLETED RULE: "this row cannot fail" is a finding about THE ROW'S CONDITIONS, not about whether the claim deserves a witness. The three outcomes, in order of preference:
  1. REWRITE the row with the conditions that make the mechanism load-bearing (here: an image-loaded frame rather than a fresh one). This is almost always the answer.
  2. DELETE it only if the claim is already covered elsewhere IN THE SAME ARTEFACT — and name the coverer. Coverage in a donor, prototype or sibling tree does not count when the bead's purpose is to stop relying on that tree.
  3. If the claim genuinely cannot be witnessed here, say so and say WHY, in the artefact — as the erasure worker did for defview coordinates, where a filename sentinel would be red on a correct build.

MAYOR APPLICATION: when a worker reports deleting a row, ask what still witnesses the claim. The report will usually not volunteer it, because the deletion feels like the finding — and it is a finding, just not a complete one.

WHAT I DID. rf2-d6ai8 flipped open three times with no comment attached. I applied the churn discriminator, verified its DELIVERABLE at source each time — requirements-mine.md carried the re-taken pass-1 entry, PR #8178 merged — and re-closed it. On the third pass I called it "churn (third status-only flip)".

WHAT I MISSED. The bead's NOTES carried an explicit unmet obligation added after the deliverable landed: "Keep this exact requirements-mine owner open until those false premises are corrected there." rf2-gvysu had also been closed as a duplicate OF d6ai8. So both owners were closed while all three false rows were still on main. The work was stranded, and it took a worker reading both beads to find it.

I substituted a different and easier check — does the thing the bead was filed to produce exist on main? Both are necessary. A bead can have its original deliverable landed AND carry a later obligation that keeps it open, and the second is invisible to a source check on the first.

THE TELL I SHOULD HAVE NOTICED: a bead that reopens THREE TIMES is not behaving like churn. Churn is a flag flipping; three flips with a duplicate closed alongside it is a signal that something is actively holding the bead open. The repetition itself was evidence and I read it as noise.

Dependency-chain gating gotcha: workers close their bead on PR CREATION (not merge), so a 'bd dep add A B' where B closes-at-PR-creation makes 'bd ready' surface A as soon as B's PR is OPENED — BEFORE B's code is on main. If A and B touch the same files (surface-conflict sequencing), dispatching A off origin/main then conflicts when B merges. FIX: for surface-conflict gates, do NOT rely on the bd dep / bd ready alone — verify the BLOCKER PR is actually MERGED (gh pr view <#> state==MERGED) before claiming+worktreeing the dependent, and create its worktree off the POST-merge origin/main. WORKTREES ACCUMULATE BECAUSE THEY ARE DIRTY, NOT BECAUSE NOBODY TRIED TO REAP THEM (2026-08-18).

A hygiene pass reaped 9 of 11 leftover worktrees whose PRs had MERGED. The two refusals were both REMOVE_REFUSED_DIRTY - git will not remove a worktree holding modified or untracked files, and the removal script surfaces each offending path prefixed [KEEP] with the message that RETRYING WILL NEVER CLEAR THIS. That is the whole mechanism behind a pile of stale worktrees: every pass reaps the clean ones and leaves the dirty ones, so the dirty ones are all that is left.

DO NOT REACH FOR --force. The script says --force DELETES the [KEEP] paths, and its own text distinguishes them from build output: an uncommitted edit, a note, a draft. On this pass one refusing worktree held a modified deps.edn plus an untracked test and an untracked script; another held a MODIFIED .github/workflows/test.yml (hot zone), a modified .claude/commands file, and a DELETED studio record.

THE CHEAP DISCRIMINATOR BEFORE DECIDING ANYTHING: check whether the [KEEP] paths already exist at origin/main. For the first worktree both untracked files were PRESENT on main - the branch's PR had merged and the worktree was simply sitting on a pre-merge commit, so its 'untracked' files were a stale local copy of landed work, at risk of nothing. That check is two git cat-file calls and it converts an alarming refusal into a nothing.

STILL LEAVE THEM. Even when the content is provably safe, force-deleting buys one worktree and risks a draft nobody has read. Leaving two dirty worktreees costs disk and a line in git worktree list.

A MERGED PR IS STRONGER EVIDENCE THAN A COMPLETION REPORT, and it is what makes an old worktree reapable at all. The hygiene rule says reap only on the agent's own completion report - correct for a worker dispatched THIS session, where a report is obtainable. For a leftover from a prior session no report exists and never will, so the rule as literally written would freeze them forever. A verifiably MERGED PR says the work is on main, which is what the report was evidence FOR. Match on exact head-ref, and re-derive the ahead-count in the same command as the delete.

DISPATCH BRIEF FIX (mayor, 2026-07-25): three workers in one session ended their turn with work committed-but-unpushed and NO PR, each waiting for a long local gate (scripts/test-fast-pr.sh spine) to finish first. The instruction 'do not end your turn with uncommitted work' is NOT sufficient — workers read it as satisfied by a local commit. Every editing brief must instead say, in this order and with the reasons: (1) PUSH as you go, not at the end, because pushed commits are the only durable worker state and a worker that dies mid-run takes local commits with it; (2) OPEN THE PR as soon as commits exist, because a PR is how work becomes visible to the merge gate and is NOT a claim of green — state any still-running gate in the '## Quality gates' section as reliance-on-CI, which is acceptable, whereas a silent omission is not; (3) the merge decision is CI's, not the worker's local run, so if a gate later reds it is a fix-worker on the existing branch and needed no waiting. Recovery when it happens: SendMessage-resume the SAME worker (it holds the branch and worktree; never dispatch a second worker onto one branch). Pair this with the two log hygiene rules workers also miss: capture gate output to a WORKTREE-LOCAL path (the machine temp dir is shared, so two concurrent workers writing one log path read each other's green), and echo the exit code explicitly (piping a gate into tail/grep returns the PIPE's status, not the runner's, so a failed run reads as '0 failures').

A DISPATCH DIRECTIVE THAT LIVES ONLY IN NOTES DOES NOT STOP DISPATCHES — put it at the TOP of the DESCRIPTION (2026-08-21, rf2-63t1i).

THE MECHANISM, and it is structural rather than careless. A mayor writing a brief reads the bead to find out what the work IS, and the work is described in the DESCRIPTION. That field is the OLDEST text on a bead by construction — corrections accrete into NOTES and comments below it. So the field a brief is naturally drawn from is precisely the field least likely to carry the current disposition. A head-truncated show makes it worse by returning the description and stopping before NOTES, but the trap survives reading the whole bead, because the description is what answers the question the mayor is actually asking.

A rule that has failed three times against the same bead is not enforced by restating it.

The banner is in the field the brief is drawn from, so it cannot be missed by the reading pattern that causes the failure. It recovered on its own and the mayor's real node_modules was verified intact at 101 throughout, so nothing was damaged — but I cost a live worker a diagnostic detour for no reason.

THE MISTAKE IS THE TRIGGER, NOT THE SCRIPT. A merged PR means the WORK landed; it does NOT mean the AGENT finished. Agents legitimately continue after opening a PR — updating the PR body, re-running a gate, hardening a mutation proof, answering a resume message. The safe trigger is the agent's own completion notification, or an explicit confirmation from it that it is done with the tree.

THE RULE: reap a worker worktree only when BOTH are true — (1) its PR is merged, AND (2) its agent has reported done (or has been confirmed dead). If a reap fails on a file lock, that is often a SIGNAL the tree is still in use; do not retry in a loop, and check whether the agent is alive before trying again.

RELATED, ALREADY KNOWN AND STILL TRUE: the guard script is correct to disarm the link before removing (that is what stops git worktree remove following it into the mayor's real node_modules), and it correctly refuses rather than forcing when the removal cannot complete. The failure mode here is entirely in WHEN I invoked it.

AN INTERRUPTED DOLT GENERATIONAL GC CAN ROLL THE BEADS TRACKER BACK MID-SESSION, AND IT LOOKS EXACTLY LIKE CORRUPTION (2026-08-03).

SYMPTOM SEQUENCE, in one 10-minute window: 'bd export' failed with 'error opening table file: table file not found: .dolt/noms/<hash>'. Then EVERY bd command — ready, list, show — exited 1. THE MISSING TABLE NAME DIFFERED BETWEEN CONSECUTIVE CALLS (18uc3mpc..., then 5l677oov...), noms/oldgen existed but was EMPTY, and the noms/ file count went 7 -> 91 across a couple of minutes. That is a generational GC rewriting table files, not disk damage.

IT RECOVERS ON ITS OWN. Roughly two minutes later bd returned exit 0 with no intervention. DO NOT rebuild the database from JSONL while this is happening — 'bd export' failing is NOT proof of data loss, and a rebuild from a checkpoint would discard everything since it.

THE REAL DAMAGE IS A PARTIAL ROLLBACK, AND IT IS SILENT. After recovery the tracker had time-travelled: a bead closed ~20 minutes earlier was back to IN_PROGRESS with its ORIGINAL 'Updated' date, and 5 note-appends were gone. But it was PARTIAL — a second close from the same pass SURVIVED. So you cannot assume all-or-nothing; verify each write individually with 'bd show'.

WHAT SAVED IT: the worker that made the writes still had them in its transcript. When bd broke I immediately messaged it to STOP all bd use and report every close/update verbatim WITH its verification evidence, then re-applied the 7 writes by hand and checkpointed at once. WITHOUT THAT REPLY THE WORK WAS UNRECOVERABLE — the JSONL checkpoint predated the writes.

RULES: (1) a tracker-mutating worker's report is a durable artefact — make its brief require verbatim reasons + evidence, not a summary; (2) checkpoint IMMEDIATELY after re-applying, do not batch; (3) row counts move under you because an automated merged-PR-audit process also commits .beads — 'HEAD had N' changing between your own checkpoints is NOT necessarily corruption; (4) beads-checkpoint.sh's shrinkage guard is the right instrument to ask 'did I lose bulk data?' — a clean round-trip at the same row count means the answer is no.

WHEN COLLAPSING DUPLICATE BEADS, THE SURVIVOR IS THE EARLIER OWNER WITH MORE CONTENT — not the one with the sharper framing (2026-08-15 16:54 AUSEST).

MEASURED ON MYSELF. rf2-15bqc and rf2-4ncab were the same finding: same four -h-fn recovery keywords, same emitters (impl/intent.cljs, impl/controlled.cljs), same Spec 009 lines. At 15:47 I closed 15bqc AS A DUPLICATE OF 4ncab. An audit then closed 4ncab AS A DUPLICATE OF 15bqc — the opposite direction.

THE AUDIT WAS RIGHT AND I LEFT IT STANDING. My reason was that 4ncab 'carries the sharper framing' — it states the CONSTRAINT ('the ids move with their emitters, or not at all') rather than only the symptom. The audit's reasons were stronger:
  - 15bqc is the EARLIER exact owner
  - it already carried the authoritative complaints.md ruling, the full emitter list, the one-pass repair AND the troubleshooting-doc tail
So it had both provenance and more content. Framing is cheap to copy forward; accumulated content and history are not.

THE RULE: prefer the earlier owner, and prefer the bead carrying more verified content. If the loser has a better framing sentence, COPY THE SENTENCE ONTO THE SURVIVOR — that costs one note. Do not close the richer bead to keep the better-worded one.

WHY NO DAMAGE WAS DONE, and this is the part that made it safe: BOTH closes carried the loser's unique evidence forward. Mine moved 15bqc's two extra surfaces (troubleshooting.md, hicasso.cljc) onto 4ncab; the audit's moved 4ncab's bench-mirror evidence onto 15bqc. Net result is one bead holding everything. THE CARRY-FORWARD IS WHAT MAKES A COLLAPSE REVERSIBLE — a close that merely says 'duplicate of X' is not.

DO NOT RE-CLOSE THE SURVIVOR. The method's own rule applies directly: the instinct to re-close a 'reverted' bead destroys a real finding and looks like tidiness. Read the notes first. Here the reopen was an audit converging on the better survivor, and the correct action was to leave it alone and record why.

CONTEXT ON WHY DUPLICATES ARISE AT ALL HERE: these two were filed HOURS APART by DIFFERENT workers approaching the same residue from opposite directions, neither visible to the other because both were mid-flight. That is rf2-a30v2's blind window one level up.

DUPLICATE deftest — CLJS WARNS, THE JVM IS SILENT. rf2-9e4lf (#6349, 2026-07-18) verified this with a standalone probe rather than assuming: a Clojure namespace defining the same deftest twice, with the FIRST body deliberately failing, reports 'Ran 1 tests... 0 failures' and emits ZERO diagnostic output. Clojure's 'already refers to' warning only fires ACROSS namespaces, so there is no JVM equivalent of shadow-cljs's :redef-in-file. CONSEQUENCE: a duplicate deftest in a .cljs/.cljc file is detectable (shadow-cljs warns on every build — rf2-qo5xk's went unread for months); the same defect in a .clj file is COMPLETELY INVISIBLE. Only the test count reveals it. PROOF TECHNIQUE (use this, not a green suite): to show a resurrected test body actually executes, temporarily INVERT one of its assertions and confirm the suite reds AT THE NEW SYMBOL NAME — that is impossible while the body is being replaced. Then revert and gate on the reverted tree. A green suite plus a +1 count is weaker: the count can rise for unrelated reasons and green proves only that nothing failed. Both instances found so far (qo5xk, 9e4lf) were genuinely DISTINCT tests collapsed onto one symbol by different causes — a rename sweep and a copy-pasted parallel test block — so archaeology first, never assume the cause from a sibling case.

WHEN DUPLICATION KEEPS RECURRING, THE DEFECT IS DISCOVERY — not the duplication (2026-08-14, rf2-040s1 worker).

THE SITUATION. A bead said two scripts independently parse the same build-summary line and asked whether to unify them. THE WORKER FOUND THREE. The third had been doing it for eleven days BEFORE the bead was filed, reached the identical verdict, and recorded the SAME reason for not reusing the others. So the bead's own trigger — 'unify when a third lane wants the line' — HAD ALREADY FIRED, unnoticed by its author.

IT REFUSED THE UNIFICATION, ON A REASON NEITHER AUTHOR HAD RECORDED: one gate's pattern is a FILTER, not merely an id capture — it deliberately FAILS on any summary whose id was not requested. An id-agnostic shared pattern would hand that gate every id the compiler prints and reopen a settled question across 54 builds. And what actually differs between the three is the SELECTION POLICY, not the regex: reconcile a requested set / every row must read zero / take the last row so a dependency's summary is not mistaken for the lane's. A shared module would remove three regexes and leave three policies.

IT ALSO ESTABLISHED THE DUPLICATION CANNOT FAIL QUIETLY: all three refuse an unreadable summary, so a compiler reformat yields three RED gates rather than a silent pass. Duplication that fails loudly is far cheaper than an abstraction that hides a policy.

THE REAL FIX WAS DISCOVERY. Two authors solved one problem against one wall and neither found the other. So the roster of readers is now stated IN ALL THREE FILES, with the full argument in one and short pointers in the others — one owner for the prose, so it cannot drift.

AND IT REPLACED THE COUNT WITH A POLICY TEST. The bead said 'unify when a third wants it'; three had arrived and the count was still wrong, so the count was never checkable. The new rule: a lane whose selection policy one of the three already implements CALLS that reader's export; a lane with a genuinely new policy writes its own and adds itself to the roster.

GENERALISE: before proposing to unify duplicates, ask what they share and what they DIFFER on. If the difference is policy rather than mechanism, unification hides the policy. And if the same duplication keeps appearing, the thing to fix is how the next author FINDS the existing one.

EIGHTH FALSE-GREEN CLASS: A CANNED STUB IS DOCUMENTATION WITH A TEST'S AUTHORITY (2026-07-25, found by the F6c worker against its own shipped work).

WHAT HAPPENED: in PR #6978 it wrote a canned MCP response envelope containing :classification :callback. THERE IS NO SUCH MEMBER — the vocabulary is closed at seven (:vector :options :ui-event :handler :fn :dynamic :spread). It had read the tool docstring's prose 'on any other classification it is a callback' as naming a VALUE, when it names the COMPLEMENT of :vector/:options. So a fixture can depict output the producer cannot emit, and the tests that read it will pass forever — while the stub sits in the one place an agent reads to learn the shape. Its own words: 'a canned stub is documentation with a test's authority.'

HOW THIS DIFFERS FROM THE OTHER SEVEN: (1)-(6) are misreading a verdict; (7) is a stale compile cache computing a verdict from stale input; (8) is a verdict computed correctly over INVENTED INPUT. No exit-code discipline catches it, and no cache-clearing catches it either.

HOW TO CATCH IT: when a diff adds or edits a canned envelope, fixture, sample response or documented example payload, check every VALUE in it against the producing source's vocabulary — not against the consumer's prose, and not against a docstring sentence. Closed vocabularies are the specific hazard: if a keyword is drawn from a fixed set, find the set. And check the combination, not just the members: two individually-valid values can name a state the producer cannot reach.

DISPATCH IMPLICATION: brief workers touching MCP descriptors, tool catalogues, canned envelopes or documented payloads to verify values against the producing source. The Pair tool catalogue is exactly this shape — tool-descriptors.edn, descriptors_data.cljs, registry.cljs, 003-Tool-Catalogue.md and the mcp-conformance end-to-end must all move together, and a fabricated value in any of them is invisible to all of them.

Event-handling pipeline atomicity (Mike CONFIRMED 2026-05-24). Architecture: interceptors (incl. the path std-interceptor) mutate the :db/:fx EFFECTS in interceptor context; app-db gets a SINGLE deferred install only after the ENTIRE chain (all :after interceptors + the flow transform) is done. Flows run at the OUTERMOST :after (framework-prepended :rf/flows, fires last) because flows read full-app-db :inputs and path's :after reshapes :db. CONTRACT: ANY throw BEFORE install (cofx, handler, interceptor :after, flow) => the deferred install simply does NOT happen => app-db UNCHANGED, NO :rf.event/db-changed, NO :fx. No partial commit (a flow throw must NOT commit prior flows' writes). The :db install is the atomic commit boundary. The ONLY post-commit stage is :fx: an fx throw surfaces an error but does NOT wind back app-db (fx side-effects http/nav/dispatch may already have fired and are irreversible). Uniform: flow-throw behaves like every other pre-install throw.

A NON-CODE EXCLUSION THAT STOPS AT COMMENTS LEAVES STRING BODIES SEARCHABLE — AND THE FIX IS TWO PROJECTIONS, NOT ONE (2026-08-06, rf2-t4j7c, PR #7620).

THE DEFECT: a gate blanked COMMENTS so prose could not stand in for a call. It deliberately KEPT string literals, and it had to — the scans own targets include the strings release, --config-merge and the require path. So the same `resetLaneBuildCache(IMPL, BUILD)` text SITTING IN A LOG LINE stood in for the call exactly as comment text had. Reproduced on unmodified main: a rider with no executable reset, carrying that text in a const string and repeated in a template, returned null from requires, clearsFirst, noLiteralId AND sameBuildId — 40 tests, 40 pass, exit 0.

THE FIX SHAPE, and it generalises: ONE SOURCE, TWO BLANKED VIEWS, both the ORIGINAL LENGTH so offset comparisons still hold across them. `code` (comments blanked, strings kept) feeds discovery, the require check and the spawn-side reads that legitimately need string text. `exec` (comments AND string bodies blanked) feeds the clear call and its build-id argument, which must be executable to count. The question is never "what is not code" in general — it is WHAT MUST THIS PARTICULAR SCAN NOT SEE, and different scans in one gate can have different answers.

THE REVERSE MUTATION IS WHAT PROVED BOTH HALVES LOAD-BEARING, and it is the better half of the proof: pointing sameBuildId back at `code` makes it FALSELY report a correctly-wired probe carrying a decoy log line as "clears DECOY but releases BUILD". So the split does not only close a false GREEN, it prevents a false RED. A projection change that only ever tightens is suspicious; check whether the looser view was also inventing findings.

AND IT WROTE THE UNCOVERED EDGE INTO THE HEADER rather than leaving it for the next audit: spawn-side reads must still see string text, so that half is deliberately unprotected. It also re-argued the failure-direction claim for the SECOND view rather than assuming it carried over, and bounded it honestly as "a direction, not a proof". When you add a projection, the safety argument does not inherit — restate it per view.

THIS IS THE THIRD ROUND ON THIS ONE GATE (comment text, then regex-in-substitution, now string bodies), each found by an audit of the previous fix. The pattern is not incompetence: each repair narrowed the aperture and revealed the next-widest way a token could masquerade as a call. Expect a masking gate to take several rounds, and expect each rounds audit to find the shape the last one made visible.

FAN-OUTS DEFEAT PRE-LOOP GUARDS — a check taken BEFORE a loop does not fence the loops later iterations. Found by rf2-sdeae (P1, #6361, 2026-07-18). rf2-qfrh4 had fenced every epoch-restore SEAM on the exact-ownership token, but three of those seams are fan-outs: the guard ran once, then the loop kept invoking callbacks that could seat a successor mid-flight. Three interleavings were constructed on the same thread, inside the callback, between the read and the write. Sharpest: the quiesce chain first hook (:machines/on-frame-restored!) destroys frame A and seats B; A second hook (:http/abort-in-flight-for-frame!) then aborts B in-flight requests — a dead frames tail mutating a live successor. RULE: when auditing an ownership or liveness guard, ask whether the guarded region contains ITERATION or CALLBACK RE-ENTRY. If it does, the guard must travel INTO the region (widen the token through the loop) rather than gate its entry. FIX SHAPE that worked: an ORDER fix, not a new gate — detach-slots! removes slots in one swap-vals!, THEN aborts the detached values, so no host side effect runs inside the retriable swap. The sibling timers/release-frame! already did this; the work-ledger table was the odd one out, so the fix converged on established local discipline instead of inventing a mechanism. BONUS SIGNAL WORTH COPYING: the adversarial re-entrancy case exposed unbounded amplification — a callback re-entering release-frame! re-read the not-yet-dropped slot and re-aborted it 1101 times in the red run. If a re-entrancy test produces a COUNT rather than a boolean, the count is the evidence. Related: rf2-uhouu (#6339) collapsed two reads into one atomic decision; this is the same discipline in the opposite direction — the decision existed and had to travel.

-> what the worker has COMMITTED git status --porcelain (inside the worktree) -> what it has NOT yet committed A worker mid-task flips between them: uncommitted early, committed at milestones, and CLEAN-BUT-COMMITTED for the whole stretch between a commit and its PR. That last state is invisible to porcelain and is exactly where mount-7mtcf sat. THE RULE IS THEREFORE: RUN BOTH, ALWAYS, AND UNION THE RESULTS. Adding a third check (PR state) separates a live holder from a rebase-merged ghost, but it does not replace either of the first two. WHY IT COSTS: an omitted holder is a stale-NARROW fence, which mayor-dispatch.md itself names as the expensive direction — two workers on one file merge-conflict and can silently revert each other. Here it cost half a cluster instead, only because the worker re-derived rather than trusting me. GENERAL FORM, since this is the second time today I have done this shape: WHEN A NEW CHECK IS ADDED BECAUSE THE OLD ONE FAILED, THE OLD ONE IS STILL REQUIRED. The new check exists because the old one was insufficient, not because it was wrong. Same error as clause 5's job-key count, where zero turned out to be necessary and not sufficient.

WHAT MY BRIEFS SAY: "Your surface is X. You are fenced out of spec/*, .github/workflows/*, package.json, shadow-cljs.edn. Worker A holds Y, worker B holds Z." That is a NAMED SURFACE plus a LIST OF FORBIDDEN PATHS. A file that is in neither is UNDEFINED, and the worker has to guess.

THE TWO FAILURES THE ENUMERATION ALLOWS: a worker crosses silently into a contended file (a real collision nobody sees until the merge), or a worker DOESN'T make a correct small change because it was not obviously permitted.

I already write the stop-and-report form for ANTICIPATED crossings (a new build id, an npm script, a new :rf.error/* id); this generalises it to the unanticipated ones, which are the only ones that surprise me.

MAYOR-SIDE COROLLARY: when a diff shows a file outside the brief's surface, READ THE FILE LIST OF EVERY OTHER LIVE WORKER BEFORE REACTING. Directory-level overlap is not collision. I check this now; I nearly did not.

THE HEAD==origin/main VERIFICATION CAN READ A STALE origin/main FOR SEVERAL COMMANDS RUNNING, AND IT LOOKS EXACTLY LIKE DIVERGENCE (2026-08-16 01:44).

WHAT I SAW. The merge sweep's closing check printed 'local==origin: NO' with local=e56fc00ccb and origin/main=401bd15991. I then ran, in order: rev-parse both refs (same mismatch), 'git fetch origin main -q', rev-parse both again (SAME mismatch), 'git pull --ff-only origin main' which printed 'Already up to date' and exited 0, and rev-parse a third time (STILL the same mismatch). Three consecutive reads agreed that the refs differed.

THEY DID NOT DIFFER. A fourth check resolved it: git rev-parse HEAD and git rev-parse origin/main both returned e56fc00ccb75a3f4f8098a5b62a515a6d1f9832d, merge-base --is-ancestor answered YES in BOTH directions, and rev-list --count was 0 both ways. The refs were identical the whole time and the SHORT read was showing a stale remote-tracking ref.

THE MECHANISM: 'git fetch origin main' and 'git pull origin main' NAME A BRANCH, so git writes FETCH_HEAD and does not necessarily update refs/remotes/origin/main. The pull can therefore be genuinely up to date while the tracking ref a later rev-parse reads still holds the previous tick's value. CLAUDE.md's rule to NAME THE REMOTE AND BRANCH on the pull is right for the pull itself — it stops the bare form no-opping against a racing audit push — but it is exactly what leaves the tracking ref behind for the verification that follows.

WHY IT MATTERS: the mayor's post-merge verification IS 'git rev-parse HEAD must equal git rev-parse origin/main'. If that comparison can read a stale ref for several commands in a row, a clean tree reports as divergence, and the remedies for real divergence — pull --rebase, force-with-lease, resetting — are all destructive against a tree that was never wrong.

WHAT SAVED IT is already written in CLAUDE.md and I nearly did not apply it: 'one mismatch is not yet evidence either ... read both refs again before believing it.' I read them a fourth time with the FULL SHAs and ancestry rather than the short form, and the phantom vanished. Note the rule says read AGAIN, not read TWICE — here it took four.

THE RELIABLE CHECK, and use this rather than repeating reads: 'git merge-base --is-ancestor HEAD origin/main' AND the reverse, or 'git rev-list --count' both ways. Ancestry resolves the objects rather than trusting a possibly-stale ref label, and it answers the question the mayor actually has — is the checkout the same tree as the remote — instead of the question the short SHAs answer, which is whether two ref labels happen to print the same characters right now.

TO FORCE THE TRACKING REF FORWARD when you do want it current: 'git fetch origin' with NO branch name, or an explicit refspec ('git fetch origin refs/heads/main:refs/remotes/origin/main'), which is the form already used in this session for worker branches and which does update the ref.

FLAKE PROOF — a run count is not always the right evidence; sometimes a MARGIN is. I briefed rf2-ybqse to prove stability with 20+ consecutive runs. Its worker (2026-07-18) correctly pushed back: focused runs could not exercise that flake at all (the bug lived in the gap between namespace LOAD and render, which a focused run collapses), and full-suite runs cost ~4 min each. It ran 20 focused + 3 full and supplied the better proof — the measured margin between the fixture's :stale-at and the render-time clock: +30461ms pre-fix (29.5s of a 60s horizon already burned), -13700ms when deliberately shrunk to falsify (reproducing the reported failure string verbatim), +60000ms post-fix. At a constant 60000ms the failure is UNREACHABLE rather than merely unobserved. RULE FOR BRIEFS: ask for proof the failure is unreachable, and let the worker choose the instrument. Repeated green runs prove absence-of-observation; a margin, an invariant, or a falsification run can prove absence-of-possibility. Demanding N runs can also mislead — N greens on a test that structurally cannot fail in that mode is a false-green about a false-green. ALSO: this class of flake (wall-clock captured in a top-level def, compared against a render-time clock) is invisible in isolation and only appears when a bundle loads all namespaces before executing any.

FREEHAND API-MANIFEST IS A SERIAL LANE for public-verb beads — the biggest merge-friction in the Freehand build wave (2026-07-23). re-frame.freehand is a FULLY-ROWED manifest surface: adding ANY public verb requires FIVE co-edited files in ONE PR — implementation/freehand/src/re_frame/freehand.cljc (facade block), spec/api-manifest.edn (REGENERATE, never hand-edit), spec/api-manifest-metadata.edn (classification row), spec/API.md (roster row + remove the declared-vacancy prose), docs/api/re-frame.freehand.md (member heading + remove vacancy prose). FOUR gates enforce it: the api-manifest gen --check entry point, api-md-check, doc-api-check, and the CLJS manifest probe under npm run test:cljs.

THE TRAP THAT COST THREE REBASES (presence PR 6713, measured — the most important part): git rebase AUTO-MERGES the generated spec/api-manifest.edn with NO conflict markers, merging the var ROWS correctly while leaving a STALE :var-count HEADER (observed 517 against a set of 519). The file looks cleanly merged and is SELF-INCONSISTENT. The drift gate then reds with "var set identical; :meta or formatting differs — regenerate", which READS LIKE a formatting or toolchain problem and sends you hunting the wrong cause. IT IS NOT A TOOLCHAIN TRAP. Cure: run the plain generator (no --check flag) to overwrite byte-exact, then --check must exit 0 AND git diff spec/api-manifest.edn must be EMPTY after that fresh run — the empty diff is the proof the committed file equals the generator output.

RULE: for a GENERATED file, a clean auto-merge is NOT evidence of correctness. Treat every rebase touching api-manifest.edn as resolve-by-REGENERATE whether or not git reported a conflict.

OTHER OPERATIONAL FACTS: (a) verb-adders are a SERIAL LANE — merge one, rebase the next onto it, and HOLD the lane still for the worker you are waiting on or it rebases forever against a moving main. (b) doc-api-check requires a member heading in docs/api for every new advanced or front-porch var. (c) the CLJS manifest probe CACHES the metadata namespace across a metadata-only edit — clear .shadow-cljs to re-verify locally. (d) INTERNAL-only beads (manifests/elision, the checker, the test surface, cell/shell correctness fixes) do NOT touch this surface and parallelize freely — dispatch those alongside verb work to keep saturation without lane contention.

MAYOR PLAYBOOK: brief every verb-adding bead with "add your metadata row, REGENERATE the manifest, add the API.md row and the docs/api member IN THE SAME PR or the gate reds", treat it as a serial-lane occupant, and hold the lane still while it rebases. This tax is real ceremony, flagged to Mike as a candidate is-this-over-engineering review — do NOT weaken the gates unilaterally, it is his call.

RESOLVED 2026-07-23 by PR #6700 — the fixture-cache warning is NO LONGER needed in Freehand worker briefs. Freehand conformance fixtures are now a shadow-cljs build dependency, so a fixture-only edit invalidates the cache and the compiled test sees the new expectations.

WHAT THE BUG WAS, kept because the shape recurs: re-frame.freehand.conformance/fixture inlined its .edn at MACRO-EXPANSION time, and shadow-cljs had no dependency edge from a test namespace to the fixture it inlined. A fixture-only edit therefore did not invalidate the build cache, and the compiled test kept asserting the PREVIOUS expectations. A green CLJS or browser conformance run after a fixture change was worthless. The JVM side was never affected.

MEASURED TWICE, INDEPENDENTLY, by two workers with no stake in each other's finding — which is why it was believed rather than argued about. The route-link slice mutated a fixture and got 484 tests / 2746 assertions / 0 failures, green on a fixture that MUST fail; its probe passed TWICE before it cleared the cache. The CI-classifier slice separately flipped FH-CALL-001 :predicates :view? true->false and saw a warm cache recompile 1 file and report 0 failures, versus 124 files and 1 failure after clearing.

⚠️ THE GENERAL LESSON, WHICH OUTLIVES THIS FIX AND IS WHY THIS MEMORY SURVIVES: a table-driven gate whose expectations are INLINED AT COMPILE TIME can silently decouple from its data. Whenever test expectations live in a separate file that a macro reads, ASK WHETHER THE BUILD SYSTEM KNOWS ABOUT THAT EDGE — and prove it the only way that counts: mutate the data WITHOUT clearing any cache and require RED. A fix verified only after a cache clear proves nothing, because that is the broken state's own behaviour.

TWO SEPARATE HOLES EXISTED ON THIS PATH; both are now closed and neither alone sufficed. rf2-drpa3.66 (#6699) made the CI jobs RUN on a fixture change — the classifier had no route for spec/conformance/freehand/fixtures/** so both newly-required host jobs skipped. rf2-drpa3.65 (#6700) made the compiled test SEE the change. Scheduling and compilation are independent failure modes; check both when a data-driven gate looks green.

Fresh worker worktrees revert bead claims: a new worktree checks out a stale-content/new-mtime .beads/issues.jsonl, and the FIRST bd invocation inside it re-imports that stale JSONL into the shared dolt DB, clobbering any claims/closes made between 'git worktree add' and the worker's first bd call. THE CHECK: when an instruction and a repository record disagree, DATE BOTH AND FIND THEIR STORES. `bd memories <topic>` returns the live ones with dates; the frozen store is the one CLAUDE.md names as retired. Controlled same-tree comparison (swap the file to main version and back): 929 TESTS both ways, but full-suite ASSERTION totals drifted run-to-run on an IDENTICAL tree — 16136 / 16141 / 16143 observed in implementation/ui — because generative suites vary their assertion counts per run. I had been quoting assertion baselines to workers (~16119, ~16132, ~16149, ~16154) as if they were stable, which invites two failures: a worker treats normal drift as a regression it caused and hunts a phantom, or treats a real small regression as drift. THE PASTE-IT-WHOLE RULE ASSUMES THE SCARCE RESOURCE IS WORKER SLOTS. LATE IN A LONG SESSION IT IS THE MAYOR'S REMAINING CONTEXT (measured 2026-08-13, third instance).

mayor-dispatch.md line 23 says paste the gate-mechanics block whole. My earlier fix for compressing it was 'dispatch fewer workers at once' - the block costs 156 lines plus 43 for the boundary block, so three parallel briefs cost over 550 lines of boilerplate.

I THEN DISPATCHED EXACTLY ONE WORKER AND STILL COMPRESSED. The measurement-window brief dropped the wedge paragraph, the read-the-clock paragraph, the artefact-naming rationale, and the hash-proves-source-not-runtime caution. Worker count was one. The remedy I had recorded did not apply.

THE ACTUAL CONSTRAINT IS THE MAYOR'S CONTEXT BUDGET, and it tightens monotonically across a session while the block stays the same size. Early ticks can afford the whole block; late ticks cannot afford it at all. So the compression is not a discipline failure that willpower fixes - it is a resource curve, and it will recur in every long session at roughly the same point.

TWO THINGS FOLLOW.

1. WHAT I DROPPED WAS NOT RANDOM, AND THAT IS THE ONE MITIGATION AVAILABLE. Each time, the load-bearing ordering survived - the arithmetic, 'detaching is CORRECT', 'do not apologise'. What went were mechanism paragraphs. If a brief must be trimmed, trim toward what the WORKER'S SITUATION cannot reach: a solo measurement window genuinely cannot hit the two-workers-wedge case, so dropping that paragraph there costs less than dropping it from a brief sent while three workers run. Say in the brief that it was trimmed and why.

2. THIS IS WORTH TELLING THE OPERATOR, because it bounds how long a mayor session runs at full fidelity. It is not a bug in the rule; the rule is right about what a worker needs. It is a limit on the mayor, and the honest response is to name it rather than to keep promising the whole block and delivering most of it.

DO NOT 'FIX' THIS BY PROPOSING READ-BY-REFERENCE. mayor-dispatch.md already ruled that question and gave its reason: a worker told to read a file may not, and the block's ordering is what a summary destroys.

GATE EXIT-CODE TRAP, SECOND VARIANT (2026-07-25, found by the rf2-kqxe6.20 worker): a BACKGROUNDED or compound gate invocation can report 'exit code 0' while its log says FAIL. The worker's first scripts/test-fast-pr.sh run was reported exit 0 while the log read 'FAIL CLJS node integration' — the 0 belonged to a TRAILING ECHO in the compound command, not to the runner. This is distinct from the known pipe variant (piping a gate through tail/grep returns the PIPE's status). So the rule needs both halves in briefs: (a) never pipe a gate through tail/grep; (b) never read the exit status of a compound or backgrounded command as the runner's — capture the runner's own status immediately into a variable (rc=$?) on the line after the runner, echo THAT, and cross-check it against the log's own PASS/FAIL lines before believing either. A gate that reports success while its log says FAIL is the single most dangerous failure mode available to a worker, because it produces a confident false green.

RELATED ROOT CAUSE worth briefing alongside it: a FRESH worker worktree has no node_modules, so shadow-cljs is not on PATH and any CLJS/node arm dies for environmental reasons that look like test failures. Fix is 'npm ci' under implementation/ inside the worktree (NOT a junction into the mayor tree — a junction makes git worktree remove destroy the mayor's real node_modules). Multiple workers hit this today. Also observed: rewrite-local-root-coord and 'implementation JS harness helpers' flake on Git-Bash fork exhaustion (0xC0000142, 'fork: Resource temporarily unavailable') when several JVMs are live, then pass uncontended — load-sensitive, not a real failure.

A GATE THAT DERIVES REACHABILITY FROM RAW YAML COUNTS COMMENTS AS EXECUTION — and 92% of the workflow corpus is comments (2026-08-06, rf2-6ckzl).

THE DEFECT. scripts/check_gate_scheduling.py answers "is this gate scheduled to run in CI?" by searching the workflow YAML. It searched the RAW file. test.yml carries paragraph-long job comments that NAME the commands they explain, so A COMMENT MENTIONING A COMMAND MARKED THAT GATE AS SCHEDULED. Measured: only 39,567 of 511,152 chars of the workflow corpus is executable — 8%. The gate was reading its answer out of the other 92%.

THE SHARPEST INSTANCE, and it is the reason this is worth a memory rather than a bug report: the test:mcp-conformance disposition pinned its ci-runs-it-directly probe on the JOB ID mcp-conformance-re-frame2-pair, which appears 8 TIMES IN RAW YAML AND ZERO TIMES IN ANY run: VALUE. Its premise had never once been confirmed by anything CI executes. A scheduling claim resting entirely on prose, in the checker whose whole job is to verify scheduling claims.

THE FIX SHAPE: derive reachability from run: VALUES ONLY - inline, block/folded scalars, and the "- run:" first-key form - excluding name:, if:, with:, the defaults: run: mapping, and comments at every level. Transitive closure preserved, no new dependency, still pure-static.

THE LOAD-BEARING VERIFICATION: identical counts before and after on the live tree (40 gates / 34 scheduled / 6 declared). That is what proves nothing real was leaning on prose, so the tightening cannot red main. A tightening that CHANGES the live counts is telling you something was depending on the loophole - read it before shipping.

WHY THIS GENERALISES. This project has found the "a comment justifying an omission is an unverified assertion" pattern five times. THIS IS THAT PATTERN ONE LEVEL UP: not a human trusting a comment, but a MACHINE CHECK trusting one. Any checker that greps a file containing both executable content and prose has this defect available to it. Ask of every static checker: WHAT SUBSET OF THE FILE IS IT ENTITLED TO READ, and is it reading only that?

TWO PROBE TRAPS CONFIRMED IN THE SAME RUN: (1) a SUBSTRING probe was satisfied by a sibling step whose name merely extended it (...-live-overflow matching ...-live) - require complete-token match; (2) a mutation that FAILED TO APPLY (Python rejected a POSIX path form) produced two "green" verdicts the worker nearly read as results. The confirm-the-mutation-applied assert is what caught it. A mutation that did not take is indistinguishable from a gate that did not fire.

TWO GATE FACTS THAT CORRECT MY OWN BRIEFS (2026-08-11, rf2-5i4e worker, PR #7833).

1. check_doc_slugs.py DOES NOT OPEN REPO-ROOT MARKDOWN — INCLUDING CLAUDE.md. Its own docstring (rf2-znup0) says repo-root markdown is out of scope and it "exits 0 on a broken link in any of them". WHY THIS IS THE NASTY SHAPE: check_doc_slugs.py is SILENT ON SUCCESS, so I already tell workers to prove coverage by planting a bogus anchor. But a plant in an OUT-OF-SCOPE file also produces silence — the proof technique and the failure mode look identical. Planting only proves coverage if you plant in a file the gate actually reads.

CORRECTED BRIEF WORDING: name the gate WITH ITS SCOPE. check_doc_slugs.py covers docs/** (including docs/design/** and docs/the-mayor-method/) and spec/**; check_readme_links.py covers repo-root markdown such as CLAUDE.md and README.md. If an edit spans both, nominate both and prove each in its own tree.

2. THE HARNESS'S REPORTED EXIT CODE IS THE LAST COMMAND'S, WHICH IS MY OWN ECHO. Live instance: `mkdocs` is not on PATH in this environment, the console script exits 127 with "command not found" — and the harness still reported the wrapper as exit 0, because the last command on the line was the `echo` writing the .exit file. (The spine's documented `python -m mkdocs` fallback, rf2-g7p7l, is what actually runs.)

So my snippet — `gate > gate.log 2>&1; echo "$?" > gate.exit` — is CORRECT, and it is correct precisely because it puts the real code in a FILE. But a worker who reads the HARNESS's reported exit instead of `cat gate.exit` sees the echo's zero. Same fail-open, one level up from the pipeline trap.

CORRECTED BRIEF WORDING, add one clause: "then READ THE .exit FILE and quote that number — not the exit code the harness reports for the command line, which is the echo's."

THE COMMON SHAPE, third instance tonight after my sweep conflating FAILURE with CANCELLED and my own piped `||` fallback: an instrument that is correct for the question it was built for, reused for a question it cannot answer. Name the scope, and read the artefact rather than the wrapper.

gh pr diff <n> -- <path> IS A LOUD FAILURE THAT A PIPELINE TURNS SILENT — use git diff for any path-scoped PR diff (2026-08-15 13:02 AUSEST; CORRECTED from an earlier wrong version of this record).

WHAT I FIRST RECORDED, AND WHY IT WAS WRONG. I wrote that gh 'accepts the pathspec, exits 0, and prints nothing. NO ERROR, NO WARNING.' A worker (rf2-g76j3, PR #8280) checked that premise and refuted it. I RE-VERIFIED MYSELF:
  gh pr diff 8279 -- .github/workflows/test.yml   -> EXIT 1, stdout 0 lines,
                                                     stderr 'accepts at most 1 arg(s), received 2'
gh does NOT accept a pathspec at all. It rejects the command loudly.

THE REAL FAILURE MODE IS THE PIPELINE, NOT THE TOOL. What I actually ran was
  gh pr diff <n> -- <path> 2>/dev/null | grep -cE '...'
and that construction destroys both halves of the evidence: 2>/dev/null discards the error message, and the pipe makes the exit status GREP's rather than gh's. grep succeeds on empty input and prints 0. So a loud, correct refusal is laundered into a confident, wrong zero.

THIS IS THE SAME DEFECT THE GATE RULES ALREADY NAME — 'never pipe a gate through a filter, because a pipeline's exit status is its last command's.' I have that rule in every worker brief and broke it in my own merge check. The rule is not about test runners specifically; it is about any command whose exit code carries the answer.

THE CORRECT FORM for a path-scoped diff of somebody's branch:
  git diff origin/main...worker/<branch> -- .github/workflows/ | grep -cE '^\+  [a-z][a-z0-9_-]*:[[:space:]]*$'
Two leading spaces, because job keys nest under jobs: — see job-key-test-needs-two-space-indent.

MEASURED ON THE KNOWN-NONZERO CASE, which is what made the disagreement visible: PR #8279 adds job key hicasso-naming-census. git returns 1; gh-with-pathspec returns 0; gh without a pathspec returns 238 lines and exit 1... no, exit 0 for the plain form. The plain form works; only the pathspec form is rejected.

THE DURABLE LESSONS, in order of value:
 1. A COMMAND THAT FAILS LOUDLY BECOMES SILENT THE MOMENT YOU PIPE IT AND REDIRECT ITS STDERR. Check exit codes on the producing command, not on the pipeline.
 2. A DISCRIMINATOR ONLY EVER TESTED ON ZERO-ANSWERS IS UNTESTED. Both defects in this one-line test — the unindented regex and this — survived because every case they had been asked genuinely had the answer zero.
 3. MY OWN DURABLE RECORDS ARE CLAIMS TOO. This one asserted a mechanism I had not isolated, and a worker refuted it in one command. Record what was MEASURED, and say which part is inference.

gh pr merge CAN FAIL SILENTLY WITH "Base branch was modified" (2026-07-26). The command returned, my script read state and got OPEN, and nothing in the summary line said why. Running the merge again WITHOUT redirecting stderr showed it: GraphQL: Base branch was modified. Review and try the merge again. (mergePullRequest).

CAUSE: main moved between the check-reading and the merge call — in this case by my own preceding merge in the same sweep. The PR was MERGEABLE / mergeStateStatus CLEAN with 72 pass / 0 fail / 0 pending, so it was genuinely green; only the base had advanced.

FIX: retry. It succeeded immediately on the second attempt. This is NOT an --admin candidate and not a gate problem.

TWO LOOP LESSONS: (1) my sweep already verifies state == MERGED after every merge, which is what caught this — keep that, and never delete a branch on the assumption a merge succeeded (a memory already records that deleting a branch pre-merge auto-closes the PR). (2) I was discarding stderr with >/dev/null 2>&1 on the merge call, which hid the reason. Send merge output somewhere readable, or re-run the merge verbatim when the state check says OPEN — the error message is the diagnosis and it costs one call.

EXPECT THIS MORE when merging several PRs in one sweep: each merge invalidates the base for the ones after it, so later merges in a batch are the likely victims. Retrying in the same pass is fine.

gh pr merge can fail with 'Pull Request has merge conflicts' AFTER the monitor reports GREEN (checks green ≠ mergeable — a sibling merge can conflict it in the gap). NEVER chain merge+cleanup in one command: verify state==MERGED before any branch/worktree deletion. Recovery if violated: the deletion output prints the tip sha — git branch <name> <sha>, push, gh pr reopen, rebase, resolve, force-with-lease.

CLAUSE 4 OF THE MERGE CRITERION FAILS CLOSED ON A CASE MISMATCH BETWEEN TWO gh COMMANDS (2026-08-13).

gh pr checks --json state returns UPPERCASE: SUCCESS, SKIPPED, IN_PROGRESS.
gh run list --json status returns lowercase: completed, queued, in_progress.

mayor-merge.md clause 4 said 'runs whose status is all COMPLETED'. A literal test of .status != "COMPLETED" therefore counts every FINISHED run as nonterminal. It reported all six open PRs as blocked (runs@sha=5 nonterminal=5, identically) when all five runs on each were completed/success. Caught only by dumping the raw JSON.

USE (.status|ascii_upcase) != "COMPLETED".

TWO THINGS WORTH KEEPING. First, the direction: unlike every other trap in the merge criterion this one fails CLOSED, so it never ships a bad merge and never announces itself either - it presents as a CI queue that will not drain, which is entirely believable and can burn ticks indefinitely. The identical reading across all six PRs was the tell; real CI does not stall six branches in lockstep.

Second, the neighbouring fail-OPEN version of the same clause: --commit takes the FULL 40-char headRefOid. An abbreviated sha matches nothing and returns [], which reads as 'no live runs' and passes clause 4 vacuously. Same clause, one argument away, opposite direction.

THE TWO gh COMMANDS IN THE MERGE CRITERION USE OPPOSITE CASE VOCABULARIES, AND A FILTER WRITTEN FOR ONE SILENTLY MISCLASSIFIES THE OTHER (2026-08-10).

  gh pr checks <pr> --json state    -> UPPERCASE:  SUCCESS, SKIPPED, IN_PROGRESS
  gh run list --commit <sha> --json status -> lowercase: completed, in_progress

CLAUSE 4 OF THE MERGE CRITERION USES THE SECOND ONE. I wrote its check as
`select(.status != "COMPLETED") | length` — copying the case from clause 2's vocabulary —
so it matched NOTHING and counted EVERY run as nonterminal. On PR #7774 it reported
"clause4 not-COMPLETED: 5" for a PR whose five runs were all `completed/success`.

THIS ONE FAILED CLOSED, WHICH IS WHY IT COST ONLY A MINUTE. An over-blocking clause 4
refuses a green PR; the method already names that failure ("a guard that blocks forever is
not safe, it is differently wrong") but it is far cheaper than the fail-open direction.
Had I written the inverse test — count runs EQUAL to "COMPLETED" and require the count to
match the total — the same typo would have passed a branch with live runs on it.

WHAT SAVED THE EARLIER MERGES. I printed the run list and read the statuses BY EYE for
every merge before this one, and lowercase `completed` reads correctly to a human. The
defect only bit when I switched from printing to counting. So: a filter you cannot eyeball
is exactly where a vocabulary mismatch hides.

THE FIX: compare case-insensitively — `select((.status|ascii_upcase) != "COMPLETED")` — or
print the values alongside the verdict so the two can never silently disagree. Prefer
printing: the criterion is read by a human every tick anyway.

THE GENERAL RULE, which this repo keeps rediscovering in its own instruments: when one
check joins two data sources, the join is where the vocabularies must be proved equal. Do
not assume a tool speaks one language because two of its subcommands describe the same
domain.

A BRANCH WITH NO *OPEN* PR IS NOT A STRAND — query --state all before calling it one (2026-08-15 14:02 AUSEST).

MEASURED TODAY. worker/settled-10lyy reported worker/rung3-hic033 as 'a stranded branch (merge-base 2026-08-12, no PR, clean worktree) carrying an unmerged budgets.md diff — live hygiene for the mayor'. Every observable it listed was true. The conclusion was wrong.

  git rev-list --count origin/main..worker/rung3-hic033   -> 5   (looks unmerged)
  gh pr list --head worker/rung3-hic033 --state all       -> #7953 MERGED
  its commit subject located in origin/main               -> present

IT IS A REBASE-MERGED GHOST. The five 'unmerged' commits are the PRE-REBASE versions of work that IS on main under different hashes. A rebase-merge rewrites commits, so the original objects stay reachable from the branch ref forever and every count-based test reports them as outstanding.

THE TWO TESTS THAT SEPARATE GHOST FROM STRAND, and both are cheap:
  1. gh pr list --head <branch> --state ALL  — the default is open-only, which is exactly how a merged PR reads as 'no PR'.
  2. locate the branch tip's commit SUBJECT in origin/main — survives the hash rewrite that defeats every sha comparison.

WHY THE ERROR IS ASYMMETRIC AND WHICH WAY IT COSTS: calling a ghost a strand wastes a dispatch re-doing landed work, or worse, revives a diff main has since moved past — the conflict-resolution-reverts-a-refactor failure. Calling a strand a ghost loses real work. So run BOTH tests rather than picking one.

THIS IS THE PR-STATE HALF OF THE FENCE RULE DOING ITS JOB — mayor-dispatch.md already says the diff alone cannot separate a live unpushed worker from a merged leftover whose fork point predates its own merge. Multiple workers have now hit it from the other side: one found FOUR branches holding a file it wanted and every one was a merged leftover; another found five, same answer; a third found three of nine. GHOSTS ARE THE COMMON CASE ON THIS REPO — roughly 70 worktrees exist and almost all are dead.

TO ASK 'DOES THIS BRANCH CARRY ANYTHING MAIN DOES NOT HAVE?', USE git cherry — NOT git rev-list --count (2026-08-13, third rev-list miss in one session).

I escalated to Mike that two guide-rewrite branches were COMPETING WHOLESALE REWRITES that conflicted and needed him to pick one. They were not competing. They had landed as a deliberate SEQUENCE, and every branch tip was PATCH-EQUIVALENT to main.

  git rev-list --count origin/main..BRANCH   read 1     <- misleading
  git cherry main BRANCH                     prints '-' <- already landed

A rebase-merge leaves the ORIGINAL commit object unreachable from main while its PATCH is fully present. rev-list counts OBJECTS; the question is about CONTENT. git cherry marks '-' for patch-equivalent and '+' for genuinely unlanded.

THE PATTERN IS BIGGER THAN THIS ONE COMMAND. A rev-list count misled three separate times in one session:
  1. liveness  - the ahead count is INVARIANT UNDER REBASE, so a working worker read as stalled (rf2-0vvw)
  2. the check band - a mid-run rollup total is a FLOOR, not a count; 92 became 93 when it settled
  3. unlanded work - object reachability is not patch equivalence (this one)

Each time the number was real and the QUESTION IT ANSWERED was not the question I was asking. Before quoting a count, say out loud what set it counts and whether that is the set you care about.

COST HERE: a false P2 escalation to the operator, a bead held at 'needs Mike' for several ticks, and three further beads fenced behind it that were never actually blocked.

A `$` ANCHOR PLACED DIRECTLY AFTER LITERAL TEXT RETURNS A FALSE ZERO IN `git grep` ON THIS CHECKOUT, AND EVERY MAYOR GOVERNING FILE IS CRLF (measured 2026-08-20).

MECHANISM. The files are stored and checked out with CRLF terminators, so a `\r` sits between the last literal character and end-of-line. `git grep` matches against that `\r`; `^` is unaffected, and `.*$` is unaffected because `.` matches the `\r`. Only literal-text-then-`$` fails, and it fails SILENTLY as "no matches".

MEASURED, on `.claude/commands/mayor-posture.md`:
  leading `^` only ........................ 1 hit
  `.*$` .................................... 1 hit
  full literal line + `$` .................. 0 hits  <-- FALSE
  same literal line, no `$` ................ 1 hit

SPREAD, and this is why it matters rather than being a curiosity: `file -b` reports CRLF for ALL of `docs/the-mayor-method/{dispatch-prompt-template,loops,bootstrap}.md`, ALL of `.claude/commands/mayor-{merge,dispatch,posture,hygiene,method-reread}.md`, and `CLAUDE.md`. `dispatch-prompt-template.md` is 900 of 900 lines CRLF. The entire surface the method-reread loop audits is affected.

HOW IT BIT. The method-reread loop's duplicate-block check ran `git grep -l "^WORKTREE BOUNDARY — MANDATORY$"` and returned EMPTY — for a heading that demonstrably exists at `dispatch-prompt-template.md:478`. Unanchored, it returns exactly 1 file, which is the correct answer. Had a second copy of that block existed, the check would have reported clean.

WHY NO DISPATCH WAS EVER HARMED. The block extraction uses `sed`, not `git grep`, and `sed` on this Git Bash STRIPS the `\r` on read — `sed -n '/^WORKTREE BOUNDARY — MANDATORY$/,/^```$/p'` still returns its 51 lines, and the extracted text is clean LF. So the paste path is sound and only the VERIFICATION path was blind. Do not "fix" the extraction.

THE RULE: never end a `git grep` pattern with a `$` straight after literal text on this repo. Drop the `$`, or use `.*$`. And this is the standing "a search that returns ZERO is not a check that passed" rule biting the mayor's own audit — run a positive control on any census whose zero you are about to believe.

GIT GREP SILENTLY MISSES HITS THAT RIPGREP RETURNS ON THIS CHECKOUT — measured 2026-08-14 23:35 AUSEST by worker/arch-hic087 during rf2-hic-087's mechanism census (PR #8258).

WHAT WAS MEASURED. An anchored hook-call-site census over implementation/hicasso/src read 14 with 'git grep -E' and 16 with rg, against a tree that was BYTE-IDENTICAL across the rebase (verified). Two hits, roughly 12% of the population, were invisible to git grep. The worker recorded the correction on its published page rather than absorbing it silently, which is the only reason it is knowable.

WHY IT MATTERS MORE THAN A TOOL PREFERENCE. Every census on this programme is a published NUMBER that later work cites — native-share, retained-tooling, mutable-globals, public-surface, allocation. A census run with git grep can be low and internally consistent, and nothing downstream can tell. A census is not reproducible unless it records the tool as well as the pattern.

THE RULE: use rg for any census whose number gets published, and RECORD THE TOOL alongside the pattern and the count. If a census must use git grep (for example to restrict to tracked files), cross-check the total with rg and say both numbers.

A SECOND TRAP FROM THE SAME BEAD, and it is Clojure-specific: A PREDICATE NAME ENDS IN '?', WHICH IS ALSO A REGEX QUANTIFIER. The worker's grep '\bscope?\b' matched 'scop' followed by an optional 'e', so it reported two LIVE evidence vars as dead code. Escape the '?' or use a fixed-string search whenever a Clojure symbol ends in '?' or '*' or '+'. In a dead-code census this fails in the dangerous direction: it deletes live code.

BOTH TRAPS SHARE ONE SHAPE — a census that is wrong reads exactly like a census that is right, because the only evidence is the number itself. That is why a positive control (seed something the census must catch, confirm it is named, remove it) is now standard on this programme's censuses.

git rm --cached DOES NOT PROTECT FILES FROM A LATER CHECKOUT — and this will bite rf2-vxgfnd.99.1 at 85 files. Found by the ai/decisions untracking worker (#6424) on 2026-07-19, in its own worktree.

THE HAZARD: `git rm --cached` leaves the file on disk IN THE BRANCH WHERE IT RUNS — but the COMMIT RECORDS A DELETION. Any later rebase, checkout, or `git reset --hard` ACROSS that commit removes the working-tree copies too, silently and with no warning. The worker rebased onto post-#6422 main and its four dossiers vanished from disk; it caught this only on a final on-disk verification and restored them.
⚠️ THE SAME THING HAPPENS IN EVERY OTHER CHECKOUT WHEN THE COMMIT MERGES. The mayor loop `git reset --hard origin/main` after a merge will delete the operator working copies. On 2026-07-19 I backed the four dossiers up to the scratchpad BEFORE merging #6424 and restored them after, so they end up UNTRACKED BUT PRESENT — which is what "should not be tracked" means. "Untrack" is not "delete".

⚠️ rf2-vxgfnd.99.1 WILL HIT THIS AT 85 FILES (ai/findings/new-substrate-synthesis + new-substrate-codex). Its brief MUST carry:
  1. Back up the full tracked ai/ set to a location OUTSIDE the repo before the untracking commit.
  2. A POST-REBASE ON-DISK RE-VERIFICATION step — after any rebase or checkout, confirm the files are still present, not just that the index is right.
  3. The same restore step in the mayor merge sequence, or the operator local working material disappears from every checkout that pulls.
  4. State explicitly whether the operator wants them KEPT on disk or genuinely DELETED — do not infer. Mike instruction was "this path should NOT be tracked", which is about the index, not the filesystem.

GENERAL FORM: an index-only operation still produces a tree-changing commit. Whenever you `git rm --cached` anything a human is still using as working material, the deletion propagates to every working tree that later checks out that commit. Back it up first; verify on disk afterwards; and say plainly to the operator that the files will vanish from their checkout unless restored.

GREPPING A GATE LOG FOR 'FAIL' HITS ITS OWN SELF-TEST CONTROL LINES — count them against a known-good run before believing a failure (2026-08-15 20:02 AUSEST).

MEASURED by worker/release-gra70 (rf2-gra70, PR #8314). Its fast-PR spine log contained 35 matches for FAIL while the run exited 0. Those 35 are CONTROL LINES of the form 'PASS ... FAILS' — a self-test asserting that a deliberately-broken input fails. The worker's discriminator was simple and right: THE SAME COUNT APPEARED IN A RUN THAT EXITED 0, so 35 is the baseline rather than a signal.

WHY THIS MATTERS: the standing rule is already 'never pipe a gate through a filter, because a pipeline's exit status is its LAST command's'. This is the mirror failure — reading the LOG instead of the exit code, and being misled in the opposite direction. One makes a failure look like a pass; the other makes a pass look like a failure. THE EXIT CODE FROM THE RUNNER'S OWN LINE IS THE VERDICT. A log grep is at best corroboration, and only against a known baseline.
