THE SESSION-UUID SCRATCHPAD PATH IS NOT ISOLATED BETWEEN CONCURRENT AGENTS (observed 2026-08-07).

WHAT HAPPENED: a worker on rf2-jr0tg wrote its PR body to a scratchpad file named pr-body.md. Mid-task the file was OVERWRITTEN with a DIFFERENT worker's PR body — the rf2-drpa3.182.12 / twoclock-182-12 lane. Both agents were spawned from the same mayor session, so both resolved the same session-scoped scratchpad directory. The worker noticed, recovered by writing to a uniquely-named file, and reported it.

WHY IT MATTERS MORE THAN IT LOOKS: this is the same defect class as two workers sharing /tmp/gate.log — the loser reads a file belonging to someone else's run and it looks entirely plausible. For a gate log that yields a green that was never earned. For a PR body it yields a PR describing another bead's work, which a reviewer would have to already know the codebase to catch. Nothing in either agent's own git status shows anything wrong.

THE RULE: a worker must never write to a fixed filename in the scratchpad. Every scratchpad artefact gets a name unique to the worker — include the bead id or the branch name (pr-body-rf2-jr0tg.md, not pr-body.md). Prefer WORKTREE-LOCAL paths over the scratchpad entirely for anything a gate or a PR depends on; the worktree genuinely is per-worker. And before believing any file the worker did not just write in that same tool call, confirm it is its own.

THE MAYOR'S SIDE: when concurrent workers are in flight, do not assume a PR body belongs to its PR. Spot-check that the body describes the bead the PR claims, especially when two workers reported close together.

THE SESSION SCRATCHPAD IS SHARED ACROSS CONCURRENT AGENTS, AND PR-BODY DRAFTS GET SILENTLY OVERWRITTEN THERE (2026-08-10, twice in one hour).

WHAT HAPPENED. Two workers independently reported the same thing. The rf2-hic-093 worker found its `pr-body.md` overwritten shortly after it created PR #7771. The rf2-dmrm worker found its `pr-body.md` replaced by a DIFFERENT agent's PR body — text about rf2-x874/hic-013/hic-011 — shortly after it created PR #7772. Neither had its worktree touched; only the scratchpad file.

WHY MY BRIEFS DID NOT PREVENT IT. Every brief already said "put every gate artefact where git ignores it" and named worktree-local paths for LOGS AND EXIT FILES. It said nothing about the PR body, so workers reasonably wrote that to the session scratchpad, which is per-session and NOT per-agent. Concurrent agents in one session share it, and a fixed basename like `pr-body.md` collides by construction.

NO HARM EITHER TIME, AND THAT IS THE HAZARD. Both PRs were created BEFORE the overwrite, so both published bodies were correct and both workers verified them afterwards. Had the ordering been reversed — draft, get clobbered, then `gh pr create --body-file` — a worker would have published ANOTHER BEAD'S PR BODY onto its own PR, with plausible-looking content and no error anywhere. The handoff records a near-miss of exactly that shape already ("one nearly pushed foreign content").

THE FIX IN EVERY BRIEF, stated as its own line rather than folded into the logs rule:
  SCRATCH FILES GO IN YOUR WORKTREE, NOT THE SESSION SCRATCHPAD. Write the PR
  body to a gitignored path INSIDE your worktree, check `git status` before
  committing, and delete it before finishing.
Worktree-local is the right default for ALL agent scratch, not just gate logs, because a worktree is per-agent by construction while the scratchpad is not.

AND THE GENERAL RULE THIS INSTANCES: a shared mutable path with a fixed basename is a collision waiting for concurrency. The same class already bit gate logs (`/tmp/gate.log`, two workers, the loser read someone else's green). When a brief names a file a worker will write, ask whether two agents would name it the same thing.

SENDMESSAGE'S OWN RESPONSE IS A RELIABLE WORKER-LIVENESS SIGNAL (discovered 2026-07-25, after four incidents that a reliable signal would have prevented).

The two response shapes mean different things:
  * 'Message queued for delivery to <id> at its next tool round.' => the agent is ALIVE and mid-task. Do not prune its worktree, do not assume its beads are discharged.
  * 'Agent "<id>" had no active task; resumed from transcript in the background with your message.' => the agent was IDLE/COMPLETE at that moment. Its worktree was prunable, and whatever it had was final.

WHY THIS MATTERS: terminality was the fact I kept lacking. I pruned three worktrees from under live workers by inferring done-ness from 'PR merged' plus a clean tree, and I merged two PRs mid-push for the same reason — the merge sweep has PR state in hand while liveness lives in task notifications that arrive asynchronously and repeat (a background agent notifies every time it stops with no live children, so one job notifies several times and 'completed' does NOT mean finished). Freshness helps but is a stale sample: a worker 45 minutes quiet turned out to be mid-write and committed 3 seconds after I looked.

HOW TO USE IT: when terminality is ambiguous and the decision is destructive or finalising (prune, close a bead, treat a merge as complete), send the worker a short status question and READ THE TOOL'S OWN RESPONSE. That is cheap, non-destructive, and definitive at the moment you ask. It also does something useful either way: an alive worker gets your update, an idle one gets resumed with it.

Note the resume side effect: messaging an idle agent RESTARTS it from its transcript. That is usually desirable (it picks up remaining work with fresh context on what changed), but it means the check is not free — do not poll with it, and do not use it on an agent whose work you want left finished.

AFTER A SESSION CLEAR, TaskList READS EMPTY WHILE PRIOR-SESSION AGENTS KEEP RUNNING — AND THEY BECOME UNREACHABLE (2026-08-15 21:35 AUSEST).

WHAT HAPPENED. A /clear handed me a fresh mayor context. TaskList returned 'No tasks found'. The handoff said 3 agents were draining. I concluded they had died with the session, and acted on it: pushed their branches and opened PRs 8322 and 8323 with a body asserting 'the authoring worker's session ended'. Mike asked 'Aren't there currently three background workers?' and he was right.

THE EVIDENCE THAT SETTLED IT, and it took one command. Count non-node_modules, non-.git files touched in each worktree in the last 25 minutes:
  retire-final    30 files, newest .scratch/rf2-local-root-109284-*/deps.edn written 8 SECONDS earlier
  hicaudit-5zmul  4767 files, implementation/core/.cpcache written 90 seconds earlier
  docsaudit-h3tke 10709 files, docs/design/hicasso/product/README.md EDITED 4 minutes earlier
Cross-check with processes: java PID 49192 started 21:32:53, node PID 109284 at 21:33:07. Live JVM gate, live node gate, live doc editing.

THE TELL I MISSED FIRST TIME. CronList in the same session returned the 5 pre-existing cron jobs. So SESSION STATE SURVIVED THE CLEAR. If the cron registry survived, agents did too. TaskList disagreeing with CronList is the discriminator, and I read only one of them.

*** AND THEY ARE UNREACHABLE. *** SendMessage to 'retire-final' and 'hicaudit-5zmul' both returned 'No agent named X is reachable.' The clear severs the agent NAME registry while the processes keep running. So the stranded sweep's step 2 — 'is there a live task to message?' — RETURNS THE STRAND ANSWER FOR A HEALTHY WORKER after a clear. Both of its liveness probes fail open in the same direction: TaskList empty AND SendMessage unreachable, on 3 workers that were all fine.

THE RULE. After any session clear, NEVER read TaskList as evidence of the fleet. Read the worktrees instead. In PowerShell: Get-ChildItem -Path <worktree> -Recurse -File -Force, filter LastWriteTime newer than 25 minutes ago, exclude node_modules and .git, then look at the NEWEST filenames. Paths under .cpcache, .scratch or implementation/out mean a gate is running; a tracked source or doc file means the worker is editing. Near-zero is a strand; thousands is a live gate.

WHAT IT COST, and why it was not worse. Two PRs opened on live workers' branches with a false provenance line, and one measurement worktree created against a box I wrongly believed was quiet. All three were cheap to reverse: PR bodies edited to say the author is live and owns the PR, worktree removed via scripts/remove-worker-worktree.sh with the canary verified at 101. NOTHING was committed from a worker's uncommitted work, which is the one error that would not have been reversible.

SECOND-ORDER CONSEQUENCE FOR THE DRAIN RULING. 'Complete when zero background agents are running' cannot be tested with TaskList after a clear. Test it with the worktree activity sweep, and only then open a measurement window.

AND A THIRD CONSEQUENCE: an unreachable live worker cannot be resumed, redirected or told anything. It will finish, or not, on its own. Do not redispatch its bead — that puts a second worker on one branch. Wait for its push.

AN EXHAUSTED SESSION ALLOWANCE KILLS WORKERS AND IS NOT CURED BY REDISPATCH (2026-08-19).

Two workers dispatched minutes apart both terminated with "Agent terminated early due to an API error: You've hit your session limit · resets 2:20pm (Australia/Sydney)". One died inside its boundary check before its first edit; the other before creating its worktree. Neither had commits; one had a single uncommitted modified file.

WHY IT MATTERS THAT THIS IS NOT AN ORDINARY STRAND. The commonest strand is a worker that backgrounded a gate and ended its turn, and that one IS cured by a message. An allowance failure is not: a replacement sent into the same exhausted window dies the same way and consumes the dispatch too. The RESET TIME is the release condition, and it is a clock rather than a state — nothing in the repo or the tracker changes at the reset, so it has to be written down.

THE DRILL: salvage the branch (push any commits — MEASURE with git rev-list --count origin/main..HEAD rather than assuming), record the reason AND the reset time on the bead, release any claim back to open, merge anything already green, and STOP dispatching until the reset.

DO NOT build a commit from a dead worker's uncommitted working tree. Let the redispatch start clean.

AND CHECK THE CLOCK BEFORE STANDING DOWN FOR LONG: on this occasion the loop's next tick arrived AFTER the reset, so the hold was already lifted and the correct move was to redispatch immediately rather than to wait.

THE SESSION SCRATCHPAD IS SHARED BETWEEN CONCURRENT AGENTS, NOT PER-AGENT (2026-08-11, observed live).

A worker had its `scratchpad/pr-body.md` OVERWRITTEN mid-task by a different agent writing an unrelated PR body for another artefact. It recovered by pulling the live PR body from GitHub and re-patching under a branch-unique filename. Nothing was lost, but only because it noticed.

I have been putting "use worktree-local scratch filenames unique to your branch" in every brief on general principle. This is the incident that makes it concrete: with six workers out, a generic name like `pr-body.md`, `gate.log` or `notes.md` in the shared scratchpad is a collision waiting to happen, and the failure mode is SILENT - the file simply contains someone else's content, and a worker that reads back what it wrote gets a plausible document about the wrong subject.

TIGHTEN THE BRIEF FROM "unique names" TO "unique names AND prefer the worktree": gate logs and scratch files should live under the worker's OWN worktree path (which is genuinely isolated) rather than in the shared scratchpad at all. Where the scratchpad must be used, the filename carries the branch name, e.g. `pr-body-<branch>.md`.

RELATED, same family: this is why every brief specifies `> <worktree>/gate.log` with an absolute worktree path rather than a bare relative filename.

SEVENTH FALSE-GREEN VECTOR: STALE SHADOW-CLJS CACHE ON AN .EDN-ONLY EDIT (2026-07-25, found by the EP-0037 routing worker). conformance-fixtures INLINES the EDN at compile time and declares no cache dependency on the .edn file — so editing ONLY a fixture .edn does not invalidate the shadow-cljs cache, and the suite recompiles from cache and reports the OLD fixture's verdict. The worker's failing CLJS conformance fixture was this, not a real failure. CI never sees it because CI compiles fresh from a cold cache; it bites LOCAL runs only, which is the worst shape — a worker debugging a red it cannot explain, or worse, a worker whose fixture fix appears not to work and who then 'fixes' something that was never broken.

WORKAROUND: after an .edn-only fixture edit, clear .shadow-cljs (or touch a .cljs/.cljc file in the same build) before believing a local CLJS result. Related known trap: a stale shadow-cljs SERVER JVM after a source-dir rename produces 'namespace not available' — check .shadow-cljs/server.pid age and kill the java pid.

THE FULL LIST OF WAYS A GREEN LIES IN THIS REPO, now seven: (1) piping a gate through tail/grep returns the pipe's status; (2) a compound or backgrounded command's trailing echo supplies a 0 while the log says FAIL — this worker hit it TWICE in one session and caught both by rc capture; (3) test-fast-pr.sh soft-skips its own mkdocs step when mkdocs is off PATH and still exits 0; (4) a .cljc test namespace missing its lane suffix is silently skipped by one runner; (5) a wrapper-reported 'exit code 0' disagreeing with a captured rc; (6) the BACKGROUNDING HARNESS reporting exit code 0 for a run whose log says rc=1; (7) this one — a stale compile cache serving an old inlined fixture.

Note that (7) is different in kind from (1)-(6): those are about MISREADING a verdict, this is about the verdict being computed from stale INPUT. So 'capture rc and cross-check the log' does not catch it. The brief line that does: 'an .edn/data-only edit may not invalidate the CLJS cache — clear .shadow-cljs before trusting a local CLJS result on a data-only change.'

SHADOW-CLJS DOES NOT WARN ON CROSS-NAMESPACE PRIVATE-VAR ACCESS. NEVER cite a warnings-fatal compile as evidence that a defn- has no out-of-namespace caller (rf2-i81n5, reproduced 2026-08-15).

THIS IS A TOOLCHAIN PROPERTY, NOT ONE GATE'S. It holds for every shadow-cljs compile in this repo -- test:cljs, browser-test, the hicasso and freehand lane compile gates, check-examples-compile.cjs, test.yml's B-spine, every release build. Do not read it as a limitation of whichever gate you happened to name.

THE CAUSE, at source in the versions actually used (shadow-cljs 3.4.10 + clojurescript 1.12.145, both read off the resolved classpath of the run). CLJS's :private-var-access warning is defaulted TRUE (analyzer.cljc:135) but is emitted in exactly one place -- (defmethod resolve* :default) at analyzer.cljc:1248-1260. shadow's install-hacks! does (replace-fn! #'ana/resolve-var shadow-resolve-var) (cljs_hacks.cljc:1273), and shadow-resolve-var resolves entirely through resolve-fqn-sym / resolve-ns-var / resolve-cljs-var, none of which tests (:private sym-ast). resolve* is never reached, so the warning can never fire. Nothing in implementation/shadow-cljs.edn disables it -- only :redef false appears.

THE REPRODUCTION. A real call to the private re-frame.hicasso.server/fresh-frame-id planted in a lane namespace: npm run test:hicasso-compile came back exit 0, '441 files, 440 compiled, 0 warnings'. The emitted JS contains the direct call -- return re_frame.hicasso.server.fresh_frame_id(...) -- so the compiler resolved it and stayed silent.

WHAT TO CITE INSTEAD. A grep / corpus sweep over tracked files is what actually answers 'does anything CALL this name'. check_naming_census.py answers a DIFFERENT question -- is the name written down in the naming ledger as public -- and treats defn- as an escape hatch with no bar attached.

JVM CLOJURE DIFFERS: there private access is a hard error, so a .cljc file is caught on the JVM half and not the CLJS half.

PRECEDENT: rf2-sc1dt's ruling listed 'Warnings-fatal Hicasso compile finds no private cross-namespace use' as acceptance evidence. That line did not hold. The privatisation itself was fine, re-established by exhaustive grep and the census moving 105 -> 103.

shadow-cljs HMR gates must wait for RUNTIME REGISTRATION, not for the app mount. The worker's send-to-runtimes (shadow/cljs/devtools/server/worker/impl.clj:55) is '(when (seq runtimes) ...)' — a runtime the worker has not met draws SILENCE, not an error, and there is no catch-up: the runtime learns about builds only by push. Registration happens when the relay handles the page's :hello (shadow/remote/relay/local.clj:252), which is sent only after the websocket opens and :welcome returns. An app mount says nothing about that: shadow's client only STARTS the connect before :init-fn paints. Positive signal to wait for = the reply to the client's post-:hello :request-clients query, observable from Node via page.on('websocket') framesent/framereceived (transit-json TEXT frames; outbound ops are never transit-cache back-references because shadow's transit-str makes a fresh writer per message). Measured on green CI: the handshake takes 0.7s (chromium) to 5.0s (webkit) while the save-to-push window is ~1.5s. rf2-odh3 / PR 7998.

When a worker edits a test namespace then runs node tests, shadow-cljs incremental compile can show a PHANTOM failure referencing the PRE-EDIT test source (a compile race). Fix: force a clean 'npx shadow-cljs compile node-test' before trusting 'node out/node-test.js'. Seen by rf2-2lb7z worker (PR #1946) — first two runs showed a stale 1-failure, clean recompile gave 0. Tell test-authoring workers to recompile-then-run after editing a test ns.

BOTH /tmp AND THE SESSION SCRATCHPAD ARE SHARED ACROSS CONCURRENT AGENTS ON THIS HOST. Two independent workers hit this on 2026-07-24, in two different directories.

INSTANCE 1 — /tmp: a worker gate log written to /tmp/gate-browser.log was overwritten by ANOTHER worker run. It read EXIT=0 and "0 failures" — plausible numbers, wrong code. The only tell was the shadow-cljs "config:" banner naming a different worktree. This defeats the capture-and-echo-the-exit-code discipline, because the captured EXIT CODE belongs to the other run too.

INSTANCE 2 — THE SCRATCHPAD: the v/->react worker had its pr-body.md OVERWRITTEN by another worker mid-task. Caught before it did damage, but a PR body is exactly the kind of file you write once and read back later without re-checking.

THE RULE, now standard in every brief: write worker-owned files to a WORKTREE-LOCAL path, not /tmp and not a bare name in the shared scratchpad. If the scratchpad must be used, make the filename UNIQUE (include the branch or bead id). And VERIFY OWNERSHIP before believing any captured artefact — for a shadow-cljs run, the "config:" banner names the worktree whose build ran; grep it and confirm it is yours.

GENERAL FORM, which is why this outlives both instances: when an assertion or an artefact rests on something OUTSIDE your process — a shared temp directory, a shared port, a shared cache, a scratchpad — ask WHO ELSE CAN WRITE IT before trusting what you read back. A file you wrote is not necessarily the file you read. This is the same family as the console-shim trap (the observer sits below your runtime) and the attribute-order trap (the serialisation carries incidental detail) — in every case the thing being measured is not the thing you think you are measuring.

MAYOR NOTE: my own boilerplate said "> /tmp/gate.log" for a long stretch of dispatches. Saturating six workers on one machine makes shared-path collision the NORMAL case, not an edge case.

SHARED SCRATCHPAD CAN OVERWRITE A LIVE WORKER'S FILE MID-TASK (2026-07-25, second occurrence, escalating). Concurrent workers share one temp root. First occurrence: a worker reached for scratchpad/pr-body.md and found ANOTHER worker's PR body already in it — caught by a stale-read refusal. Second occurrence: the R6 worker's own scratchpad file was ACTIVELY OVERWRITTEN mid-task by a different PR's body content, and it only noticed because a python string-replace threw on a missing substring. Its own assessment: 'a silent overwrite of a body file could have published the wrong description' — i.e. gh pr edit --body-file could publish another PR's text under your PR.

AGENT-QUALIFIED FILENAMES ARE NOT SUFFICIENT — the second victim was already using them. Brief workers to: (1) write PR bodies inside their OWN WORKTREE (a gitignored path like <worktree>/ai/gate-logs/ or <worktree>/.worker/), never the shared session scratchpad; (2) verify content immediately before publishing — re-read the file and confirm it contains an expected marker unique to THIS PR; (3) treat a string-replace that fails to find its substring as a CORRUPTION SIGNAL, not a bug in the pattern. The R6 worker's recovery is the right pattern: it treated the live PR body on GitHub as the source of truth and rebuilt from that rather than trusting local state.

Related mayor-side trap from the same session: Git Bash /tmp and Windows Python /tmp are DIFFERENT paths. Python raised FileNotFoundError while a following 'gh pr edit --body-file /tmp/...' happily re-uploaded the UNMODIFIED file — a chain that reported success while doing nothing. Gate any publish on the editing step's own return code.

A SHELL IS NOT A NEUTRAL CARRIER OF A PATTERN — a mangled plant refutes a real defect (2026-08-14, rf2-mwr2 worker).

WHAT HAPPENED. A worker set out to red a control against buggy code by planting a config that should trigger the defect. The control came back REFUSING — the reading that says "no defect here". That is a false refutation of a defect that is real.

THE CAUSE: the plant went through a bash-to-python round trip, which ate one backslash. The plant wrote \. where real EDN writes \. — so the code's string-literal sub-pattern never matched the plant at all. The gate refused for the WRONG REASON, and the refusal looked exactly like "your premise is false".

RE-RUN FROM A FILE CARRYING THE LITERAL VERBATIM, the defect appeared instantly.

WHY THIS IS WORSE THAN A PLANT THAT SIMPLY FAILS TO RED. A green sabotage is a known signal to stop. But a plant that produces the RIGHT-LOOKING NEGATIVE — a refusal, an exit 1 for an unrelated reason, a "not applicable" — reads as evidence about the subject rather than about the harness. The worker nearly closed a real defect as unreproducible.

THE RULE. When planting anything containing backslashes, quotes, dollar signs or braces, write the plant to a FILE with the literal bytes and have the code read that file. Never pass it through a shell argument, a heredoc that interpolates, or a language round trip. Then verify the plant landed as intended by reading the bytes back — git hash-object, or a byte comparison against what you meant to write — BEFORE interpreting what the gate said about it.

THE SAME BEAD'S HISTORY MAKES THE POINT TWICE. Its original audit finding was refuted at source because an exclusion pattern was READ rather than EVALUATED against the real value — re-frame.freehand.bench.* does not match re-frame.bench.*. Both errors are the same shape: reasoning about a pattern instead of running it against the real bytes.

AN 86-MINUTE SILENCE IS NOT EVIDENCE A WORKER IS DEAD, AND A FINISHER DISPATCHED ON THAT INFERENCE BECOMES A SECOND EXECUTOR ON THE SAME BEADS (2026-08-18).

WHAT HAPPENED: worker xrayroster-2 went quiet for 86 minutes - clean tree, no file activity, two unanswered messages, and a local tip that was not a descendant of what it had pushed. I read that as stranded, salvaged its branch (correct and cheap), and ALSO dispatched a finisher to rebuild the work from current trunk (not correct). It was alive the whole time. It resumed on my message, finished, and produced PR #8440. The finisher independently produced PR #8450. Two PRs, same three beads, several hours of duplicated work.

THE DISCRIMINATORS I HAD ALL POINTED THE SAME WRONG WAY. Idle worktree, clean status, unanswered messages, stale tip - every one of them is equally consistent with a worker that is THINKING, or blocked on a long backgrounded gate, or between turns. None of them distinguishes dead from busy. The harness's running-agent report is the only signal that answers the actual question, and I did not have one.

THE RULE: SALVAGE IS CHEAP AND REVERSIBLE; A SECOND DISPATCH IS NEITHER. Pushing a stranded branch to a salvage ref costs nothing, destroys nothing, and is right even if the worker is alive. Dispatching a finisher spends a full worker and creates a merge race. So on silence: salvage immediately, message, and WAIT. Dispatch a replacement only on positive evidence of death - a completion notification, an explicit allowance-exhausted report, or a harness report showing no running agent.

WHEN IT HAS ALREADY HAPPENED: do not close the loser's PR before asking what it has that the winner lacks. Here the file counts were 21 vs 18 and the SMALLER one was the better artefact - it covered the third bead (spec/017) that the larger missed. File count is not scope. Ask the losing worker for its delta by file and by substance, keep anything unique, then close.

SEE ALSO the same day: a hygiene pass deleted that finisher's branch on a survey taken minutes earlier reading ahead=0; it had committed in the interval. Both failures are one root - a mayor acting on an inference about a worker's state instead of on evidence from the worker itself.

A GATE THAT IS SILENT ON SUCCESS GIVES AN EXIT 0 THAT CANNOT BE DISTINGUISHED FROM IT SKIPPING YOUR FILE (observed 2026-08-07, PR #7638).

WHAT HAPPENED: a worker ran 'python scripts/check_provenance_pins.py --changed-since origin/main' and got exit 0 with NO OUTPUT AT ALL. That is exactly what the gate prints when it selects your page and finds nothing wrong — and also exactly what it would print if it selected NO pages, or skipped yours. The worker re-ran with --verbose specifically so the claim 'it stayed green on that page' was evidence rather than inference. The verbose run showed '1 files, 5 cited pins' — proving the page was actually examined.

WHY THIS IS THE SAME DEFECT CLASS THE GATE ITSELF POLICES: a fail-open is a check that passes without checking. A silent exit 0 lets a worker report 'the gate is green on my change' when the gate may never have looked at it. check_doc_slugs.py has the same property — silent on success.

THE RULE: for any gate that is silent on success, run it with --verbose (or its equivalent) and QUOTE THE LINE SHOWING IT SELECTED YOUR FILES. 'exit 0' alone is not evidence the gate covered the surface; it is only evidence the gate did not fail. This is the same reasoning as never nominating a gate whose exclusion list omits the tree being edited — mkdocs --strict exits 0 over docs/design/** having verified nothing.

FOR THE MAYOR: when a worker reports a silent gate at exit 0 with no selection evidence, ask which files it selected before treating the surface as covered.

SUPERSEDED IN ITS CONCLUSION — see audit-reopens-are-recorded-as-comments-not-notes. The diagnostic half below is right; the 'so re-closing was correct' half was WRONG and produced a wrong re-close on 2026-08-21.

WHAT IS STILL TRUE. A bd close can revert ALONE, and that is not the whole-database time-travel CLAUDE.md documents. Re-check EVERY close the session made: a reverted .beads export takes the whole batch, so if 7 of 8 held (as here), the JSONL remedy is the wrong diagnosis.

WHAT THE ISOLATED REVERSION ACTUALLY MEANS, and this is the correction: one bead reverting while the batch holds is evidence it was reopened DELIBERATELY, by the merged-PR audit hook. It is not evidence of a lost write. Trace it: git log --format=%H --since=... -- .beads/issues.jsonl, read the bead out of each commit, and the flip attributes to an exact commit — here chore(beads): audit PR #8619, which dropped close_reason and closed_at.

AND THE FINDING LIVES IN A COMMENT, NOT IN NOTES. Grepping notes for AUDIT-REOPEN returned silence while the marker sat in bd comments at 2026-08-21T00:41:23Z. comment_count rising across the reopening commit is itself the proof. Read comments FIRST.

SIXTH FALSE-GREEN VECTOR, and this one is THE HARNESS ITSELF (2026-07-25). A worker's backgrounded gate reported success while the gate had failed: sh scripts/test-fast-pr.sh was backgrounded on timeout, and the task-completion NOTIFICATION said 'exit code 0' while the script itself had printed rc=1 in its log. The worker caught it only by READING THE LOG rather than believing the notification.

So the list of ways a green can lie in this repo is now: (1) piping a gate through tail/grep returns the pipe's status; (2) a compound or backgrounded command's trailing echo supplies a 0 while the log says FAIL; (3) test-fast-pr.sh soft-skips its own mkdocs step when mkdocs is off PATH and still exits 0; (4) a .cljc test namespace missing its lane suffix is silently skipped by one runner; (5) a wrapper-reported 'exit code 0' disagreeing with a captured rc (the v/custom-element slice hit this, and the captured 1 was correct — it is what surfaced a live defect); and now (6) the BACKGROUNDING HARNESS reporting exit code 0 for a run whose log says rc=1.

WHY IT MATTERS BEYOND ONE WORKER: (6) breaks the mitigation for (1)-(3). 'Capture rc immediately and never pipe' is defeated if the layer REPORTING the rc is itself wrong. So the brief line must be stronger than 'capture the exit code': it must be 'cross-check the captured rc against the log's own PASS/FAIL lines, and treat any disagreement as failure until proven otherwise.' I have been writing that in briefs; this is the incident that justifies it, so keep it.

THE UNDERLYING FAILURE was environmental and worth knowing on its own: a FRESH WORKTREE HAS NO implementation/node_modules, so shadow-cljs is not on PATH and the 'CLJS node integration' step dies. Everything before that step was genuinely green. Fix is npm ci inside the worker's OWN worktree — never a junction into the mayor tree, which once deleted the mayor's real node_modules.

Worker gotcha (2026-06-10, bit hiqtk8 #3700): the CI gate 'Verify skill ↔ MCP allowed-tools drift' is a MULTI-script job; one axis is check_skill_implementor_partition_drift.py rule L7 (BEAD-ID-LEAK) = user-facing skill leaves (SKILL.md / README.md / references/*.md under skills/) must carry ZERO 'rf2-' bead ids. A worker that adds an explanatory parenthetical like '(... removed per rf2-XXXXX)' into a skill doc FAILS this gate. FIX: strip the tracker-id, keep the substantive sentence. BRIEF RULE: any worker editing skills/ must NOT cite rf2- bead ids in skill prose.

A NEW :rf.error/* REFUSAL MUST TOUCH spec/009-Instrumentation.md, SO A BLANKET "NEVER TOUCH spec/**" FENCE IS WRONG (2026-08-11, rf2-hic-035 / PR #7876).

WHAT HAPPENED. I fence every dispatch with "HOT ZONE, sequential and never parallel: shadow-cljs.edn, deps.edn, spec/**, .github/workflows/** — STOP and report rather than editing." The rf2-hic-035 worker edited spec/009-Instrumentation.md anyway, flagged it in its PR body, and was RIGHT to. Its reason: check_keyword_catalogue_drift.py CHECK A REDS ANY PR THAT EMITS AN UNCATALOGUED :rf.error/*. So a diff adding a refusal cannot be green without its catalogue row. A blanket fence would forbid every new refusal in the repo.

THE DISTINCTION THE FENCE WAS MISSING. The hot-zone rule exists to stop two workers colliding on one file, and it is right about the files it names. But spec/009 has TWO kinds of edit and they carry completely different collision risk:
  - A CATALOGUE ROW appended for a refusal the same PR introduces. Mechanically forced by a gate, append-only, and unique to that refusal's id — two workers adding different refusals do not collide.
  - A NORMATIVE PROSE change to the instrumentation contract. That is genuine hot-zone work and stays sequential.
The same shape almost certainly applies to docs/design/hicasso/product/complaints.md, which carries the parallel row.

HOW TO FENCE IT INSTEAD. Say: "spec/009-Instrumentation.md — you MAY append the catalogue row your own new refusal requires, because check_keyword_catalogue_drift.py CHECK A reds a PR without it. You may NOT change its normative prose or any row you did not introduce; that is sequential hot-zone work — report it." Same for complaints.md.

TWO WIDER LESSONS, and the second matters more.

FIRST: a fence that forbids what a GATE REQUIRES is not a safe fence, it is an unsatisfiable one. The worker's options were to break the fence or ship a red PR. When a brief and a gate disagree, the brief is wrong — check what the gates demand of the surface before writing the fence.

SECOND, AND IT IS THE REAL FINDING: the bead's own WORKER PROTOCOL did not list spec/** at all; only my dispatch brief did. The worker noticed the discrepancy and told me. That is the bead-governs-over-brief rule working, and it points at a mayor habit worth breaking — pasting a STANDARD fence list into every brief without asking whether this particular bead's work can live inside it. A boilerplate fence reads as careful and is not; it is the same reflex as a boilerplate gate list, and it fails the same way.

THE FAST-PR SPINE'S CLJS TIER REDS IN ANY FRESH WORKTREE THAT HAS NO node_modules — and that is NOT a failure of the change under test (2026-08-15 16:51 AUSEST).

MEASURED on PR #8307 (rf2-hic-060, the hicasso API reference). The worker captured spine EXIT=1 whose SOLE failure was the last step, 'CLJS node integration'. Its diff was markdown, a nav entry and a digest roster — nothing a CLJS build reads. The cause was that its worktree had no node_modules.

WHY THIS IS A TRAP RATHER THAN AN INCONVENIENCE: the two ways to get node_modules into a worktree are not equally safe.
  npm ci --prefix implementation  -- correct, but costs minutes
  a junction to the mayor's real node_modules -- fast, and TWICE followed by a later git worktree remove that emptied the mayor's REAL directory, exit 0, silently
So a doc-only worker is choosing between a slow install it does not need and the single most destructive operation in this repo. #8307's worker correctly declined BOTH and reported the red honestly.

HOW TO READ IT, as the mayor:
  1. A red spine is never waved through on a worker's reassurance. Read the failing STEP.
  2. If the sole failure is the CLJS/node tier AND the diff reaches no CLJS surface, the spine result is uninformative rather than adverse — CI decides it, and CI has node_modules.
  3. CONFIRM the classifier agrees: the diff's own surface flags say whether the CLJS lane is required. #8307 reported cljs_node_test=true, so CI would run it for real.
  4. Then judge on the PR's CI rollup, not on the local spine.

WHAT NOT TO CONCLUDE: this does not make a red spine acceptable in general. A red spine on a code change is a red change. The discrimination is entirely 'does the failing tier read anything the diff touched'.

BRIEFING CORRECTION THAT FOLLOWS: telling a doc-only worker 'the spine is proportionate, run it' sets up exactly this. For a markdown/nav/roster diff, name the doc gates and say the spine's CLJS tier will red without node_modules, so it should either run npm ci deliberately or skip the spine with that reason stated. Do not leave the worker to discover it and then have to defend a red.

MEASURED SPINE DURATION, while correcting the record: 29m47s captured by worker/epochroster-t7qh8 under contention, against a harness ceiling of 10 minutes. My briefs have said '~25 minutes'. The decision it feeds — detach and poll within the turn — is unchanged at either figure, so the number is decoration on a true statement; state the FACT (the spine exceeds the ceiling; detach it) rather than the constant.

A SPINE FAILURE NAMING NAMESPACES YOUR DIFF CANNOT REACH IS PROBABLY JUNCTION CONTENTION, NOT YOUR CHANGE (2026-08-14).

WHAT WAS SEEN. A worker's fast-PR spine reported FAIL CLJS node integration — a shadow-cljs par-compile abort naming re-frame.schemas.* fixtures, with NO underlying error printed. Its diff could not reach implementation/schemas. test:cljs ran green directly both before and after, with identical counts. No stale shadow-cljs server pid in its worktree.

THE LIKELIEST CAUSE: contention on the implementation/node_modules JUNCTION that worker worktrees link at the mayor checkout's real directory. Several workers compiling at once through one physical node_modules can abort a par-compile with no diagnostic.

THE DISCRIMINATOR, and it is cheap: (a) can the diff reach the named namespaces at all? (b) does the focused suite for those namespaces pass directly, before and after, at identical counts? (c) is there a stale server pid in the worktree? If the answers are no, yes and no, it is contention rather than a defect.

WHY THIS MATTERS FOR THE MAYOR. A worker that reads such a failure as its own will chase a phantom, or worse, weaken something to make it green. Brief workers that a par-compile abort with no printed error and namespaces outside their diff is a KNOWN environment mode: re-run it, and if it clears, say so and move on. Do not let it become a fix.

AND IT SCALES WITH FLEET SIZE. Six concurrent workers all junctioned at one node_modules is the condition. Expect more of this at saturation, not less. If it becomes frequent, the repair is per-worktree node_modules rather than a junction — but that costs disk and setup time on every dispatch, so it is a trade rather than an obvious win.

THE FAST-PR SPINE'S 'CLJS node integration' FAILURE IN A FRESH WORKTREE IS CONDITIONAL ON THE CLASSIFIER, NOT AUTOMATIC (established 2026-08-17).

THE CLAIM I HAD BEEN PUTTING IN BRIEFS: 'expect scripts/test-fast-pr.sh to exit 1 in a fresh worktree with no implementation/node_modules, on the CLJS node integration lane failing to resolve shadow-cljs'. Three workers hit exactly that and reported it, so the claim looked settled.

IT IS NOT GENERAL. rf2-r70kn's worker (PR #8432) ran the same spine on a documentation-only diff and it exited 0. Its log line 3 reads: 'fast PR spine: docs=true jvm=false node=false (classified)'. The classifier gated the node lane out before anything could need shadow-cljs. So the failure depends on whether the DIFF classifies node=true, not on whether node_modules is present.

WHY IT MATTERS RATHER THAN BEING TRIVIA: a brief that predicts a red teaches the worker to expect one and discount it. A worker that then gets a red for a REAL reason has been pre-supplied with an innocent explanation for it. That is the same fail-open shape as a gate nominated over an excluded path — except the brief is the thing doing it.

FOR THE NEXT BRIEF: say 'if your diff classifies node=true the spine's CLJS node integration lane needs implementation/node_modules; a fresh worktree has none. Read the classifier line the spine prints and report it alongside the exit code.' Never assert the red unconditionally. And keep the standing advice not to junction into the mayor's node_modules to green an irrelevant lane — that hazard is unchanged and has emptied the real tree twice.

`test:script-policy` AND `test:script-helpers` ARE ONE GATE IN TWO HALVES, AND RUNNING ONLY ONE IS HOW A REAL DEFECT REACHED CI (2026-08-11, rf2-hic-016 / PR #7896).

WHAT HAPPENED. The scripted-IME-witness PR went red on `JS harness self-tests (quiet reporters + path policy)`. The job HAD run the harness in full — this was not an install failure — and the assertion was genuine:

  FAIL every navigation passes an EXPLICIT timeout — none inherits Playwright's 30s default
       (rf2-dczpv, rf2-bhjzn, rf2-taj9b)
  + [ "implementation/hicasso/testbed/spec.cjs: .goto(`${base}?arm-ms=${ARM_MS}`, { waitUntil: 'commit' })" ]
  at implementation/scripts/_navigation-ceiling-policy.test.cjs:253

The armed-edges repair had added the repo's ONLY `.goto` in any `spec.cjs`, with no `timeout:`. `_navigation-ceiling-policy.test.cjs` sweeps every first-party `.cjs`/`.mjs` and requires each navigation to name its own ceiling, because a bare one inherits Playwright's anonymous 30-second default.

THE MECHANISM WORTH REMEMBERING. CI's step and `scripts/test-fast-pr.sh:1355` both run `npm run test:script-policy && npm run test:script-helpers`. The original worker ran ONLY `test:script-helpers` — the half where it had wired its own self-test — and the offended suite lives in the OTHER half. So its local green was real and irrelevant.

**THE SPINE DOES DECIDE THIS GATE.** `check_fast_pr_gap.py --list` does NOT name the JS-harness gate among the 96 checks the spine leaves undecided. A full spine run would have caught it. This was not a spine-gap; it was a worker running a subset of the spine.

WHAT TO PUT IN A BRIEF touching `implementation/scripts/**`, any `spec.cjs`, or any first-party `.cjs`/`.mjs`:
  Run BOTH halves as CI does, from `implementation/`: `npm run test:script-policy && npm run test:script-helpers`. Running only the half you added a test to is not running the gate. And if you add a `.goto` anywhere, it must name its own `timeout:` — a missing ceiling must REFUSE rather than default, because `timeout: undefined` silently reinstates the 30s default (the choice `examples/scripts/spec-helpers.cjs` already makes).

THE WIDER RULE, and this is the third instance this week: a gate named for one thing ("quiet reporters + path policy") can own assertions about something else entirely. Neither of the mayor's two guesses at the cause was right. Read the job log and let it name the assertion — never infer the failing rule from the gate's title or from the diff.

THE SPINE SKIPS EVERYTHING WHEN THERE IS NO DIFF, so a POST-MERGE verification run proves nothing unless you pass --all (2026-08-05).

THE MECHANISM: scripts/test-fast-pr.sh classifies surfaces from the diff against origin/main. In a checkout whose commits are ALREADY MERGED, there is no diff, so it self-classifies docs=false jvm=false node=false and exits 0 having run nothing of consequence. The rf2-l0wfx worker hit this while re-verifying after I merged its PR out from under it: the plain spine went green while skipping the docs lane its EP-0038 edit needed. It re-ran with --all and got a real result.

WHY THIS MATTERS BEYOND ONE WORKER: I have twice merged a PR while its worker was still verifying. The natural recovery - "re-run the gates against merged main" - is exactly the case where the plain spine is vacuous. So the recovery from my mistake has its own fail-open, and a worker following it would report PASS having tested nothing.

THE RULE: any verification run in a checkout with no diff against origin/main MUST use --all. If a report says "re-ran the spine against merged main, exit 0", ask whether it was --all; a bare pass there is the same shape as the tools/template lane skipped on main, and as check_doc_slugs.py exiting 0 over TESTING.md which it never opens.

ALSO WORTH KNOWING, from the same run: the --all log contains a FAIL token that is a self-test DESCRIPTION string - "a single standalone failure is flagged as the red namespace (FAIL path)". Grepping the log for FAIL finds it. Read the runner's own terminal marker, not a grep.

Staging explicit paths does NOT keep .beads out of a worker commit. bd auto-stages .beads/issues.jsonl on any command that touches the tracker -- including read-only 'bd show' at the start of a task. So a later 'git add <explicit docs paths> && git commit' commits the ALREADY-STAGED .beads path too, silently: CLAUDE.md's 'stage explicit paths instead of git add -A' is necessary but NOT sufficient. Hit on rf2-r7nyt (PR 7595): first commit carried .beads/issues.jsonl at 2 insertions / 9 deletions -- tracker time-travel -- despite every git add naming only docs files. DETECT with 'git diff --numstat origin/main..HEAD' (compare COMMITS, not the working tree: plain 'git diff origin/main' also shows the uncommitted bd export and looks the same, so it cannot distinguish). FIX without losing the message: save it ('git log --format=%B -n 1 > msg'), 'git reset --soft origin/main', 'git restore --source=origin/main --staged .beads/issues.jsonl', re-commit -F msg, force-with-lease. Do this BEFORE any bd mutation, and never 'git checkout' .beads after a bd close. Worker worktrees have no pre-commit hook protection against this -- the installed hook guards the 90%-shrink floor, not the worker-surface boundary, unless scripts/install-git-hooks.sh has been run in the clone.

Worker worktrees can leave stale JVM processes (live-ssr, shadow-cljs server) holding ports after worktree removal. rf2-rk8gc worker hit this with port 8031 held by orphaned 'java' PID from story-deprecate-rhs worktree (long removed). Worth checking ports 8030/8031/8767/9630 if examples gate fails unexpectedly with a port-binding error.

(1) A sweep that extracts backticked path tokens and tests them against git ls-files MUST run a second pass for RELATIVE citations resolved against the citing file's own directory - 'draft-guide/05-forms.md' is not repo-anchored, and an anchored-only sweep silently returned a clean-looking result that missed the bead's own confirmed instances. Always name a file the pattern should match and confirm it does before trusting a zero. (2) rf2-0yp7w both MOVED and RENUMBERED the hicasso guide: draft-guide/05-interop.md is the shipped 09-interop.md, and docs/core/hicasso/05-interop.md does not exist (05 is forms). A naive directory swap would have repointed five citations at the WRONG chapter. Mechanical rule that partitions the corpus generations: a citation is safely repointable iff docs/core/<same-name> exists; ones that fail name an older generation and read as records. (3) The governing pointer-vs-record test in practice: a stale POINTER is present-tense prose whose claim is still TRUE at the new address (repoint it, nothing is falsified); a RECORD sits in a blob table, quotes a ruling VERBATIM, narrates the move in past tense, or counts occurrences (leave it). Backticked prose tokens are invisible to check_doc_slugs.py, so NO gate catches this class.

STALE .shadow-cljs CLASSPATH MIMICS THE shadow.resource UNBOUND-VAR RACE — two different causes, one identical error string (2026-07-23).

THE SYMPTOM, identical in both cases: `unbound fn: #(quote shadow.resource/slurp-resource)`, surfacing as a compile failure (seen in scripts/api-manifest/probe/).

CAUSE A — STALE CLASSPATH (benign, one-time): commit 6328dca436 changed the shadow-cljs :source-path classpath root from spec/conformance to spec/. Any worktree with a WARM .shadow-cljs still holds the old classpath.edn and fails this way after pulling that commit. CURE: delete .shadow-cljs in that worktree and recompile (1811 files, 0 warnings observed). Every warm worktree that pulls that commit needs the one-time clear — expect this across a whole wave of workers, not just one.

CAUSE B — THE REAL RACE (rf2-sff2s, recurring as rf2-drpa3.78): requiring-resolve performs its first resolve BEFORE entering the namespace require lock; shadow/resource.clj ships un-AOT-d so it compiles from source on first use, and shadow-cljs macroexpands in parallel — a thread arriving mid-load gets the interned-but-UNBOUND Var. Cured per-consumer by a namespace-local delay, and process-wide by one shared choke point that enters the serialized require path before resolving.

⚠️ WHY THIS PAIRING IS DANGEROUS: a worker fixing the race can read a stale-classpath failure as its bug reproducing, or conclude its fix failed when it actually worked. And a worker hitting the stale classpath can waste a cycle believing it found a concurrency defect.

THE DISCRIMINATOR: a shadow-cljs COMPILE failure is not reliable evidence of the race in either direction. The race must be evidenced by a CONCURRENCY PROBE in a clean Clojure process — one thread cold-loading shadow.resource, an observer resolving the same Var and reporting its state — which observes the Var directly and does not depend on any build. If clearing .shadow-cljs makes the failure vanish, it was Cause A.

MAYOR RULE: when a wave of workers is running warm worktrees and a source-path or classpath-root change lands on main, expect this error across several of them and say so in briefs; do not let it be diagnosed independently five times.

"STATE THE CONDITION, NOT THE ENUMERATION" EARNED ITS KEEP FOUR TIMES IN ONE DAY — AND THE FOURTH IS THE CLEANEST PROOF (2026-08-06, rf2-lr1rn).

THE CASE. I relayed a filing saying two rows of spec/002s tier table were affected by the new ambient-refusal exception: `override` untouched, `scope` bitten. Both were right. BUT THE SPLIT IS THREE ROWS — `hold` is touched too, because `capture-frame`s NO-ARG form resolves ambiently IN ORDER TO capture, so it refuses inside a refusing extent. (The 1-arity never consults the resolver and still carries; nothing HELD is refused — the refusal reaches the ambient capture that STARTS a hold, not the carrying that follows.)

WHY THIS IS THE CLEANEST PROOF OF THE RULE: 002s Resolver-surface section ALREADY LISTS "no-arg rf/capture-frame" among its ambient-resolving operations. So writing the CONDITION — "resolving a frame ambiently inside a refusing extent" — COVERS THE THIRD ROW FOR FREE, while the two-row ENUMERATION I relayed would have silently excluded it. The condition was not merely more durable; it was more CORRECT ON THE DAY, against a fact neither I nor the filing worker knew.

THE OTHER THREE INSTANCES TODAY, all the same shape — an enumeration under-counting its own class: an audit named 2 occurrences of a claim and there were 3 (the third in a provenance section outside the charge); a bead named 4 call sites of require-frame-provider-target! and there were 9; a pages table listed 4 verdicts against an instrument whose own docstring is headed "## The five verdicts".

AND A RELATED GOING-BEYOND-THE-BRIEF THAT WAS RIGHT: 002s "The error and its ladder" section presented a CLOSED two-way discrimination — absent target vs bad explicit target — into which a refusal fits NEITHER. Fixing only the missing tier would have left 002 telling an implementer to emit :rf.error/no-frame-context for a refused resolution. When you add a third case to a system, CHECK WHETHER SOMETHING NEARBY CLAIMS THE CASES ARE EXHAUSTIVE.

THE REASON IT STAYED SMALL, worth keeping as the test for "does this belong here?": 002s invariant is already "frame identity is carried, not found". A refusing extent is THAT INVARIANT ENFORCED STRICTLY — the refusal deletes the FINDING, never the CARRYING. So it needed a section, not an apparatus. When a new mechanism looks like it needs a home in a normative spec, ask whether it is a NEW law or an existing law applied harder; the second needs far less text.

StoryUI planning context: remember Story has an MCP surface and an associated skill. Future Story UI/spec work should treat human UI, Story MCP, and Story skill as related entry points over the same variant/plan/result/evidence substrate, not separate runtime models.

THE STRANDED SWEEP'S ACTIVITY TEST IS BLIND FOR A WORKTREE YOUNGER THAN ITS OWN WINDOW, AND IT FAILS IN BOTH DIRECTIONS. Measured 2026-08-21.

THE TEST: `find <worktree> -newermt '20 minutes ago' -type f | grep -v '/\.git/' | wc -l`, where near-zero is the strand signature.

WHAT I MEASURED. Four worktrees dispatched roughly 10 minutes earlier read 4945, 4946, 4945 and 4945 touched files — near-identical across four independent workers, which is the tell. Reading the NEWEST FILENAMES, as the loop instructs, settled it: the newest files in every tree were alphabetically-adjacent `docs/design/hicasso/studio/*.md` pages that no worker had any business touching. They are CHECKOUT artefacts. `git worktree add` writes the whole tree, so a window wider than the worktree's age swallows the checkout and returns a large number for a tree where nothing has happened.

IT FAILS OPEN: a genuinely dead worker in a fresh worktree reads thousands of touched files and looks alive.

NARROWING THE WINDOW DOES NOT FIX IT — it just moves the failure. The same four read 1 file at 3 minutes, which is the strand signature, while one of that same cohort reported DONE with a merged-quality PR minutes later. A worker that is READING touches nothing, which is `mayor-hygiene.md`'s write-clock problem: the metric observes writes, and reading is most of the early work.

SO FOR A WORKTREE YOUNGER THAN ABOUT 20 MINUTES, NEITHER READING IS EVIDENCE. Do not report a fresh cohort as swept on this test. What discriminates instead, in order: the harness's own running-agent report, which observes the AGENT rather than its output; a cohort sibling that has already reported done, which is direct evidence the fleet is healthy; and only then SendMessage, which costs a live worker a turn (rf2-y7tu4 measured three such costs in one day).

THE FILENAME READ IS THE LOAD-BEARING HALF, not the count. The loop already says to read the newest filenames and that instruction is what caught this; a count alone would have been believed.

THE STRANDED SWEEP IS STRUCTURALLY BLIND HERE, BECAUSE WORKERS HOLD BEADS THAT ARE STILL MARKED open (2026-08-15 22:14 AUSEST).

WHAT I OBSERVED. `bd list --status in_progress --limit 0` returned NOTHING — zero in-progress beads — at a moment when worker/retire-final was demonstrably alive: 80 files touched in 15 minutes and a fresh JVM gate started 3 seconds before I looked. That worker holds rf2-0yp7w.4, rf2-0yp7w.6 and rf2-0yp7w.10, and ALL THREE READ open.

SO THE SWEEP'S PRIMARY INPUT IS EMPTY BY CONSTRUCTION, NOT BY HEALTH. The loop is written as "look for in-progress beads; if no live worker holds one, it may be stranded". Here the set is empty whether or not anything is stranded, so the loop cannot fire in either direction. A clean sweep means nothing when nothing is ever in the set.

*** THIS RE-READS A STATISTIC IN THE HANDOFF. *** It records "In progress: 0 — 15 CONSECUTIVE CLEAN STRANDED SWEEPS" as evidence of health. Some or all of that streak may be this blindness rather than an absence of strands: 15 consecutive reads of an empty set. Do not quote that streak as assurance.

WHY IT MATTERS CONCRETELY. If retire-final dies mid-gate, the sweep finds no in-progress bead to recover. Its 3 beads sit open, look dispatchable, and the NEXT DISPATCH TICK IS FREE TO SEND A SECOND WORKER AT THEM — which is the two-workers-on-one-branch failure the method spends a section forbidding. The blindness converts a strand into a collision.

THE INSTRUMENT THAT DOES WORK, and it is the one this session has been using all along: the worktree activity sweep. Count non-node_modules, non-.git files touched in each worker worktree in the last N minutes and read the NEWEST filenames — .cpcache / .scratch / implementation/out mean a gate is running, a tracked source or doc file means the worker is editing, near-zero means a strand. Cross-check with a process listing filtered to recent start times. That test is keyed to the WORKTREE, which is where the truth is, rather than to a bead field nobody is setting.

TWO POSSIBLE FIXES, neither taken yet because it is the operator's call which:
  (a) dispatches set `bd update <id> --claim` (or --status in_progress) as part of the brief, so the field carries the fact; or
  (b) the sweep stops reading the field and reads worktrees, and mayor-posture.md is rewritten to say so.
(b) is the smaller change and matches what actually works. (a) is more honest to the tracker but relies on every future brief remembering, which is the kind of rule that decays.

UNTIL THEN: never report "0 in progress, sweep clean" as a health signal without the worktree sweep beside it. The first number is not evidence.

A SUBSTRATE FIX APPLIED IN ONE CONSUMER MUST BE SWEPT ACROSS EVERY CONSUMER OF THAT SUBSTRATE — rf2-8cnxg shipped in the observation port and was hit again, unfixed, in arm1's runtime (found 2026-08-07).

THE SHAPE. re-frame's observation port learned that a Reagent-hosted subscription must be ACTIVATED before it is watched — observation.cljc:1959-1982, 'ACTIVATE, then watch, then observe — and the order is the whole fix for rf2-8cnxg ... every ViewCell over a Reagent-hosted subscription rendered ONCE and never again.' Months later, arm1's Hicasso runtime attached to the same substrate with subscribe -> deref -> add-watch and NO activation, and reproduced the identical symptom. Nothing connected the two: the fix lived in the port, the bug lived in a second consumer, and no gate spanned both.

WHY IT HID SO LONG. The candidate's own bench segment installs the UIx adapter, every p0-heap row is mount-hold-release with no write, and the write-driving arms were floor/reagent/uix only. The defect needed a WRITE driven at that arm with the RATOM adapter installed — a combination the programme had never run until an allocation row demanded it. A defect that requires an untried combination of axes is invisible to every suite that varies one axis at a time.

THE RULE. When a substrate-level fix lands, grep for every OTHER site performing the same attachment sequence and check each. Under the ratom family a subscription is a bare reagent.ratom/Reaction built WITHOUT :auto-run, and a Reaction learns its sources only through deref-capture — so a plain deref outside *ratom-context* leaves 'watching' nil and the node is in nobody's watcher set. Any code that does subscribe -> deref -> add-watch without activate-derived-value! has this bug, silently, and looks like it works because it paints correctly at mount.

THE TELL, for diagnosis: stale by EVERY write since mount, not stale by one. A drain/flush fault reads stale-by-1 invariably; a never-activated reaction is deaf from birth. That arithmetic separated the two hypotheses here without running anything.

SUSTAINED API 529 OUTAGE — THE MAYOR PLAYBOOK, learned 2026-07-26 when six workers were killed inside about twenty minutes.

WHAT IT LOOKS LIKE: task-notifications with status=failed and "API Error: 529 Overloaded", each carrying the worker last sentence — which is usually mid-diagnosis and genuinely valuable. Not stopped for cause, nothing wrong with the work.

THE MISTAKE I MADE FIRST: resuming them. SendMessage-resume during a live outage burns a worker turn and dies on contact — I resumed three and all three died again immediately, one of them twice. Resuming is correct AFTER the window, useless during it. The tell that you are still inside the window is a resumed agent failing within a minute with the same 529.

THE CORRECT POSTURE, in priority order:
1. STOP RESUMING. Each attempt costs a turn and returns nothing. The cron loop will retry; let it.
2. DO NOT DISPATCH NEW WORK. A bigger in-flight bubble is a proportionally bigger crash surface, and every new worker is another thing to recover.
3. SWITCH TO DURABILITY. Sweep every worktree: for each, compare local HEAD against git ls-remote for its branch, and count uncommitted files excluding .beads. Classify pushed / UNPUSHED / NO-REMOTE. Pushed commits survive anything; uncommitted files survive only as long as nobody reaps the worktree.
4. PROTECT THE AT-RISK ONE ON ITS BEAD. The mayor must NOT commit another worker uncommitted WIP (only that worker knows whether it forms a coherent change). But the mayor DOES control reaping — so the mitigation is to record on the bead that the worktree holds N uncommitted files, name the path and branch, and mark it EXEMPT from the hygiene loop zero-commit/clean/no-PR reap rule. That converts an invisible risk into a written one.
5. Message the still-live workers to commit and push immediately, WITH the reason — a live worker can still act even while resumes of dead ones fail.

FRESHNESS-CHECK TRAP HIT DURING THE SAME PASS, worth its own line: a find over a worktree for recently-touched files reports .beads/* churn, because bd re-exports into EVERY worktree from any worktree. Exclude .beads, .git, node_modules, .shadow-cljs and .cpcache or a cold worktree reads as warm. And even then, a count of ~4500 touched files is an npm ci or an mkdocs build, not liveness — the file COUNT is a proxy for a recent build, not for a running agent. The only reliable liveness signal remains the SendMessage response shape ("queued for delivery" = alive; "had no active task, resumed from transcript" = was idle).

AND THE THING THAT MADE THIS SURVIVABLE: push-as-you-go was already in every brief. Four of seven workers had their commits on origin and lost nothing. The one that was genuinely at risk was the one that had not committed yet. That single instruction is worth more than the entire recovery procedure.

THE EVIDENCE. The claim "the repair arrives a macrotask later" was corrected FOUR times across THREE PRs, and each correction was found by the NEXT merged-PR audit rather than by the repair before it:

  3. implementation/hicasso/test/.../reincarnation_seams_cljs_test.cljs:39-40 — a test docstring.
Every individual repair was bounded and correct. The PROCESS was wrong: three round-trips of mayor, worker and CI for what one `git grep` would have closed.

THE PRACTICE: when a bead corrects a stale factual claim, the brief says SWEEP EVERY CARRIER. `git grep` the exact wording over TRACKED files, read every hit, dispose of each in the one PR, and list in the PR body what was changed and what was left correct. "Bounded repair" should bound the CHANGE, not the SEARCH.

TWO CAUTIONS THAT MAKE THE SWEEP HARDER THAN IT LOOKS, both earned here:
  - THE PHRASE IS OFTEN CORRECT ELSEWHERE. invariants.md L150's timer-callback row says "one macrotask later" and is RIGHT, because a timer callback is a macrotask. The React-controlled deferral under rf2-hic-014 is also correctly a macrotask, and its repair is unreachable by this one. `git grep "macrotask later"` also hits core/substrate/spine.cljs, the react_shared_suite and two arm1 bench tests. Reading every hit is the work; the grep is only the index.
  - NAME THE DISCRIMINATOR IN THE BRIEF, or the worker cannot tell the stale hits from the correct ones. Here it is WHO SCHEDULES THE DEFERRAL: the runtime's own collector (repaired to a microtask) versus React or a timer (still a macrotask). Without that sentence a sweep either under-corrects or breaks correct prose.

THIS IS THE SAME DEFECT CLASS AS THE CENSUS'S THIRD SPECIES — text that matches the search and is not about the subject — and as the "confident sentence outliving its behaviour" shape the Checkpoint 1 review named. All three are one thing: a claim and its carriers drift apart, and only an exhaustive read reunites them.

A SWEEP'S GENERATOR DEFINES WHICH FAILURE DIRECTIONS IT CAN EVER FIND (2026-08-11, rf2-skpf worker, PR #7811).

THE CASE. PR #7803 swept 1,728 quoted-fence prefix triples against the real MkDocs renderer to characterise a docs-gate defect, and its numbers held up. But EVERY shape that generator emits has BALANCED backtick runs on lines 1 and 3. So the inline-masking defect could only ever manifest there as pairing that should not happen — a FALSE POSITIVE. The false-negative half needs an ODD backtick-run count either side of a boundary, a shape the fence-triple generator CANNOT EMIT BY CONSTRUCTION.

Result: in that domain the defect was 188/188 false positives and its expensive half was invisible. Not because 1,728 was too few — because the generator excluded the direction. Running 17,280 would have found nothing more.

THE LESSON, in the worker's words: 'a sweep generator defines its reachable failure directions, and the direction it excludes is invisible no matter how many shapes you run.' A sweep's SIZE is not its coverage; its GENERATOR is. So a big clean sweep is not evidence of absence outside the directions its generator can express — and the false-negative direction is usually the expensive one, because it is the one where a checker stays silent.

THE COUNTERMEASURE THAT WORKED: two probes over the same boundary, each mapping the disagreement onto the OPPOSITE error direction (a mask probe and a wrap probe over the same middle line), so neither direction can hide. When commissioning or reading a sweep, ask: what shapes can this generator NOT produce, and which error direction does that make unreachable? Put the answer in the report.

MAYOR APPLICATION: when a worker reports 'N shapes swept, zero disagreements', that is a claim about the generator, not about the surface. Ask for the generator's excluded shapes before treating it as clearance.

AFTER A CONTEXT CLEAR, PRIOR-SESSION AGENTS STAY ALIVE BUT GO INVISIBLE TO TaskList — AND I USED TaskList AS THE LIVENESS SOURCE (2026-08-10).

WHAT I DID WRONG. Recovering from a /clear, the handoff said the rf2-vsgq worker on worker/hmrbrowser-vsgq was "live and resumed". I called TaskList; it returned "No tasks found". I trusted the tool over the handoff, concluded the agent was dead, and dispatched a fresh fix-worker into that SAME worktree on that SAME branch. Two executors then ran on one branch — the exact thing "no concurrent workers same branch" forbids.

HOW IT SURFACED. Not from any check of mine. The original agent's own completion report flagged it: "A commit I did not author appeared on my branch at 15:50 — 13e9750dc9 ... it may be a second executor in this worktree." It was mine.

NO HARM, BUT ONLY BY LUCK. Both agents happened to fix different halves of the same red gate (one renamespaced the :dev-http build id, the other added the README build->port row), the commits did not conflict, and PR #7768 merged green. Nothing about that outcome was guaranteed.

THE ROOT CAUSE IS A TOOL BOUNDARY, NOT A JUDGEMENT CALL. TaskList reports the CURRENT session's task registry. A /clear starts a new registry. Agents spawned before the clear keep running and keep pushing commits, but they are absent from it. An empty TaskList after a clear therefore means "this session has spawned nothing yet", NEVER "no workers are running". It also returned empty immediately after I spawned six agents, so it is not a reliable liveness source in this harness at all.

WHAT TO USE INSTEAD, in order:
  1. The worktree list under the re-frame2-worktrees sibling — a live worker owns a worktree, and a finished one removes its own.
  2. Whether the branch's commit count has MOVED since the last tick. bootstrap.md already names this as the cheap reliable discriminator; a moved count says alive. A still count says nothing and never authorises a reap.
  3. Whether SendMessage finds a live task to deliver to.

A HANDOFF DOCUMENT OUTRANKS AN EMPTY TaskList. The handoff was written by the session that spawned those agents and it was right; the tool was answering a narrower question than the one I asked it.

AND THE SAFE MOVE WAS AVAILABLE AND CHEAP: SendMessage to resume the existing worker keeps its full context and cannot create a second executor. Never re-dispatch a fresh worker over one that may still be live — resume it.

TENTH FALSE-GREEN VARIANT: report-changed-surfaces.sh TAKES PATHS, NOT REFS, AND SILENTLY REPORTS NOTHING CHANGED (2026-07-26, hit by the scaffold-floor worker on itself).

Invoking scripts/.../report-changed-surfaces.sh origin/main treats "origin/main" as a literal FILE PATH. No such path changed, so it prints every surface false and exits successfully — i.e. "your diff touches nothing, no gate needs to run." Re-run on the real changed paths, it correctly armed examples_compile=true. There is no error, no usage message, and no hint that the argument was misread.

WHY IT MATTERS BEYOND ONE INVOCATION: this is the classifier that decides which CI jobs arm. A caller who passes a ref gets a confident all-false answer, which is exactly the answer that means "skip everything". It is the same failure direction as check-beads-pr-boundary.sh exiting 0 with no base ref — a gate-adjacent script that cannot understand its input and reports the benign case rather than refusing.

DIRECTLY RELEVANT RIGHT NOW: the ci-arming worker is editing this very script to add JVM arms for tools/machines-viz and tools/testbed-support. It must pass real paths when testing its own arms, or it will see all-false and conclude its arm does not work — or worse, conclude the arm works when it has not exercised it.

GENERAL RULE, now with two instances: a script in the gate path that accepts an argument should refuse an argument it cannot interpret, not fall through to the empty result. When touching either of these, prefer making the misuse loud over documenting the correct usage.

THE BASH TOOL SILENTLY STRIPS BACKSLASHES FROM HEREDOC STRINGS ON THIS WINDOWS SETUP (2026-07-26).

Found by the checker-residuals worker while probing a char-literal guard: a heredoc probe string lost its backslashes, so the probe read as a FALSE NEGATIVE — the guard looked broken when the input had been mangled before it arrived. It rewrote every probe as a FILE under its own worktree and the results reversed.

THIS IS THE SAME FAMILY AS THE KNOWN git worktree add BACKSLASH STRIPPING, which is already recorded, but the surface is different and more insidious: a worktree path failing is loud, whereas a mangled PROBE STRING silently changes what you are testing. Any probe involving backslashes, char literals, regex escapes or line continuations must be written to a FILE, not passed through a heredoc.

AND IT COST A REAL VERDICT IN THE SAME SESSION, in a second form: that worker plant C did not apply because of a LINE-CONTINUATION BACKSLASH in the anchor, and the self-test returned rc=0 — INDISTINGUISHABLE FROM A GATE THAT MISSED THE DEFECT. Only the mandated "confirm the diff applied before reading the verdict" protocol caught it. That is the twelfth false-signal class firing in the wild and being caught by the exact rule written for it.

SO THE RULE COMPOUNDS: for any mutation or probe whose payload contains a backslash, (1) write it to a file rather than a heredoc, and (2) confirm it applied by git diff --stat AND by grepping the token back out. Either check alone would have missed one of the two failures above.

A THIRD FINDING FROM THE SAME WORKER, unrelated but worth the same memory: a PRIME-SUFFIXED SYMBOL (db-prime, tags-prime) reads as a QUOTE to the bijection walker regex — 352 occurrences in the tree, the same class the existing backslash-quote lookbehind was written for, and a FALSE-GREEN direction. Latent rather than live because all 352 sit inside binding vectors the walk cannot reach. Closed with one lookbehind. The lesson: when a regex already has a lookbehind for one lookalike, ASK WHAT ELSE LOOKS LIKE THAT — the second instance is usually already in the tree.

The core JVM suite (implementation/core clojure -M:test) runs ~10min under concurrent worker/mayor JVM load — right at the 600s foreground tool limit. This is the ROOT of the 'workers strand on backgrounded gates' pattern: a worker can't reliably foreground it when the machine is contended, so it backgrounds the gate + ends its turn with work uncommitted + no PR. THE CROSS-BASE CHECK: TWO PRs EACH GREEN AGAINST A BASE LACKING THE OTHER CAN STILL BREAK IN COMBINATION (2026-07-26).

A worker did this unprompted and it is the practice I most want to adopt. Its work and PR #7081 were EACH GREEN against a base that did not contain the other. Rather than assume the combination was fine, it built a THROWAWAY WORKTREE AT origin/main WITH BOTH MERGED and ran the suite: freehand JVM 1156/7707, 0F 0E. Then removed the worktree.

WHY THIS MATTERS AT SATURATION: I run up to six workers, each rebasing onto a moving main, and I merge on green. Every green I act on was measured against a base THAT NO LONGER EXISTS by the time I merge. Nineteen PRs today merged a state older than the worker tip; several pairs touched adjacent surfaces. THE MERGE LOOP HAS NO CROSS-BASE SIGNAL AT ALL — CI re-runs on the merge commit, but I do not wait for it.

WHEN TO REQUIRE IT: when two live PRs touch the SAME artefact or adjacent seams — for example one editing implementation/freehand/src and another editing implementation/freehand/test, or two both moving spec/009 rows. It is cheap: one throwaway worktree at origin/main, both branches merged, the ONE suite that spans both surfaces. Not the whole spine.

WHEN NOT TO: disjoint surfaces. Most of the time the fence system already guarantees it, and this would be ceremony.
