THE MERGED-PR AUDIT CAN DESTRUCTIVELY OVERWRITE A BEAD'S ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA (2026-07-25, found by EP-0037 review gate 2). This is a process defect in a process I do not control, and it silently destroys the only record of what a slice promised.

WHAT HAPPENED: R1's and R2's slice acceptance criteria were REWRITTEN — both the title AND the description — into the audit's follow-through text. PRs #6875/#6877 name rf2-kqxe6.5/.6 as the slice owners; their original criteria no longer exist anywhere. By contrast the audits of .3 and .7 APPENDED their findings, leaving the criteria intact. That difference is exactly why an independent completeness review could verify .3 and .7 and could NOT verify .5 and .6. Named casualty: the R2 tooling clause ended up with no bead at all.

WHY IT MATTERS BEYOND ONE EPIC: acceptance criteria are the only durable record of what was promised. A merged-PR audit's job is to record what it found, and it is very good at that — it caught a keyword-as-Var false green, a load-order privacy defect, a declared-:on-* classification defect and a census extent bug. But an audit that overwrites the promise it is auditing removes the ability to check completeness later, and the loss is invisible: the bead still reads coherently, just as the audit's narrative rather than as the slice's contract.

MAYOR ACTIONS: (1) treat audit notes as APPEND-ONLY when I write them myself, and say so in briefs — findings go in notes, never over a description; (2) when a bead's description reads as audit narrative rather than as acceptance criteria, suspect this and check git history of .beads for the original; (3) rf2-twpp6 tracks the append-only repair for the two affected beads; (4) when commissioning a completeness review, tell it that a bead whose criteria were overwritten is UNVERIFIABLE and should be reported as such rather than passed — gate 2 worked this out unprompted and it is the reason its verdict is trustworthy.

GENERALISABLE FORM: any automated process that writes into the tracker can destroy the state a later reviewer needs. Prefer append. If a tool overwrites, the tracker's git history is the only recovery path — which is another reason the .beads export must keep being committed on the heartbeat.

THE MID-WRITE RACE ACTUALLY FIRED TODAY AND AN EMPTY EXPORT REACHED main (2026-07-26).

WHAT HAPPENED: commit 4d8042d80d ("chore(beads): audit merged PR #7063") committed .beads/issues.jsonl AT ZERO ROWS. The previous commit d1c49b1164 had 2573. The working tree, the index and HEAD were all empty and git status was CLEAN, so nothing looked wrong — the file simply was not there any more.

THE DATABASE WAS NEVER AT RISK. Dolt is the source of truth; bd list returned every bead normally throughout. Recovery was one command: scripts/beads-checkpoint.sh, which runs bd export and REGENERATES from Dolt rather than trusting the working file, then refuses an empty or badly shrunken result. It committed 2576 rows over a HEAD of 0. That refusal-plus-regenerate design is exactly why the script exists instead of a hand-rolled git add.

THE MECHANISM, now observed rather than theorised: a process ran git add on the export WHILE a bd operation was rewriting it, and snapshotted the zero-length intermediate. I hit the same window myself twenty minutes earlier — read the export as 0 rows with bd.exe alive — and did NOT commit, which is the only reason my own pass was clean. The audit process hit it and did commit.

TWO RULES THAT FOLLOW, and the first is cheap enough to be unconditional:
  1. GUARD EVERY CHECKPOINT ON A ROW COUNT. Never commit the export without asserting it is above a floor (2000+ here). The checkpoint script already does this; anything else that touches the file must too.
  2. AN EMPTY EXPORT IS NOT A DATA LOSS EVENT — IT IS A REGENERATION EVENT. Do not panic-restore from git history: git checkout of an older export would TIME-TRAVEL THE TRACKER, reopening closed beads and vanishing new ones. Always regenerate from Dolt.

AND A DETECTION NOTE: I nearly reported "0 open beads" as a real number. The tell was that it disagreed with the previous pass by 49. WHEN A COUNT MOVES TO ZERO, SUSPECT THE INSTRUMENT BEFORE THE WORLD — that is the tenth measurement error of this class I have caught today, and the only one that would have been consequential.

THE REOPEN TAXONOMY HAS A THIRD CLASS, AND I MISSED IT TWICE (2026-07-26).

I recorded two classes: (A) WEAK-CLOSE reopens, where the close said the job was ARMED rather than CATCHING and the audit had nothing to verify against — mine to prevent; and (B) NEW-RESIDUAL reopens, where a fully-evidenced close was accepted and the audit found something ELSE in the merged code — the audit working as designed.

THE REOPENS WORKER FOUND A THIRD, and it is distinct from both: (C) THE CLOSE ITSELF INTRODUCED THE DEFECT. rf2-12g5z was reopened against PR #7028 OWN NEW TEXT — spec/Privacy.md claimed "every production error record shipped off-box carries one too", which is false because error_emit.cljc:216 returns nil for three shapes and the emitter conditionally assocs the slot. The audit ACCEPTED the original finding and objected to the prose the fix added. In the worker words: "neither residual missed nor original re-asserted".

WHY C MATTERS SEPARATELY: A is a discipline failure I can fix by writing better close reasons. B is discovery I cannot reduce. C IS A REVIEW GAP — the fix was right and its accompanying claim was wrong, which no amount of close-reason rigour catches, because the close reason is describing a fix that IS correct. The remedy is different again: when a fix adds NEW PROSE asserting a general property, that prose needs the same evidence standard as the code. A sentence like "every production record carries X" is a UNIVERSAL CLAIM and should be checked against the conditional that emits X.

AND A FOURTH BUCKET THAT IS NOT A REOPEN AT ALL: rf2-ia904 reads like a reopen of rf2-2z9u3 but was FILED NEW by the #7042 audit. rf2-2z9u3 stays correctly closed. So "the bead is open again" has at least four causes and only one of them is my fault. Before treating an open-looking bead as a reopen, ASK WHICH OF THE FOUR IT IS — the worker did this per bead and it changed what each one owed.

PRACTICAL CONSEQUENCE FOR THE BACKLOG NUMBER: I have been reporting roughly one reopen per merged PR as partly my defect. The honest split is now: A is mine, B and D are the system working, and C is a review gap that belongs to whoever wrote the accompanying prose. Only A responds to better closing.

The skill↔MCP drift gate has TWO distinct failure modes — do NOT assume flake (learned 2026-07-18, rf2-92dlh). (1) The TRANSIENT flake: 'Verify skill ↔ MCP allowed-tools drift' fails under concurrent-PR load; structurally impossible when the diff has 0 skills/MCP files → --admin-justifiable. (2) A REAL main-red drift: when a PR adds/changes MCP server tools WITHOUT reconciling the consumer skills' allowed-tools + the retro drift-set, check_skill_mcp_drift.py --ci reports real findings and the gate is RED ON MAIN — every subsequent PR inherits that red. I conflated the two: rf2-vxgfnd.95.8 added 5 re-frame2-pair MCP tools (explain-render/read-view-*) without updating skills/re-frame2-pair/SKILL.md allowed-tools + scripts/check_skill_mcp_drift.py's re-frame2-pair-retro intentional_server_only set, so main's drift gate went REAL-red — and I kept --admin-ing PRs past it as 'the flake' for many merges until .95.10's spine run surfaced it (rf2-92dlh). FIX GOING FORWARD: when the drift gate is red, VERIFY main's own drift state — run/check  (or check main's gate run). If it exits non-zero (real findings), it is NOT a flake — file/dispatch a fix (allow-list the new tools in SKILL.md + the retro drift-set) instead of --admin-ing PRs past it. Only --admin when main's drift gate is GREEN and the PR's red is the load flake (0 skills/MCP diff).

THE SPEC 009 CO-EDIT INVARIANT HAS A THIRD ARM: the core JVM error-catalogue conformance test exercise literal. A new ALWAYS-ON :rf.error/* id needs THREE co-edits in the same PR, not two: (1) the spec/009-Instrumentation.md catalogue row; (2) the Spec-Schemas.md row; (3) an entry in implementation/core/test/re_frame/error_catalogue_channel_conformance_test.clj exercise literal (~line 590) AND something that actually exercises/emits it (a register-error-listener! drive or equivalent). The test asserts parsed-always-on-set-equals-the-exercise-literal — a catalogue always-on row with no matching literal entry fails with only-in-catalogue: (:the-new-id).
DISCOVERED 2026-07-19 when #6440 (rf2-vxgfnd.143 custom-element conflict law) added :rf.error/custom-element-conflict always-on and its JVM core gate went red. The ui-artefact worker ran check_keyword_catalogue_drift.py (Python) + the ui suite, but NOT cd implementation/core && clojure -M:test, so it never saw the conformance failure. ⚠️ AND A CORRECTION TO MY OWN FLAKE HEURISTIC: I diagnosed this as a CI flake because "the diff touches 0 files under implementation/core/ and JVM core is green on main." THAT REASONING IS WRONG for cross-artefact conformance tests. The real touched surface was spec/009-Instrumentation.md (the catalogue), which the PR DID touch; a CORE test parses that shared spec file and compares it to a literal. So "diff has no core SOURCE files" does NOT imply "core gate cannot be affected" — a gate in artefact A can read a shared artefact-agnostic file (spec/009, Spec-Schemas, Conventions) that the diff edited. The flake signature must be: diff cannot affect the failing gate THROUGH ANY PATH INCLUDING SHARED SPEC FILES A GATE PARSES — not merely "no source files of that artefact in the diff." I nearly --admin-merged past a genuine touched-surface gate. The rule holds: a failing touched-surface gate is NEVER an --admin candidate; when unsure whether it is touched, READ THE FAILURE (it named the test, the file, the exact only-in-catalogue id) before concluding flake.

THE LOAD-BEARING TYPE MUTANT IS THE ONE THAT IS VALID IN A SIBLING CATEGORY (2026-08-06, rf2-am6qs, PR #7605).

Tightening three `:where` slots from `:any` to `:symbol`, the worker mutated four types at each slot — string, number, map, and a BARE KEYWORD. It named the keyword as the load-bearing one, and the reason is the generalisable part: OTHER CATEGORIES IN THE SAME CORPUS GENUINELY CARRY `:where :event`, `:where :flow-eval`, `:where :reactive`. So `:any` was not admitting arbitrary garbage — IT WAS ADMITTING A SPELLING THAT IS CORRECT ONE ROW OVER.

WHY THAT MATTERS FOR HOW YOU CHOOSE MUTANTS: a string/number/map mutant proves the slot rejects nonsense, which nobody was going to write. The keyword mutant proves it rejects THE MISTAKE SOMEONE WILL ACTUALLY MAKE — copying a neighbouring row. When picking negative cases for a schema slot, look for a value that is VALID IN AN ADJACENT DECLARATION and use that; the plainly-absurd mutants are the cheap ones and prove the least.

CONTROL SHAPE WORTH COPYING: each mutant had to be REJECTED by the shipped `:symbol` AND ACCEPTED by an `:any` control rebuilt from that slots OWN shipped schema, with a minimal base so only the `:where` type can be under test. Without the acceptance half you have not shown the TIGHTENING is what did the work rather than something else in the base.

AND THE CENSUS DID NOT TRANSFER, which is why it had to be redone per slot: the brief told the worker not to assume the previous slots answer carried, and the beads own call-site list was INCOMPLETE. Beyond the four sites it named there were five more through `require-frame-provider-target!` — `re-frame.freehand.substrate/frame-provider`, `v/->react`, `re-frame.ui/frame-provider` (twice, once via `require-scope-frame!`) and `re-frame.ui/->react`. A bead enumerating call sites is a starting point, never the population.

RESULT: all three tightened, no `:where` slot in Spec-Schemas.md is `:any` any more, and spec/009 needed NO edit because no row disagreed.

THE THREE-POINT CONTROL'S REFUSAL IS A DENOMINATOR-CLASS FAULT, NOT A ROW-CLASS ONE — diagnosed 2026-08-07 from 42 refused runs across two ensembles (rf2-8a746).

TWO INDEPENDENTLY FATAL HALVES.
(1) THE PREDICTION IS WRONG. 2.0101x is the statistic's expectation only if T is AFFINE in the dirty set over [1,200]. On the published TaskDuration clock it is not: marginal cost is 12.6 us/cell over [1,100] and 6.8 over [100,200]. True centre is 1.55x, which sits 2.6% above the band's own rejection edge of 1.5076 — so half of every run's blocks fall out the bottom ON A PERFECTLY QUIET BOX.
(2) THE STATISTIC IS ILL-CONDITIONED. Differencing away the constant also throws away the PEDESTAL that made relative noise look small, leaving a denominator of 1.25 ms carrying 0.60 ms of dispersion — 2.09 sigma from zero. Even with the centre corrected only ~60% of blocks land in band, and a strict every-one-of-18 rule turns that into P(pass) ~ 1e-4.

THE DECISIVE CONTROL EXPERIMENT: ctl3Layout — the SAME statistic on LayoutDuration over the IDENTICAL blocks and samples — reads 1.9681 / 1.9801 with marginals affine to 5% and no sign-gate firing in 756 blocks. So the arithmetic, door, tare and aggregation are all sound; the PAGE is not affine on the counter the row is published on. The non-layout half carries it: 7.13 -> 1.83 us/cell, a 3.9x collapse.

WHY ctl-2x SURVIVES AND ctl3 DOES NOT — this is the transferable lesson: ctl-2x's denominator is a LEVEL (the floor's whole tared reading, ~4.5 ms) carrying the same ~0.4 ms of estimator error, so 9% relative against ctl3's 48%; and its centre sits 20% above the edge against ctl3's 4%. Distance-above-edge and per-block scatter, raised to the strict-rule exponent, reproduce every pass rate in the programme. A DIFFERENCE-OF-DIFFERENCES DENOMINATOR IS THE FAULT. The invariance argument ('an additive constant cancels in each difference') is true of the LEVEL and is not the problem; what destroys it is the error in each arm's ESTIMATE of that level, which is independent between arms and ADDS. Measured corr(T(1),T(100)) = 0.43, so differencing removes only 40% of the denominator's variance where the argument assumes nearly all.

THE DEGENERATES ARE THE SAME FAULT, NOT A SECOND ONE: den=+0.019 ms -> 86x, den=+0.026 ms -> 114x, and in 9 of the 10 worst blocks T(1) is elevated — it enters BOTH differences, so it drives the smaller one to zero first.

RE-SITING THE POINTS DOES NOT RESCUE IT. Re-adjudicating the same committed blocks at 100/200/300 (above the knee) gives 1.9975 / 2.0777 against a prediction of 2.0000 — the affine premise holds there — but den halves to 0.70 ms while its IQR does not, and in-band blocks FALL from 47% to 33%. Span the knee and the centre is wrong; avoid it and the denominator is gone.

THE ONLY CONSTRUCTION THE EVIDENCE SUPPORTS has a denominator that is a LEVEL rather than a difference. That is a decision about what the lane measures and belongs to the operator.

THE HARNESS DOES NOT SIGNAL A CAPPED TOOL CALL — IT BACKGROUNDS IT, AND THE GATE KEEPS RUNNING (measured 2026-08-07 on rf2-ketqy, PR #7642). CORRECTED: an earlier version of this memory said the harness kills the parent and orphans the child. That model was wrong and the fix built on it would not have worked.

MEASURED, not inferred. Capped at 90s, a backgrounded 'sh scripts/test-fast-pr.sh' kept running after the tool returned — its log grew 41822 to 49220 bytes and two more stages completed. TaskStop behaves identically: reports success, kills nothing, fires no trap. So there is no signal, and a signal handler alone can never see this case.

TWO FURTHER MEASUREMENTS THAT KILL THE OBVIOUS FIXES:
- 'kill the child PROCESS GROUP' would kill the CALLER. Every child shares the caller's PGID under Git Bash.
- bash DEFERS a trapped signal until the foreground child returns — measured at 22 seconds (SIGTERM at t+3s to a script running 'sleep 25'; handler ran at t+25s). So even when a signal IS delivered, a trap is late.
- 'taskkill /F /T' is silently mangled by Git Bash into 'taskkill F:/ ...'. Behind the customary '|| true' it is a NO-OP that looks like it worked. Needs MSYS_NO_PATHCONV=1 and MSYS2_ARG_CONV_EXCL='*'; Cygwin ignores both.

THE DAMAGE the orphan does: it keeps writing to the SAME log as the relaunch (two writers, NUL-riddled output), and its 'npm run test:cljs' unlinks out/node-test.js underneath the next run's per-namespace isolation sweep, which then reds with 'the bundle changed on disk during the sweep' and MODULE_NOT_FOUND. That red is the sweep working correctly and is indistinguishable from an isolation regression in the worker's own diff. The culprit java.exe is invisible to 'ps -ef' entirely.

THE SHIPPED REMEDY (PR #7642): a trap for the genuinely-signalled cases PLUS the same reap invoked at the START of the next run — the only moment it can act, because the path that actually bites delivers no signal. Not a lock: the second run never waits or refuses.

DISCRIMINATORS, unchanged and still the useful part: LAUNCH failure ('Command failed:') = spawn contention. 'changed on disk during the sweep' = a live orphan; kill it and re-run quiet. ASSERTION mismatch = real.

GATE LOGS MUST NOT GO TO /tmp UNDER MULTI-AGENT LOAD — /tmp is SHARED across concurrently running worker agents on this box, so one worker gate log silently OVERWRITES another. Found 2026-07-24 by the rf2-drpa3.112 SSR worker, which nearly shipped a false green.

THE MECHANISM: worker A runs "npm run test:browser > /tmp/gate-browser.log 2>&1". Worker B, running concurrently in a DIFFERENT worktree, writes the same path. A then reads a log that is really B run. In the observed case the log EXIT=0 and reported "0 failures" — every number looked right. The ONLY tell was the shadow-cljs banner naming the WRONG worktree (pilot-react-interop-46 instead of the reader own).

WHY THIS IS NASTY: it defeats the standard exit-code discipline. The capture-to-a-file-and-echo-the-exit-code rule was adopted precisely because piping into tail/grep discards the runner exit status. But if the FILE ITSELF belongs to another agent, the captured exit code is ALSO another agent — a correct technique reading the wrong evidence. Both the summary AND the exit code agree, and both are about someone else run.

THE FIX, now standard in every dispatch brief: write gate logs to the SESSION SCRATCHPAD or a worktree-local path, never a bare /tmp name. e.g.
  <gate> > "$WT/gate-<name>.log" 2>&1; echo "EXIT=$?"; tail -30 "$WT/gate-<name>.log"
And VERIFY OWNERSHIP: the shadow-cljs "config:" banner line names the worktree whose build ran. Grep it and confirm it is YOURS before believing any number in that file. That is the cheap proof.

MAYOR NOTE: my own standing gate-discipline boilerplate said "> /tmp/gate.log". That instruction is now known-unsafe whenever more than one worker runs at a time, which is the normal case at saturation. Update the boilerplate; do not keep handing workers a colliding path.

GENERAL FORM: this joins the roster of ways green has meant nothing-was-measured here. The others are about a check that could not fail; this one is about a check that MEASURED SOMEBODY ELSE. When an assertion rests on an artefact OUTSIDE your process (a shared temp file, a shared port, a shared cache), ask WHO ELSE CAN WRITE IT before trusting what you read.

I CHOSE BETWEEN TWO DUPLICATE PRs ON WHETHER EACH TOUCHED THE FILE A BEAD NAMED. THAT TEST ANSWERED A DIFFERENT QUESTION THAN THE BEAD ASKED, AND I GOT IT BACKWARDS (2026-08-18).

THE TRACKER SILENTLY REVERTS CLOSURES TO OPEN, REPEATEDLY, AND ONLY A PER-TICK AUDIT CATCHES IT (observed twice on 2026-08-07: 2 beads, then 5).

WHAT HAPPENS. Beads closed with a verified reason read OPEN again a few ticks later, with no action of mine in between. First occurrence reverted rf2-2rtt6.56 and rf2-2rtt6.62. Second reverted rf2-kqac1, rf2-drpa3.182.12, rf2-2rtt6.103, rf2-ketqy and rf2-cvvb7 — every one of which had a PR I could verify MERGED at the moment of re-closing.

WHY VERIFYING AT CLOSE TIME IS NOT ENOUGH. I verified each of these CLOSED immediately after closing. They reverted anyway. So the audit has to run EVERY tick against the full list of everything closed this session, not just the recent ones — the second wave included beads closed many ticks earlier.

HOW TO AUDIT SO THE AUDIT ITSELF DOES NOT LIE: key on the STABLE BEAD ID, never an internal row UUID (a re-import regenerates UUIDs and a UUID-keyed diff reports phantom losses), and read the STATUS FIELD rather than grepping the whole record (the word 'open' appears inside titles). 'bd show <id> | head -1 | grep -oE CLOSED|OPEN|DEFERRED' is enough.

WHAT MAKES RE-CLOSING CHEAP: the close REASON is the durable artefact. If it names the PR number and the concrete evidence, re-closing is a thirty-second job of verifying 'gh pr view <n> --json state' still reads MERGED and pasting the reason back. If the original close said only 'done', a revert costs a full re-investigation. Write close reasons for the revert you have not had yet.

THIS IS THE SAME DEFECT CLASS THE PROJECT KEEPS FINDING IN ITS OWN INSTRUMENTS: a state that reports success while the underlying fact has moved. Treat the tracker as untrusted for closure state, exactly as you treat a statusCheckRollup.

TRUE-CONCLUSION-DEAD-REASONING — a documented defect class, seen twice on 2026-07-19 and subtler than plain drift.

DEFINITION: a document states a correct conclusion resting on an inference that has since been invalidated. Nothing looks wrong — the conclusion checks out — so a reviewer confirms the conclusion and moves on. But the NEXT reader follows the stated reason, finds it false, and "corrects" the conclusion in the wrong direction. The rot is in the justification, not the claim.

INSTANCE 1 (rf2-0qsp5, #6386): spec/005-StateMachines.md derived :rf.machine/join-dispatch target protection FROM its REJECT-tier membership. Worker verdict: "The conclusion is true; the inference is precisely what the split invalidated." Preserving the reasoning would have re-merged the two fx policies the next time anyone extended it.

INSTANCE 2 (rf2-vxgfnd.188, #6391, worse): the canonical W1 rule table declared SEVEN verbs unavailable — ui/adapter, local, effect, ui/event, ui/handler, ui/render-fn, ui/dispatch-fn. ALL SEVEN SHIP, exported from ui.cljc. MIG-16/17/18 "this gates" conclusions stayed TRUE, but the reason inverted: from "the verb has not shipped yet" to "the decision belongs to the human". Retiering alone would have let the next reader check whether S3 shipped, find it had, and UNGATE RULES THAT MUST STAY GATED. The worker rewrote the reasons and left the tiers.

HOW TO CATCH IT: when reconciling a document against code, verify the DERIVATION, not just the conclusion. Ask "if the stated reason were false, would the conclusion change?" If yes and the reason IS false, the conclusion is correct by luck and the next edit will break it.
HOW TO FIX IT: rewrite the reason, keep the conclusion. Do NOT retier/restate/delete the conclusion just because its stated basis collapsed.

RELATED, SAME FAMILY: a bead PREDICTION can be wrong too. rf2-vxgfnd.188 own preliminary map predicted six rule retirements; ALL SIX were refuted against shipped code (one, R-X7, had NO DETECTOR AT ALL and became a new rule; R-S3 was missing the cursor WRITE side). A worker trusting the bead analysis would have deleted six live rules. The bead is authoritative about WHAT TO DO, never about WHAT IS TRUE — always re-verify its factual claims against the code.

ALSO: my brief framed 36-vs-34 rules as "one book has two rules the other lacks". Wrong — the books cut the same work at different GRANULARITIES (one by construct area, one by detector), many-to-many both ways, so the deliverable was a crosswalk not a diff. When two artefacts disagree on a COUNT, check whether they share a unit before assuming they disagree on content.

TRUTHFUL-BUT-LATE vs FABRICATED — the discriminator for unfenced async writes. Established by the rf2-2amkm worker (#6410) when it RE-VERIFIED rather than inherited a judgement rf2-6pfpt (#6405) had left.

THE TEST: when a callback settles after its subject is gone, ask whether the value it writes is TRUE-BUT-STALE or FABRICATED-ABOUT-NOTHING.
  - TRUTHFUL-BUT-LATE: runner-events/run-step! emits an unfenced emit-trace! for an abandoned stepper session. The step REALLY RAN and REALLY produced that result; only the timing is wrong. #6410 checked every trace listener under tools/story/src and none consumes :rf.story.play/step. Verdict: LEAVE UNFENCED. Fencing it would mean inventing session identity for a public one-shot executor whose recorded verdict is already fenced caller-side.
  - FABRICATED: the a11y sites. (swap! run-state assoc frame-id :done) over a map the frame was dissoc-d from RESURRECTS the entry — measured 10/10 RED with 19 failures and ZERO ERRORS, so nothing throws. The phantom slot reads :done and the resurrected violations-by-frame entry beside it is exactly what browser/register-a11y-reader! serves to :rf.assert/a11y — A TORN-DOWN FRAME REPORTING A CLEAN VERDICT. Verdict: FENCE IT.
Same defect shape, opposite correct action. Do not blanket-fence every unfenced .then; ask what the write ASSERTS.

MECHANISM REFINEMENT worth copying: #6410 stamped the run token INTO the slot rather than beside it, so "existence and identity are one question with one answer, and every present and future clearing path revokes the claim with no side atom to keep in step". Strictly better than a parallel token map, which a new clearing path can silently fail to update.

⚠️ (inc nil) IS 1 ON CLJS. That is why this class never throws — it silently rebuilds state instead. Never test for it by expecting an exception; assert the slot is ABSENT and the status is the terminal value.

TWO PROSE SOURCES THAT AGREE WITH EACH OTHER ARE NOT EVIDENCE (2026-08-14, rf2-7cuns worker, self-caught).

WHAT IT CAUGHT IN ITS OWN DIFF. It wrote "188 digest-pinned fenced blocks" into a new declaration, having copied the figure from a workflow comment AND a script docstring. Its own words: "two prose sources that agree with each other, which is not evidence." IT THEN RAN THE CHECKER — 188 blocks across 25 pages, 177 Clojure, 34 verb sites — and only then kept the number.

AND THE NEAR-MISS PROVES THE POINT: the same script's docstring says "23 CHAPTERS" where the live run reports 25 PAGES. That tree already carries a stale count. Had it cited that one instead, two agreeing prose sources would have propagated a wrong figure into a third place.

WHY AGREEMENT IS WEAK EVIDENCE HERE: prose figures are COPIED, not derived. Two documents agreeing usually means one was copied from the other, or both from a third — so agreement measures propagation, not truth. THE ONLY EVIDENCE IS RUNNING THE THING.

THE COMPANION FAILURE, from the same evening: a worker's description of ANOTHER worker's diff was wrong, and I relayed it as fact. It reported deletions at specific lines; the PR's author measured its own diff as 20 added, 0 removed, 540 lines away. A WORKER'S ACCOUNT OF A THIRD PARTY'S WORK IS A CLAIM AT TWO REMOVES — weaker than its account of its own, which is already a claim.

THE RULE: never quote a count you did not derive, and never relay one worker's description of another's diff without saying whose reading it is. If it matters, read the diff.

TWO CLJS/CLOJURE TRAPS found by the rf2-ycz3k worker (#6415) WHILE building, not by a gate.

(1) NAMESPACE-CLOBBERING FACADE DEF. Naming a namespace re-frame.ssr.boundary and then exporting (def boundary ...) from the facade compiles to `re_frame.ssr.boundary = re_frame.ssr.boundary.boundary;` — THE ASSIGNMENT DESTROYS THE NAMESPACE OBJECT. Shipping bug, found only because the worker exercised the built artefact. RULE: never let a facade export share its bare name with a namespace segment under the same root. Fix structurally (rename the ns; keep the authoring name) rather than renaming the public verb.

(2) clojure.test HAS NO MAP FIXTURES — and the failure mode is a SILENT GREEN. A map is IFn, so `(use-fixtures :each {:before f :after g})` composes to a function that returns nil WITHOUT RUNNING THE TEST BODY. Output is "Ran 0 tests ... 0 failures", exit 0. The worker caught it ONLY because the suite count did not move off 456. RULE: use a plain fn fixture `(fn [t] (before) (t) (after))`. And this is the concrete reason every brief must demand a NON-ZERO, PLAUSIBLE test count rather than a green exit — "Ran 0 tests" is the single most common false green in this repo, and it has now appeared via (a) a bare `clojure -M:test -n <ns>` from implementation/, (b) a CLJS runner selecting no namespace after a rename, and (c) a map fixture swallowing the whole body.

ALSO FROM #6415, worth copying: it proved its own hydration harness by feeding it KNOWN-BAD HTML first, and a separate non-vacuity assertion then caught its OWN first version rendering an empty client tree and passing. Two independent controls on the harness before trusting any result from it.
AND: reset-failed-boundaries! is now the FIFTH process-global defonce table keyed outside app-db (with request-slots, response-slots, pending-error-traces, installed-payloads). Any test that touches one MUST reset it or it leaks into siblings — #6389 CI failure was exactly that.

DC-09 TWO-CLOCK ENVELOPE, MEASURED (rf2-drpa3.182.12, PR #7179, HeadlessChrome 147, dev build :optimizations :none goog.DEBUG true). Sustained semantic rate ~190/s at 0 dirty siblings, ~49/s at 200. 60 Hz crossing is comfortable to 50 siblings and breaks between 50 and 200; 120 Hz never clears p95 in a dev build; 240 Hz is unreachable because the BROWSER stops offering first, not because the framework refuses.

THREE STRUCTURAL FACTS worth reusing before re-measuring anything on this surface:
1. PEAK BACKLOG IS 1, at every offered rate and both sibling loads, with rf/dispatch (async). The setInterval callback IS the main thread, so overload manifests as OFFER LOSS at the host, never as a growing queue; latency stays bounded at one crossing and the settlement tail stayed <=5.4 ms even at 240 Hz requested against a 20 ms crossing. This is why no throttle/debounce/coalesce verb is warranted — the browser already back-pressures. CAVEAT: measured with a TIMER. Coalesced pointermove / pointerrawupdate bursts can deliver several events to one task and are the only shape that could exceed backlog 1; do not quote this for raw-pointer bursts without re-measuring.
2. THE EVENT HALF IS FLAT, THE COMMIT HALF SCALES. Splitting the window at the instant dispatch-sync returns: :event-ms (router, interceptors, reducer, app-db install, 300 subscription notifications) is 3-4 ms whether 1 or 201 cells moved; :commit-ms goes 0.4 -> 17.5 ms at ~0.085 ms per dirtied cell. An expensive crossing is expensive in React, not in re-frame — attribute before optimising.
3. WHERE YOU READ THE SUB COSTS MORE THAN HOW MUCH CHANGED. Reading a high-rate value in a view that ALSO builds a collection costs a CONSTANT 40-44 ms more than reading it one boundary down — independent of payload size (Vega 96 leaves 45.6->5.0 ms, Spread 900 leaves 63->18.8 ms) — while moving THREE FEWER DOM nodes. Same 'one leaf of app-db changed', 8-19x apart. Guidance: if a high-rate value must cross into app-db, read its subscription at the boundary that USES it.

EQUALITY IS FREE AND FREEHAND ALREADY ELIDES. Fresh-but-rf=-equal is indistinguishable from stable-reference (0.2-0.3 ms at 96 leaves, 0.4-0.6 at 900) and repaints nothing; a full structural walk of a 900-leaf map is under a millisecond. Behavior :update ran exactly 52 times for 52 changed crossings and ZERO times for stable or fresh-equal ones — elision is VALUE-based (rf=), not identity-based. Proved by counting, not by reading the runtime. No equality hook is warranted.

INSTRUMENT NOTES for the next perf bead in a browser:
* A COMPUTED-DURATION POSITIVE CONTROL DOUBLES AS A CONTENTION METER. A busy-wait of exactly 4.00 ms riding in every cell read p50 4.0 with overshoot never above 0.3 ms — which is what let the numbers be published without the usual 'other agents were running' caveat. On a loaded box it would have said so in every table simultaneously. Cheap, and it retires the standing wall-clock-is-unreliable worry per-run instead of per-repo.
* A COMPUTED-SIZE CONTROL CATCHES A KNOB THAT DOES NOT TURN. Predicted DOM mutation counts (host-only 1, fresh-equal 0, one-leaf k+1) matched measured at all 15 mode x rung combinations, and the driven arm independently reproduced exactly 201.0 per crossing. MutationObserver.takeRecords() answers SYNCHRONOUSLY, which is the only reason it can be read inside a flushSync-bracketed window.

A TWO-VALUED PROBE CONFLATES 'REJECTED' WITH 'CRASHED', SO TWO VALIDATORS THAT BOTH EXPLODE AGREE (rf2-dhl4d, 2026-08-03).

THE MECHANISM, and it is the best fail-open diagnosis this project has produced. A viz<->engine parity ratchet compared two validators by asking each "do you accept this definition?" — a BOOLEAN. On CLJS, engine-accepts? wrapped the call in (catch :default ... false). So when the engine raised a host ClassCastException on a non-Named key, the probe recorded FALSE — indistinguishable from a clean, documented rejection. The viz side crashed the same way. TWO VALIDATORS THAT BOTH EXPLODE AGREE, and the ratchet stayed green over a live crash in a security gate.

THE FIX IS THE SHAPE, NOT THE CASE: make the probe THREE-VALUED — :accept / :reject / :host-throw — plus a definition-validation-is-total assertion. Proof it now sees the divergence: (engine :reject, viz :host-throw).

GENERALISE IT. Any comparison harness that reduces its subjects to a boolean, or that catches broadly and maps the catch onto one of the two legitimate outcomes, is fail-open BY CONSTRUCTION — parity ratchets, differential tests, golden-file comparators, A/B benchmark agreement checks. Ask of every such harness: WHAT DOES IT RECORD WHEN THE SUBJECT CRASHES? If the answer is "the same thing as one of the normal outcomes", it cannot see the failure class it exists to catch.

The method's rule is right: verify a restore by hashing the bytes, never by reading git diff, because 'unchanged' and 'never applied' produce the same diff. But the INSTRUMENT matters and sha256sum is the wrong one on this checkout.

WHAT HAPPENED: a worker planted a fault, ran the gate red, restored, and 'sha256sum -c' FAILED on a restore that was actually correct. Git's LF->CRLF conversion rewrote the working file during a rebase checkout AFTER the baseline hash was taken. The bytes on disk genuinely differed; the CONTENT did not.

USE git hash-object against the committed blob instead. It normalises line endings the same way git does, so it compares what git compares. Both reads agreed at c37e900... where sha256sum had disagreed.

WHY THIS MATTERS MORE THAN IT LOOKS: a false 'restore failed' is not merely noise. The worker's next move is to re-apply the restore, or to doubt the whole sabotage result - and the sabotage result is the deliverable. An instrument that misreports is the same defect class as the hollow gate it was being used to prove.

Pair it with the other half already recorded: a hash proves the SOURCE changed, not that the RUNTIME saw it. A fault outside the build's module graph compiles into nothing and the sabotage run comes back green for an unrelated reason.

A STATUS AUDIT KEYED ON A BARE ID STRING READS ANOTHER RECORD'S STATUS (2026-08-13, my own tool misreporting).

WHAT HAPPENED: verifying that five beads had really been deferred, I grepped the committed export for the bead id in quotes:

  grep '"rf2-hic-092"' .beads/issues.jsonl | grep -o '"status":"[a-z]*"' | head -1

It reported rf2-hic-092 as CLOSED. The bead was in fact DEFERRED - bd show said so, with the deferral date. The grep had matched the FIRST LINE CONTAINING that id string, which was a DIFFERENT bead whose dependency list or note text mentions rf2-hic-092. I then read that other record's status as this bead's.

Four of the five happened to be right, which is worse than all five being wrong: a spot-check would have passed.

THE FIX IS ONE CHARACTER OF PRECISION - key on the id FIELD:

  grep '"id":"rf2-hic-092"'

WHY THIS IS THE SAME DEFECT CLASS THE METHOD ALREADY NAMES. mayor-hygiene.md warns that gh pr list --search 'head:<branch>' substring-matches and returns a SIBLING branch's PR, so you must ask for headRefName and compare equality yourself. This is that rule in a second place. The general form: AN ID IS NOT A SEARCH TERM. Any tracker, VCS or CI query that accepts a bare string will substring-match it, and the record it returns will look entirely plausible because it is a real record - just not yours.

AND NOTE WHICH DIRECTION IT FAILED. It reported a live bead as closed, i.e. it manufactured a false alarm rather than hiding a real one. Reversed - reporting a closed bead as open - it would have sent a worker at finished work. Both are available from the same bug.

THE DISCIPLINE: a verification tool that misreports is the same defect class as the bug it was written to catch. Cross-check the export against the database (bd show) rather than trusting either alone; here the disagreement between the two is what exposed the grep.

VERIFYING THAT AN ARTEFACT IS THE RIGHT KIND IS NOT VERIFYING THAT THE REQUIREMENT STILL EXISTS (2026-08-11, rf2-r7zq / rf2-5gka).

WHAT HAPPENED, and it is a two-layer miss. rf2-r7zq blocked rf2-5gka on a "target-side advance-clock!".
  - LAYER 1, which a previous mayor got wrong: closing the bead because SOMETHING named advance-clock! had landed. It had — three of them — but all were the wrong KIND (a test-kit harness facility, plus two other substrates' runtimes). That mayor recorded afterwards that "the property I verified and praised is exactly what makes it unusable".
  - LAYER 2, which I then got wrong: I verified the kind carefully, avoided layer 1, wrote a detailed note proving none of the three served — AND NEVER ASKED WHETHER THE REQUIREMENT STILL STOOD. It did not. rf2-5gka carried an operator-directed DELEGATED DECISION: OPTION C — "add nothing to Hicasso... Nothing to build" — recorded about TWO HOURS BEFORE my note. The migration had already resolved as retire-with-the-donor.

So the more careful check still failed, one level up. Guarding against the previous error is not the same as being right.

THE RULE: when bead A blocks bead B, read B's OWN notes bottom-up before doing anything about A. A ruling on B can retire A's entire reason for existing, and nothing on A will say so — dependency edges carry no news. The direction that bites is downstream-to-upstream, which is the direction nobody reads.

TWO PRACTICES THAT MAKE IT CHEAP:
  - Before dispatching or noting on a blocker, run `bd show <the-blocked-bead>` and read its notes bottom-up. One command.
  - When you record a verification on a bead, state explicitly what you did NOT check. My note said "the grep is not the check; the check is which artefact ships it" — true, and it framed the question so narrowly that the larger one became invisible.

HOW IT WAS CAUGHT, which is worth copying: the worker did not assert the timing, it BISECTED `.beads/issues.jsonl` per commit with `git show <sha>:.beads/issues.jsonl | grep -c` and produced the two intervals. (A `git log -S` over that file timed out at 120s — exit 143 — so per-commit bisect is the working technique on this tracker file.)

THE OUTCOME WAS STILL GOOD, because the brief asked for analysis first and said a reasoned refusal was an acceptable deliverable. The worker wrote no code, created no worktree, opened no PR, and returned the one fact that made all of it unnecessary. A phase-1 refusal on a bead with a subtle trap is worth more than a built facility in the wrong artefact — and this one also corrected a standing dependency edge that would have kept mis-blocking rf2-5gka.

WHAT THE MERGED-PR AUDIT REOPENS, MEASURED — AND IT IS A DEFECT IN MY CLOSE REASONS, NOT IN THE AUDIT (2026-07-26).

THE MEASUREMENT. Of the open beads carrying audit-reopen language, the largest cluster by type is TEST / FIXTURE / GATE beads — 7 of 16, ahead of donor (4), spec-prose (3) and privacy (3). All 16 name an explicit residual.

THE DISCRIMINATOR, and it is clean. Gate beads I closed today WITH a mutation proof written into the close reason have stayed closed: rf2-4hc9p (3 mutation references), rf2-wns8d (8), rf2-xwa4n (3), rf2-kqxe6.25 (4). Gate beads that got REOPENED carry ZERO mutation references in their notes: rf2-wq17m (0), rf2-as6bg (0). Small n, but the mechanism is obvious once seen.

WHY IT HAPPENS. A gate bead asks "arm this check". The audit asks "does the check CATCH the thing". A close reason that says the job was added, the roster was widened, or the suite is green gives the audit NOTHING TO VERIFY AGAINST — so it reopens and writes the residual itself. A close reason carrying the planted defect, the gate reddening, the restore and the green gives it the verification already done, and it stays closed.

THE RULE: when closing a gate, fixture, census, lane or CI-arming bead, the close reason MUST carry the mutation proof — the specific defect planted, the observed red with counts, the restore, the green. "The job runs" is not "the job catches". If a worker did not supply one, that is a reason to ask for it BEFORE closing, not to close and let the audit find it.

CORROBORATING EVIDENCE FROM TODAY, all of it the same shape: rf2-wns8d proved a shipped deftest was a TAUTOLOGY by mutating the production wrapper and watching the deftest stay GREEN. rf2-4hc9p proved the pre-repair bijection gate was green on all seven planted defects and red on the one prose fixture — exactly inverted. The ci-arming worker found engine_grammar_parity_test.cljc armed on two lanes and matching NEITHER build ns-regexp, so it ran nowhere. In every case the arming was real and the catching was absent, which is precisely the distinction a close reason must record.

SECOND-ORDER POINT WORTH KEEPING: this means the audit reopen rate is partly MY OUTPUT, not just its diligence. Roughly one reopen per merged PR looked like an immovable property of running an audit; a meaningful share of it is gate beads closed on arming rather than on catching. That is fixable from my side.

WHEN A GUARD IS WARRANTED UNDER "TRUST THE PROGRAMMER" — the principle that reconciles three decisions I made today (2026-07-26).

The three look contradictory on their face:
  1. rf2-bk7z5 — CLOSED, refusing to validate :role against its documented closed set.
  2. rf2-8o66x — DEFERRED, refusing a performance regression gate.
  3. The empty-export finding — FILED, asking for a row floor in the pre-commit hook.

Two refusals and one request, all under the same posture. The distinguishing principle is not size, cost or priority. It is:

  A GUARD IS WARRANTED WHEN THE FAILURE IS SILENT AND HAS ALREADY HAPPENED. IT IS NOT WARRANTED WHEN THE PROGRAMMER CAN SEE THE FAILURE, OR WHEN THE FAILURE CANNOT OCCUR.

Applied:
  1. :role validation — the failure CANNOT OCCUR. Every producer is in-namespace; no caller can pass an invalid role. Enforcing it adds a failure mode, a message to maintain and a test to keep green, and catches nothing. That is a nag-diagnostic.
  2. The perf gate — the failure would be NOISE, not signal. The no-substrate floor drifted 37% across rounds, larger than most effects being measured, so the gate would red on nothing. And a false red is expensive here precisely because the standing rule is that a failing test on a touched surface is never a flake.
  3. The row floor — the failure IS SILENT AND HAS HAPPENED TWICE, six weeks apart, by the same mechanism. An empty tracker with a CLEAN git status is exactly what a programmer cannot see. That is not distrust; it is the only way the fact becomes visible at all.

SO "TRUST THE PROGRAMMER" IS NOT "ASSUME NOTHING GOES WRONG". It is: DO NOT GUARD AGAINST WHAT THE PROGRAMMER CAN ALREADY SEE. A loud crash needs no guard — it is already a signal. A wrong value that renders visibly needs no guard. What needs a guard is the state that looks correct: an empty file with a clean status, a gate green on a defect it was built to catch, a test armed on two lanes and selected by neither.

THE COROLLARY IS THE ONE I HAVE BEEN UNDER-USING: this principle is also a REJECTION criterion with teeth. Most proposed guards fail it, because most proposed failures are either impossible or loud. Ask which of the three cases a proposal is in before pricing it, and the answer usually decides the bead without further analysis.

AND IT EXPLAINS WHY THE ERGONOMICS CLAUSE IS A DETECTOR RATHER THAN A BRAKE: a bad diagnostic is the same defect class inverted. The failure IS visible, but it points somewhere useless — an author told to add a key the source already has, or handed a JSON encoding error naming a reified malli class. That is a signal that lies rather than a signal that is missing, and both are worth fixing where a merely-absent convenience is not.

WHERE A FINDING BELONGS WHEN ITS PREMISE IS AN OPEN RULING (2026-07-25, articulated by the R6 worker and worth adopting): a finding whose premise depends on how an OPEN P1 gets ruled belongs on the PR, NOT in the tracker, until that ruling lands.

Concrete case: R6's guide audit found seven canonical recipes omitting an explicit {:sensitive ...} map and recorded the roster on its PR rather than filing beads. rf2-kqxe6.20 then shipped option A — the framework retains its own carrier classification — and the finding DISSOLVED COMPLETELY: those seven recipes had been describing the correct spelling all along; the framework was what needed fixing. Had the roster been beaded, the tracker would now hold a bead instructing people to add boilerplate that spec/012 and the auth how-to explicitly FORBID.

So the test is not 'is this finding real?' but 'is this finding real under every live ruling?'. If the answer depends on a pending decision, park it on the PR where it dies quietly if the ruling moots it, instead of in the tracker where it becomes durable instruction. A dissolved finding is a GOOD outcome to be stated plainly, not salvaged — the R6 worker struck its own roster in the PR comment so nobody would act on it.

`.claude/commands/*.md` AND `CLAUDE.md` ARE GATED — BY check_readme_links.py, NOT by check_doc_slugs.py (2026-08-11, rf2-j689 / PR #7887).

I HAVE BRIEFED THIS WRONG. Twice in one day I told a worker that `.claude/commands/*.md` "may have no automated gate at all" and to verify by hand. That is false, and the worker on rf2-j689 established the real mapping at source:

- `scripts/check_readme_links.py` OWNS repo-root markdown — its docstring names `CLAUDE.md` — and, per rf2-1yy75, also resolves markdown path references inside `.claude/commands/*.md`.
- `scripts/check_doc_slugs.py` EXPLICITLY DOES NOT COVER `CLAUDE.md`. Its own notes warn that briefs have nominated it and received a GREEN EXIT VERIFYING NOTHING — the precise fail-open defect this project spends its days hunting, arriving through the brief rather than through the code.
- `docs/the-mayor-method/` IS inside the mkdocs site build (proved by `python -m mkdocs build --strict` producing `site/the-mayor-method/`), and `check_doc_slugs.py` enrols that tree explicitly via FENCED_DOC_LINK_TREES.

THE COVERAGE IS REAL BUT NARROW, and the worker proved the boundary rather than assuming it. Its FIRST negative control was INVALID and it said so instead of burying it: a bogus `scripts/*.sh` path planted in `mayor-merge.md` was NOT flagged, exit 0, because the resolver matches `.md` references only. Re-run with a `.md` path, it failed correctly and named the file and line. So the gate catches broken MARKDOWN references in those files and nothing else — it will not notice a wrong command string, a broken shell path, or prose that contradicts itself.

WHAT TO PUT IN A BRIEF FROM NOW ON, for a diff touching CLAUDE.md or .claude/commands/**:
  Run `python scripts/check_readme_links.py` — it owns repo-root markdown and resolves `.md` references inside `.claude/commands/*.md`. Do NOT nominate `check_doc_slugs.py` for `CLAUDE.md`; it does not cover it and exits green having verified nothing. Prove the gate reaches your file with a negative control that breaks a MARKDOWN reference — a broken script path will not be caught, and a control that fails to fail proves nothing.

THE WIDER RULE THIS IS THE THIRD INSTANCE OF: never state a surface's gate coverage in a brief from memory. Establish it, or tell the worker to establish it and report. A brief that names the wrong gate is worse than one that names none, because the worker then trusts a green that means nothing — and the mayor reads that green as evidence.

WIDE RENAME SWEEPS — check whether the rename silently DISABLES a gate rather than failing it. rf2-lgeron (#6356, 2026-07-18) found the landmine before sweeping 593 alias sites: doc_api_check.clj extracts references for the alias list ["rf" "story"], so renaming story -> rf.story in docs/story/api/** drops ~15 refs; the min-references floor is 20 against a live ~50, so the gate does NOT trip and the Story API page quietly loses reference checking. A green CI would have certified a switched-off check. RULE: before any mechanical rename, grep the GATES for the old token — a checker that counts or allow-lists the thing you are renaming must move in the same PR. Second trap from the same bead: routing/ as an alias is textually indistinguishable from the sanctioned :routing/* late-bind HOOK KEYS (:routing/extra-route-keys, :routing/on-frame-destroyed!), and the same holds for :epoch/* and :schemas/* — a blind sweep corrupts the DI seam grammar. Same family as rf2-bcjpq5 finding :routing/match-url also exists as a conformance CAPABILITY TAG. ALWAYS check for same-spelling distinct meanings before a bulk edit. Third: a sweep spanning surfaces held by live workers cannot be complete-in-one — report the site count and let the mayor sequence it.

THE WINDOWS ENCODING HAZARD IS NARROWER THAN I FIRST WROTE — argv survives, stdout redirects and bd pipes do not (2026-08-14, sharpened by the rf2-3lrb worker after it broke its own rule and verified rather than assumed).

WHAT ACTUALLY MANGLES TEXT:
- `bd show --json` PIPED through the shell: U+2014 comes back as replacement characters.
- Python writing to stdout under a REDIRECT: the console encoding is cp1252, so `python -c ... > file` mangles the same way.

WHAT SURVIVES INTACT: passing UTF-8 through ARGV. The worker wrote a bead comment with a `$(cat file)` substitution — exactly the console-crossing it had just documented against — then verified instead of panicking: it landed verbatim, all four em dashes intact, zero U+FFFD. So the earlier blanket rule "no text crosses a console" was too wide and would have banned a safe path.

THE WORKING RULE: read with `bd show --json` REDIRECTED to a file and parse it as UTF-8; write with `bd update --body-file` from a UTF-8 file; do intermediate reporting from inside Python with an EXPLICIT encoding rather than bare stdout. argv is fine.

VERIFIED ACROSS THREE SCRIPTED PASSES over bead descriptions (19, 19 and 1): zero U+FFFD in every one.

COMPANION TRAP, worse because it fails silently and coherently: bd export from the wrong working directory auto-discovers a DIFFERENT database — see [[bd-export-from-wrong-cwd-returns-a-different-database]]. Run it from the repo root and cross-check against `bd stats`.

WINDOWS JUNCTION DETECTION - two wrong answers before the right one, both recorded here so neither gets retried. (1) `cmd /c dir /AL <path>` from the Bash tool prints only the cmd banner, no listing, so every directory reports 'not a junction'. (2) `fsutil file queryfileid` DOES NOT share the target's id - a control junction reported a DIFFERENT id from its target, so this test calls a real junction 'not a junction' too. THE WORKING DETECTOR, validated against a deliberately-created control junction: the `ReparsePoint` attribute plus `LinkType`/`Target` via PowerShell `Get-Item -Force`. Belt-and-braces that also validated: `[IO.Directory]::Delete(path, $false)` unlinks a junction leaving the target's contents intact, and refuses a populated real directory - safe to run before every `git worktree remove`. THIS IS NOT THEORETICAL: a worker worktree's implementation/node_modules was confirmed a live junction into the mayor's real node_modules, the exact configuration that destroyed it once already. ALWAYS validate a detector against a control junction you create yourself before trusting it. Supersedes [[junction-detection-via-cmd-c-dir-al-path]].

Windows unclean-shutdown can ZERO-FILL .git/config (12KB of \0), breaking ALL git ('fatal: bad config line 1'). Diagnose: od -c .git/config shows all \0; scan .git top-level for other all-null files (only config was hit). Recover: back up the corrupt file, reconstruct config from surviving data — remote URL from .git/FETCH_HEAD, committer identity from recent commit objects (read with config moved aside), core/* Windows defaults; restore beads.role via 'git config beads.role maintainer'. Verify with git fsck-lite (cat-file -e HEAD + HEAD^{tree}), ls-remote, and 'only tracked file modified is the expected one' (a zero-filled tracked file would show as modified). Happened 2026-07-08.

A WITNESS DERIVED FROM THE FIX INHERITS THE FIX'S BLIND SPOTS — five instances in one session (2026-08-10/11, hicasso).

THE SHAPE: a test or table whose STATED SCOPE EXCEEDS THE CASES IT ACTUALLY DRIVES. Each was green, each was honest, each claimed more than it checked.

1. rf2-hic-020 — a runtime/kit parity table claiming both arms of the raw escape, driving only the VALID raw component.
2. rf2-hic-007 — a completeness test claiming all six constructor fields unforgeable, running only where declaring! had already supplied real values; outside every extent the guarantee did not hold.
3. rf2-hic-012 — a comment recording the EXPECTED result as though it were the measured one, contradicted by the very row it annotated.
4. rf2-hic-021 — a round-trip check whose both directions ranged over ids THAT EXIST, so thirteen taught refusals with no id at all satisfied it VACUOUSLY (fail-open).
5. rf2-hic-022 — a shadow-detection walker whose letfn arm reads [nm params] and collects params only when the second node is a VECTOR; in multi-arity letfn it is a LIST, so every arity is missed. PR body and README both claimed letfn was covered.

WHY IT RECURS, and it is not carelessness: the witness is written FROM the fix, so it drives the shapes the author had in mind while fixing. The shapes that break it are exactly the ones the author did not think of — the same set. Test-after-fix is structurally biased toward passing.

THE COUNTERMEASURE, now standing in briefs: DERIVE THE WITNESS FROM THE GRAMMAR OF THE THING, NOT FROM THE FIX. Enumerate the legal shapes of the construct (for letfn: single-arity vector, multi-arity lists, docstring/prepost variants) and drive each. Require the PR body to state which shapes of the grammar were driven AND which were not — the second list is the valuable one, and writing it is what surfaces the gap.

SISTER RULE: see sweep-generator-defines-reachable-failure-directions — a generator's excluded shapes make a whole error DIRECTION invisible. Same disease at a different scale: coverage is defined by what the instrument can express, not by how much of it you ran.

A DEFECT-WITNESS TEST AND ITS FIX ARE MUTUALLY INVALIDATING — merging both without flipping the witness REDS MAIN, in either order. Cost a P0 red-on-main on 2026-07-24.

THE MECHANISM: a validation pilot reproduces a known hazard and writes it down as a LIVE TEST asserting the CURRENT (broken) behaviour. A separate slice FIXES that hazard. Each PR is green against a main lacking the other. Merge both and the witness test fails, because the defect it documents no longer exists.

THE CONCRETE CASE: the dropdown pilot independently reproduced the ref-composition hazard and shipped `a-behavior-and-a-top-layer-state-on-one-element-lose-a-ref` — a test that PASSES ONLY WHILE THE BUG IS PRESENT. I merged the pilot, then merged the ref-composition fix, and main went red with 2 failures. Every other gate stayed green, so it read like a mystery regression in a slice that had been CLEAN as a PR.

⚠️ WHAT MAKES THIS WORTH A MEMORY IS THAT I HAD ALREADY IDENTIFIED THE PATTERN AND FAILED TO APPLY IT. Days earlier I wrote into a different brief: "both pilots assert the current REFUSAL in a test, so the blocked cell re-opens loudly. THOSE ASSERTIONS WILL START FAILING WHEN YOU SUCCEED — update them deliberately as part of this slice." I understood it for the compiled-browser refusal and did not carry it to the very next fix I merged. Recognising a hazard in one place does not transfer it to another unless it becomes a CHECK.

THE CHECK, now standing — BEFORE MERGING ANY FIX, ASK: does a merged test currently ASSERT THE DEFECT THIS FIXES? If yes, the flip belongs in the SAME PR as the fix, or main goes red the moment both are in.
  git grep -l "<hazard keyword>" implementation/**/test/
Pilot and validation suites are the usual home, because documenting current-state honestly is exactly what they are FOR.

THE REPAIR IS A FLIP, NOT A DELETE, and it has three parts:
  1. Assert the FIXED behaviour positively (both participants ran), never loosen to tolerate either outcome — that discards the only coverage of the combination.
  2. RENAME the test. A name asserting the opposite of its body is a trap for the next reader.
  3. Sweep for SIBLING witnesses in the same suite rather than discovering them one merge at a time.

⚠️ AND THE DIAGNOSTIC LESSON: the failure looked like a regression in the fix. The worker got it right by READING CI OWN LOG for the failing test NAME and MESSAGE — the name said "lose-a-ref" and the message said "one of the two refs was lost", which is the test DOCUMENTING a defect, not detecting one. A test name that describes a BUG rather than a PROPERTY is the tell. My own grep for the failure lines used a pattern chosen before I knew what the output looked like and returned only the namespace roster — capture the log to a file and read it.

GENERAL FORM: this WILL recur wherever validation pilots run alongside active development, which is the whole point of running them. It is a property of the arrangement, not a mistake by either author.

WORKER 'BACKGROUND-GATES-THEN-END-TURN' PATTERN: several workers (xray-tail, m90brg-finish, schemas-5a5qwp) did the full implementation + committed-or-staged it, then spawned their gate runs (npm run test:cljs, JVM suites) as BACKGROUND tasks and ENDED THEIR TURN saying 'I'll pick up when the background tests report' — leaving the work uncommitted/unpushed with the bead still IN_PROGRESS. The harness fires a completion notification but there's no PR. RECOGNITION: worker 'completed' but result says 'background test runs still executing / I'll wait for completion' + worktree shows modified>0, commits/pushed=0. RECOVERY (fast, no work lost): SendMessage-resume the SAME agent → tell it to run gates in the FOREGROUND (wait inline), commit, rebase, push, gh pr create, bd close. Its WIP survives. PREVENTION: put 'run gates in the FOREGROUND — do NOT background them or end your turn waiting on a background task' in dispatch briefs (already added to recent ones; the pattern still recurs, so keep the resume-recovery reflex). NOT a stall — the work is done, just the push step remains.

Worker brief gate-scope lesson (2026-06-09): do NOT require a worker to run the FULL gate matrix locally (all per-artefact clojure -M:test + npm test:cljs/test:browser + elision + mcp-conformance + xray-feature-gate). Reserve full-local-suite only for the very few beads where CI can't cover it. Applies to future B7/B9 + any big core bead.
