THE node_modules CANARY IS ONLY A CANARY IF BOTH READINGS USE THE SAME FLAGS — 'ls' AND 'ls -A' DIFFER BY EXACTLY THE DOTFILES AND EITHER IS A CORRECT COUNT (measured 2026-08-23 14:30 AUSEST).

WHAT HAPPENED. A worker removing its node_modules junction re-counted the mayor's real tree and reported 103 entries, 'up from the 101 I recorded at the start (npx added two), so it did not drop'. My own baseline had read 101 all session. Two careful measurements, two numbers, and a plausible story attached to the difference.

NEITHER NUMBER WAS WRONG AND NOTHING HAD CHANGED. 'ls implementation/node_modules | wc -l' returns 101; 'ls -A' returns 103. The gap is exactly the two dotfile entries. The decisive control was the write clock rather than either count: the newest entry in that directory by mtime is from AUGUST 11, so nothing was written there today at all — no addition by npx, no deletion by the junction removal.

WHY THIS MATTERS MORE THAN IT LOOKS. The canary exists to detect a silent deletion through a junction, and it detects one by COMPARING two counts. A comparison across a flag change is not a comparison: the same two dotfiles read as a drop of two in one direction and a gain of two in the other, and the reading arrives attached to a confident explanation, because whoever measured it will reach for a cause. Here the invented cause was 'npx added two', which is exactly the shape that survives review.

THE RULE: capture both sides of a canary with the SAME command, in the same shell, at runtime — the method already says a remembered constant cannot detect a delta, and this is the same failure one level down, where the constant is remembered but the INSTRUMENT is not. When two counts disagree, reach for a third signal that is not a count: the directory's newest modification time answers 'did anything change here' without depending on which entries you chose to enumerate.

THE THREE BLOCKS THAT TRAVEL VERBATIM INTO A DISPATCH HAVE THREE DIFFERENT SHAPES, AND ONLY ONE OPENS WITH A SELF-NAMING FRAME (2026-08-23, PR #8726).

Measured in docs/the-mayor-method/dispatch-prompt-template.md:

- The worktree boundary block: payload is a FENCED text block (52 lines / 2,930 chars incl. fences). Mayor-facing rationale sits BEFORE the fence; a note about the mayor-side commit guard sits AFTER it.
- The common preamble: payload is a FENCED text block (61 lines / 3,990 chars incl. fences), opening immediately under the heading. Its mayor-facing paragraph sits AFTER the closing fence, at the TAIL.
- Gate mechanics: NO fence. Heading down to the rule before '## Reviewing what comes back'. It alone opens with '**This section is the gate-mechanics block.**' naming itself, where it stops, and the neighbouring section it is not.

SO THE OPERATIVE RULE IS: where the payload is FENCED, take the FENCE and everything outside it is yours. The frame-dropping instruction applies only to the unfenced block.

WHY IT MATTERS: PR #8723 (mine, merged 90 minutes earlier) asserted 'Each block opens by naming itself and saying where it stops' — true of ONE of three. The cost is directional: a mayor taught that mayor-facing prose lives at the OPEN checks the open of the common preamble, finds a fence, pastes the heading-to-heading range, and ships the tail paragraph ('A pass that concludes only in the ignored tree...') into a worker brief. That is the exact failure the paragraph exists to prevent, reintroduced at the other end of the same block.

A HABIT ABOUT WHICH END THE MAYOR-FACING PROSE LIVES AT IS WRONG HALF THE TIME. The two fenced blocks put it on opposite sides.

TO ASK WHETHER A BRANCH HAS A PR, USE THE API'S EXACT head= FILTER RATHER THAN SCANNING PR PAGES (2026-08-23).

THE COMMAND: gh api -X GET repos/<owner>/<repo>/pulls -f state=all -f 'head=<owner>:<branch>' 
It queries the WHOLE pull-request set by exact head ref and returns [] when there is none. No paging, no substring matching, no window to be wrong about.

WHY IT MATTERS HERE. The hygiene loop's rule is 'never delete a branch whose PR is not verifiably MERGED, keyed on exact headRefName equality'. I had been answering it by pulling gh pr list --state all --limit 400 and equality-filtering in Python. That is correct as far as it goes and it has TWO failure modes the head filter does not:

1. THE WINDOW. 400 PRs covered #8326-#8726. Both orphan branches' tips date from 2026-08-11 and 2026-08-15, whose PRs would sit BELOW that window -- the scan's zero was a zero over the wrong range, and it read exactly like a zero over the right one. Widening to pages 5-6 reached #8126 and still could not prove absence, only extend it.

2. THE COST. Each widening is another API round trip and another chance to mis-set the range. The head filter answers in one call and its answer is total.

MEASURED: head=day8:worker/receipts-hic081 and head=day8:worker/retire-delete each return 'NO PR of any state', confirming what the paged scan could only suggest. Both branches therefore carry genuinely-new work (git cherry '+' counts 3 and 1) that has never been proposed for merge, and under the rule they can never be deleted on evidence -- only on the operator's explicit word.

THE GENERAL SHAPE: when a rule says 'compare for equality yourself', prefer an instrument that takes equality as INPUT over one that returns a page you then filter. The filter is right; the page is the risk.

bd show PRINTS COMMENTS LAST, SO piping bd show <id> to tail LANDS IN COMMENTS AND NOT ON THE NEWEST NOTE (2026-08-23, hit twice in one session).

THE SECTION ORDER bd show emits: DESCRIPTION, then NOTES, then DEPENDS ON / BLOCKS / DISCOVERED, then COMMENTS. Comments are ordered by their OWN dates and can be far older than the newest note. So a tail of the whole output reads old text that LOOKS newest because it is last on screen.

MEASURED ON TWO BEADS THE SAME AFTERNOON:
- rf2-85og2: 1299 lines total, NOTES span 42-567, COMMENTS span 572-1299. A tail landed at ~line 1290 on a comment saying the bead still owes a quiet-box window and that a second driver plus donor arm "wants its own bead". The genuine newest note (2026-08-22 17:06:29) says the OPPOSITE: the quiet-box half is satisfied and authorised, U1/U2's window was taken in PR #8676, and what remains wants an operator ruling or a subject that does not yet exist.
- rf2-9wmqd: same shape. Its own banner names the cause in its own words -- "bd show prints COMMENTS last, so the bottom of its output is two superseded worker reports saying item (c) is still owed. It is not." Item (c) landed in PR #8680.

BOTH ERRORS RAN IN THE SAME DIRECTION: they reported work as OWED that had already been done, which reads as diligence and manufactures a backlog that does not exist.

THE METHOD ALREADY SAYS a tail "is not a read-the-newest method". What it does not say is the mechanism on THIS tool, which is what makes the failure reproducible rather than occasional.

WHAT TO DO INSTEAD:
1. Find the section boundaries first -- grep -nE on line-anchored DESCRIPTION|NOTES|COMMENTS|DEPENDS ON|BLOCKS|DISCOVERED over the captured output -- then read the TAIL OF THE NOTES BLOCK only.
2. Confirm with bd history <id> --json by walking adjacent snapshot pairs newest-first to the first change in a text-bearing field; that gives the real mutation time of the newest note.
3. On any bead whose notes run to tens of thousands of characters, ADD A SCANNABLE BANNER as the newest note. rf2-9wmqd's banner is the model and states its own justification: the notes were ~50,000 characters with no scannable marker, so each tick re-derived the answer at that cost.

# hic-063 — [OPERATOR-ACTIVATED] Pilot applications

**Phase**: 6 · **Wave**: — (activates when the operator nominates pilots; blocks nothing) · **Est.**: L · **Depends**: hic-060, hic-061
**Surface**: pilot support work as it arises

## Goal
Two real pilot applications each migrate/ship at least one substantial screen without framework-author intervention — the adoption proof §13 requires.

## Deliverables (on activation)
Onboarding both pilots on the released artefact + docs only; a friction log (every question they had to ask a human is a docs or API defect — file each as a bead); the §13 evidence: install, develop, test, diagnose, production-build, upgrade unaided.

## Acceptance (on activation)
Both pilots shipping; the friction log dispositioned; no critical public API change across one release candidate.

## Worker notes
This bead cannot be autonomous — it needs the operator's nominations. Everything else in the set proceeds without it; record nominations here when made.

---
[Worker context — applies to every hic bead]
PATH MAP: the normative documents are published in-tree by bead rf2-hic-000:
- docs/design/hicasso/product/decision-brief.md  (= synth.md / "the decision brief")
- docs/design/hicasso/product/specification.md   (= "spec SN" / synth-codex.md)
- docs/design/hicasso/product/lanes/<name>.md    (= codex/<name>.md)
References to `fable/...` are operator-local provenance; workers do not need them.
PROPOSED-ID MAP: "hic-NNN" in any bead text = tracker id rf2-hic-NNN. The dependency manifest is authoritative over prose Depends lines.
WORKER PROTOCOL (mandatory):
1. Run the worker worktree guard before edits: sh scripts/assert-worker-worktree.sh; report WORKTREE_ROOT.
2. Read first: the path-mapped documents this bead names.
3. Gates: foreground a gate that fits inside the harness ceiling; DETACH one that does not and poll BOTH its log and its `.exit` file in a bounded loop within the same turn — never end the turn waiting for a completion event. Never pipe a gate through `tail` or any filter; redirect to a log and echo the runner's own exit code on the same command line. Commit and open the PR before ending the turn. DOC-SURFACE GATE: for an edit confined to docs/design/hicasso/, `mkdocs build --strict` is NOT the gate — mkdocs.yml's exclude_docs keeps that tree out of the site. `scripts/check_doc_slugs.py` validates its markdown link targets and heading anchors, and `scripts/check_provenance_pins.py` validates changed pages under docs/design/hicasso/; nothing validates its tables, rendering or nav, so verify anchors and table column counts BY HAND and say so in the PR body.
4. Never `git stash`. Commit first, then rebase.
5. Never commit `.beads/issues.jsonl` or `.beads/metadata.json` from a worker branch — they are whole-database EXPORTS, not database files, and your branch carries the snapshot taken when its worktree was created, so committing one TIME-TRAVELS the tracker: beads closed since reopen, beads filed since vanish (PR #6677 did exactly this, 135 insertions / 136 deletions of pure collateral). Any other database-derived path likewise. The human-authored config — `.beads/README.md`, `.beads/config.yaml`, `.beads/.gitignore`, `.beads/hooks/**` — IS fair game. CLAUDE.md's Beads durability section is the authority.
6. Beads touching tools/xray/ update tools/xray/spec/* in the same PR (or state "spec unchanged because X").
7. Hot-zone files only if this bead flags them — and the hot zone INCLUDES the spec/*.md hot files (spec/004-Views.md, spec/002-Frames.md, spec/API.md, spec/Conventions.md among others), not just implementation/shadow-cljs.edn, implementation/deps.edn and .github/workflows/*. CLAUDE.md's Workflow section carries the canonical list; read it there rather than treating this line as complete.
8. No AI attribution in commits or PRs.
9. If you created a node_modules junction, remove it as your last act.
10. Checkpoint findings become real bd issues AND a row in docs/design/hicasso/product/correction-ledger.md. The checkpoint's own report PR writes the `open` row; a CORRECTIVE PR never edits that file — every later transition is the ledger keeper's. Read the file's own stated protocol before touching it.

THE REMOVAL SCRIPT'S CANARY CANNOT COMMIT THE COUNT-BOTH-SIDES-DIFFERENTLY ERROR; MY MANUAL ONE CAN (verified 2026-08-23 20:25 AUSEST by reading the tool, not the doc).

WHAT I VERIFIED. scripts/remove-worker-worktree.sh computes its before AND after canary through ONE shell function, signature(), so no flag mismatch between the two sides is reachable. It is also three-part rather than a count: immediate-entries/recursive-files/sentinels-present, e.g. 103/2933/2, where the sentinels are .bin and shadow-cljs/package.json. Its own comment says why the immediate count alone is half-blind — a partial recursive delete can empty the files under every package while leaving all the top-level package directories standing, so before == after would report healthy over real damage. The recursive count sees exactly that shape.

MEASURED LIVE THIS TICK: 103/2933/2, matching the figure the script's own header documents. Tool and tree agree.

SO THE FAILURE I DOCUMENTED IN loops.md IS A MAYOR-SIDE FAILURE ONLY. That addition — count both sides the same way, because a hiding form one side and a showing form the other turns the comparison into an offset that can CANCEL a real loss of its own size — is addressed to a mayor capturing counts by hand in a hygiene census, which is exactly where it happened. It is not a claim about the script, and a later pass should not read it as one or "fix" a tool that is already immune.

PRACTICAL: my hygiene census uses ls -A (shows hidden) = 103, which agrees with the script's find -mindepth 1 -maxdepth 1. The bare ls form reads 101 and is the one to avoid. Two hidden entries: .bin and .package-lock.json.

AND THE DECISIVE CONTROL IS STILL THE CLOCK. Newest-entry mtime has read 2026-08-11 14:16:13 across every census this session; an unmoved clock refutes a compensating-offset story that three matching counts alone cannot.

MY PHRASE PROBES FAIL ON SENTENCE-INITIAL CAPITALS AND NARROW WINDOWS, AND EVERY FAILURE MANUFACTURES A FINDING (four instances 2026-08-23, one method-reread pass).

WHAT HAPPENED. Checking quotes I had been attributing to the method tree, a case-sensitive single-line grep returned NOT FOUND on four of five. Three of the four were VERBATIM PRESENT and my probe missed them:

* "cite the check you made" — the tree begins the sentence "Cite the check you made, or say plainly that you are summarising and from what."
* "where a reader-side rule has failed repeatedly" — the tree has "Where a reader-side rule has failed repeatedly, more text is usually not the repair."
* "Merge state is the test for a BRANCH" — the tree has lowercase "branch"; I had uppercased it myself and then searched for my own alteration.

The fourth, a principle I attributed to the tree in a merged PR body, read as INVENTED under a 180-character context window and turned out to be stated THREE TIMES once I widened the window and varied the phrasing.

THREE COMPOUNDING CAUSES, all mine. (1) Case: re-typing a phrase from memory drops the sentence-initial capital, and grep is case-sensitive by default. (2) Window: a fixed -oE context window centred on a short term misses the statement that sits just outside it. (3) Wrapping: these files wrap near 95 characters, so ANY quoted sentence longer than a clause spans a line break and a single-line grep cannot see it — flatten with tr '\n' ' ' first.

DIRECTION OF THE ERROR IS ALWAYS THE SAME AND ALWAYS THE EXPENSIVE ONE: absent-when-present. It reads as discovering drift, and acting on it means "fixing" a document that is already correct, or filing a correction against a merged PR that needs none. I was one step from both.

THE CONTROL THAT CAUGHT IT, and it is cheap: run a POSITIVE CONTROL through the same instrument before believing a zero — a phrase you have already confirmed present must come back. Mine returned the right two files, which is what licensed trusting the remaining zeros, and then widening and case-folding dissolved three of them anyway.

RELATED: the tree's own rule already governs the underlying slip — cite the check you made, or say plainly that you are summarising and from what. Reap is "Reap only on the worker's own report", not my paraphrase "a quotable completion report". When quoting the method to the operator, copy the string out of the file rather than retyping it.

PROVE "NOTHING CHANGED ON THE TRACKER SINCE MY LAST PASS" FROM THE EXPORT DIFF, NOT FROM MEMORY OR A RE-READ (2026-08-23).

THE PROBLEM. The backlog-reread loop fires hourly and says do NOT rely on memory. On a static board that reads as an instruction to re-read fourteen long beads every hour, which is exactly what the method's own reread loop calls spending context for nothing. But "I remember it was the same" is not evidence either.

THE INSTRUMENT, two halves that together cover the whole window:

1. COMMITTED MUTATIONS: git log --since=<last pass> -- .beads/issues.jsonl gives the checkpoint commits spanning the window; git diff <first>..<last> -- .beads/issues.jsonl shows exactly which records changed. Parse the +/- lines as JSON and collect the id field to get the changed BEAD IDS.
2. UNCOMMITTED MUTATIONS: git status --porcelain -- .beads/. bd AUTO-STAGES on every mutation but never commits, so a clean export proves no tracker write since the last checkpoint.

MEASURED THIS PASS: the window carried exactly ONE changed line, and parsing it returned id=None. That None was not a null to wave through -- inspecting it showed {"_type":"memory", ...}, my own bd remember record. So: ZERO bead mutations in the window, proven, and the deep re-read of all fourteen was genuinely null.

THE TRAP INSIDE THE INSTRUMENT: the export holds more than issues. Memory records share the file and carry no id, so an id-keyed parse reports None rather than nothing. Read what the None was before calling the diff empty -- a records-changed count of 1 with zero bead ids is a DIFFERENT fact from a diff of zero lines, and only one of them is "nothing happened".

WHAT THIS DOES NOT COVER. Two of the loop's four things depend on the WORLD changing rather than the bead: a fence clears when a PR merges or a worker dies, and neither touches the tracker. So pair the export diff with: HEAD == origin/main unchanged (no merges), and the worktree sweep. If the trunk has not moved and no bead has mutated, all four things are provably null.

READ A WORKER'S LIVENESS CLOCK IN ITS OWN METADATA DIRECTORY, NOT AT <worktree>/.git -- AND ALWAYS PRINT THE DATE (2026-08-23, two sweeps wrong on the first, one on the second).

TRAP 1 -- THE PATH. In a LINKED git worktree, .git is a FILE containing "gitdir: <path>", not a directory. So "find <worktree>/.git -maxdepth 1 -type f -printf %T@" measures the mtime of that one-line pointer and reports it as the worker's metadata clock. It fails quiet: a plausible timestamp comes back, no error. MEASURED: on worktree pr-audit-8445 the wrong form read 2026-08-23 03:13:05 while the real gitdir clock was 21:14:02 -- an 18-hour error, in the direction that reads as DEATH. I nearly recorded a live, actively-fetching worker as quiescent.

RESOLUTION: gd=$(git -C "$wt" rev-parse --git-dir); find "$gd" -type f -printf '%TY-%Tm-%Td %TH:%TM:%TS %f\n' | sort -r | head. For a linked worktree that resolves to <main>/.git/worktrees/<name>/, holding that worktree's OWN FETCH_HEAD, HEAD, index and ORIG_HEAD.

TRAP 2 -- THE FORMAT. Printing %TH:%TM without %TY-%Tm-%Td makes a four-week-old file read as tonight. MEASURED: three frozen husks printed "20:45" beside a live worker's "22:07" in the same table, and the 20:45 was 2026-07-25. The conclusion survived only because the number contradicted an earlier reading and I re-measured with dates. In a liveness table -- where the whole question is how old something is -- a bare time is not a timestamp. ALWAYS carry the date.

WHICH FILE ANSWERS WHAT, measured on pr-audit-8445:
* FETCH_HEAD -- moves on every fetch, so it is the POLLING clock. Movement is proof of life and needs no corroboration; stillness proves nothing. Read it twice 30-60s apart.
* index -- moves when the worker actually stages work. Its index wrote at 11:41:02 and the commit "chore(beads): audit PR #8721" landed at 11:43:26, two minutes later. That gap VALIDATES index-mtime as the "is it producing?" clock, distinct from the fetch clock.

THE METHOD TREE ALREADY SAYS THE FIRST HALF, better than I was practising it: the fetch-head file lives in "that item's OWN metadata directory, which each linked worktree gets its own copy of", and "movement is proof of life and needs no corroboration". Both failures were mine, not the document's, so the repair is this memory rather than more text in the tree.

DO NOT confuse the mayor's .git/FETCH_HEAD with the worker's. Both move; only the worker's proves the WORKER is alive. Check the path you actually measured.

bd show --json CARRIES ONLY FORWARD EDGES: enumerating CHILDREN through it returns a VACUOUS ZERO (2026-08-23).

MEASURED. A bead's JSON record carries exactly two list fields: labels and dependencies. There is NO children, discovered, discovered_from or blocks key. So a probe like [x for x in d.get('children',[])] finds nothing because it looked at nothing -- and a blank from a wrong field name is indistinguishable on screen from a blank meaning "no such edges exist".

THE BACKLOG LOOP ASKS FOR EXACTLY THIS ENUMERATION and warns that a prefix scan misses generated ids -- a child of rf2-hic-090 can be rf2-8mlfj, sharing nothing. So the JSON route looks like the rigorous answer to that warning and is worse than the prefix scan: the prefix scan at least finds the same-family ones.

THE WORKING INSTRUMENT is the TEXT output, whose reverse edges live in sections the JSON does not project:
  bd show <id> | awk '/^(BLOCKS|DISCOVERED)/{f=1} /^(COMMENTS|LABELS)/{f=0} f' | grep -oE 'rf2-[a-z0-9-]+' | sort -u
Run over fourteen open beads this returned nine with reverse edges and four ids never examined before (rf2-xomo, rf2-sxhu, rf2-8mlfj, rf2-v04s) -- all closed days earlier, so the pass was null, but only the text route could establish that.

THE CONTROL THAT CAUGHT IT: when a structural probe returns zero across EVERY item, dump the record's actual keys before believing it. One command -- print every list-valued field with its length -- showed labels and dependencies and nothing else, which is what turned a clean null into a known gap.

GENERAL SHAPE, and it is the day's recurring one: a query against a field that does not exist fails silently and reassuringly. Confirm the field exists before trusting its emptiness.

A COSMETIC PIPE DESTROYS AN EXIT CODE EXACTLY AS A FILTERING PIPE DOES -- and it does not feel like piping a gate (2026-08-24).

WHAT I DID. Checking whether this checkout's git hooks were armed:
    sh scripts/install-git-hooks.sh --check 2>&1 | sed 's/^/  /'
    echo "exit=$?"
That $? is SED'S status, not the script's. It printed 0 and told me nothing. The guard happened to be armed, so the wrong instrument agreed with the truth -- which is the worst outcome, because nothing on screen disputes it.

WHY IT SLIPPED PAST A RULE I HAD JUST WRITTEN DOWN. The method tree says "Never pipe a gate through a filter. A pipeline's exit status is its LAST command's, so a red runner reads green", and I had put the same discipline into two PR bodies hours earlier. But I did not read this as piping a gate: the pipe was there to INDENT output for readability, not to filter anything, and it was a guard-check rather than a test runner. Neither distinction matters to the shell. Any pipe -- sed, head, tr, cat, tee -- replaces the status you wanted with the formatter's, and formatters essentially always succeed, so the answer is a reassuring 0 whatever happened upstream.

THE CORRECT FORM, one command line, one shell:
    out=$(cmd 2>&1); rc=$?
    printf '%s\n' "$out" | sed 's/^/  /'   # format AFTER capturing rc
Capture first, decorate second. And when a --check style probe returns 0 with ZERO BYTES of output, corroborate independently rather than trusting it -- here, ls -l on .git/hooks/pre-commit (present, executable, 4585 bytes) plus the script's own header line "--check  # exit 0 if installed & current, 1 otherwise", which establishes that silence-on-success is the designed contract.

GENERALISE: I add "| sed 's/^/  /'" to almost every command for readable output. Every one of those pipes silently voids $? for the command I actually care about. If the line's purpose is to learn an exit code, it must not end in a pipe -- no exceptions for formatting.

title: loops.md's remedy pointer opens the template at its top, not at Fences
description:

title: nightly-red tracking issue stays silent after night one: seven reds, one notification, no bead
description:
Split out of rf2-2ohy's third acceptance item, which asked whether the
rf2-6sg25 alerting failed to surface seven consecutive nightly reds.

MEASURED 2026-08-23 13:36 AUSEST, and the answer is that THE ALERT FIRED
CORRECTLY. Issue #8423 'Nightly `expensive tests` is red' was opened
2026-08-16T16:01:50Z — the first red night — labelled `nightly-red`,
assigned to mike-thompson-day8, and its body named the exact failing step:
`Browser, bundle, examples, Story/Xray gates -> Gate — production elision,
browser (test:browser-prod-elision)`. It was edited every night since and
last updated 2026-08-22T16:02:05Z carrying `reds=7 greens=0`. The
alerting self-test step passed on every one of those runs. So the first
disjunct in rf2-2ohy's premise — 'the alerting did not fire' — is FALSE.
Nothing in .github/scripts/nightly_failure_alert.py is broken, and this
bead is NOT a request to change its signature logic.

WHAT ACTUALLY HAPPENED is the second disjunct: the issue went unseen for
seven days, and the alerter's own body says why, in its own words:

  'It is edited in place — which notifies nobody — while the same steps
  keep failing, and comments only when a step that was not failing starts
  to.'

That is a deliberate anti-spam design and it is defensible. The observed
cost of it is that a red lane produces EXACTLY ONE notification, on night
one, and then six nights of silence — and the one notification competes
with normal PR traffic in the same inbox. Seven days later the redness was
found by a manual PR-activity sweep, not by the alert, and no bead existed
until that sweep filed rf2-2ohy.

THE GAP, stated narrowly: nothing escalates a `nightly-red` issue that
stays open, and nothing bridges a GitHub issue into the beads tracker,
which is where work is actually dispatched from in this repo. The alert
lands in a channel the working loop does not read.

NOT PROPOSING A REMEDY — this is an operator call, and there are at least
three shapes with different costs, so it should not be picked by a worker:
  (a) re-notify on an age threshold (comment, not edit, after N reds) —
      cheapest, stays inside the existing script;
  (b) have the mayor loop read open `nightly-red` issues each tick;
  (c) have the alerter file/refresh a bead directly, so nightly redness
      enters the same queue as everything else.
(a) risks the spam the current design avoids. (c) is the most useful and
the most machinery. Mike to rule.

EVIDENCE: gh issue view 8423; gh run list --workflow expensive-tests.yml;
.github/workflows/expensive-tests.yml lines 558-616 (the 'Nightly result ->
tracking issue' job, which succeeded on all seven red runs).

ACCEPTANCE: a ruling on whether nightly redness should escalate past night
one, and if so which shape. If the ruling is 'leave it as is, the mayor
sweep is the backstop', close this — that is a legitimate outcome and the
evidence above is the record of what that choice costs.
notes:
*** AWAITING MIKE — NOT DISPATCHABLE. WHOLLY AN OPERATOR CALL. *** Fence recorded by the mayor's dispatch tick 2026-08-23 13:41 AUSEST at tip e1a1faf9c8, quoting this bead's own description rather than re-reasoning it.

WHY IT IS NOT DISPATCHABLE: the bead states it in terms — 'NOT PROPOSING A REMEDY — this is an operator call, and there are at least three shapes with different costs, so it should not be picked by a worker.' A worker sent here would have to choose between (a) re-notify on an age threshold, (b) the mayor loop reads open nightly-red issues each tick, and (c) the alerter files or refreshes a bead directly. Those differ in cost and in how much machinery they add, which is a judgement rather than a task.

DISCHARGED BY: Mike ruling on whether nightly redness should escalate past night one, and if so which of the three shapes. 'Leave it as is, the mayor sweep is the backstop' is a legitimate ruling and closes this bead — the bead says so itself, and the evidence it carries then stands as the record of what that choice costs.

WHAT IT IS NOT, and this matters because the parent bead's premise said otherwise: the alerting is NOT broken. This bead REFUTED that premise with measurement — issue #8423 opened on the first red night, labelled, assigned, naming the exact failing step, edited every night since, with the alerting self-test passing on all seven runs. Do not dispatch anything at .github/scripts/nightly_failure_alert.py's signature logic; nothing there is wrong.

THE COST OF THIS HOLD, priced rather than asserted: nothing is queued behind it and no bead is blocked by it. What it costs is the thing that already happened once — seven consecutive red nights on the superset backstop, found by a manual sweep on day seven rather than by the channel built to report it. That cost recurs at the same rate as nightly redness itself, which over the last nine nights was seven times in nine.

NO HOT-ZONE SEQUENCING IS NEEDED. I had expected to fence this behind rf2-2ohy's worker because a remedy would touch .github/workflows/*, which is hot-zone and currently that worker's. That fence is unnecessary: this bead cannot be dispatched at all until it is ruled, and by then that worker will be long finished.
BACKLOG REREAD 2026-08-23 17:05 AUSEST, tip 69a464c76b. THE PRICE OF THIS HOLD HAS CHANGED SINCE IT WAS RECORDED, and the bead's evidence needs the update so the ruling is made on current facts rather than on the state that prompted the bead.

WHAT THE 13:41 FENCE PRICES: "That cost recurs at the same rate as nightly redness itself, which over the last nine nights was seven times in nine."

THAT RATE WAS MEASURED WHILE THE ROOT CAUSE WAS LIVE, AND IT IS NOT LIVE NOW. Verified at source this tick, one item at a time:

  rf2-2ohy                          CLOSED (the browser-prod-elision abort, fixed by PR #8724)
  expensive-tests on main, 04:11    workflow_dispatch, completed/SUCCESS
  expensive-tests on the fix branch completed/SUCCESS at 03:38
  last SCHEDULED run                2026-08-22T15:24, failure -- i.e. BEFORE the fix landed

So the first SCHEDULED exercise of the fix has not happened yet; it is tonight. The lane is proven green on main by dispatch, and the 7-in-9 figure describes a condition that has been repaired.

AND THE ALERTER CARRIES A RECOVERY POLICY THIS BEAD'S DESCRIPTION DOES NOT MENTION. Issue #8423's body reads, at this tick, "reds=7 greens=1" and states: "This issue closes automatically after 3 consecutive green runs -- the gap exists so an intermittent gate that passes tonight does not close and reopen the issue every other night." The 04:11 dispatch already counted as the first green.

WHY THAT MATTERS TO THE RULING RATHER THAN CLOSING IT. The "edited in place, notifies nobody" characterisation is TRUE OF THE RED DIRECTION ONLY. Recovery is automatic, bounded and hysteresis-guarded; it is the escalation on SUSTAINED redness that is absent. That narrows the question rather than answering it, and narrowing is worth recording: the three shapes are still the three shapes, but option (a) -- re-notify on an age threshold -- is now visibly the mirror of a policy the alerter ALREADY implements in the other direction, which is an argument about symmetry rather than about adding machinery.

THE HOLD'S COST, RE-PRICED. Still nothing queued behind it, still no bead blocked by it. What it costs is no longer a 7-in-9 recurring toll; it is the next unrelated breakage going unreported for as many nights as it takes somebody to sweep manually. That is a lower expected cost and a WORSE-SHAPED one -- rarer, and silent exactly when nobody is looking for it, which is when it will next bite.

NOTHING TO DISPATCH AND NOTHING CHANGED ABOUT DISPATCHABILITY. This stays wholly an operator call on the same three shapes, and "leave it as is, the mayor sweep is the backstop" stays a legitimate closing ruling.

ONE THING TO WATCH RATHER THAN FILE: if tonight's scheduled run is green, #8423 goes to greens=2 and closes itself after the third. If it is red, the fix did not hold under the scheduled trigger and rf2-2ohy wants reopening -- but that is a question for the merge tick tomorrow, not a bead today.

  2026-08-22T15:24  schedule           completed/FAILURE  8c118b7dc2   <- the last red, BEFORE the fix

So the first SCHEDULED exercise of PR #8724's cache-blocking fix passed. The lane is now proven green
under the trigger that was failing, not only under manual dispatch. rf2-2ohy STAYS CLOSED — no reopen.

THE TRACKING ISSUE HAS MOVED TOO, and its own counter is the evidence: issue #8423 now reads
'reds=7 greens=2' where it read 'reds=7 greens=1' before tonight. It auto-closes after THREE
consecutive greens, so it stays open one more night by design — the gap exists so an intermittent gate
does not close and reopen the issue. Expect it to close after tomorrow's scheduled run.

WHAT THIS DOES NOT DISCHARGE: this bead's own subject, which is the ALERTING gap rather than the test
failure — seven reds produced one notification. That question is untouched by tonight's green and is

value:
A WORKTREE'S INDEX CLOCK MEASURES THAT WORKTREE, NOT THE FUNCTION IT WAS DISPATCHED FOR (2026-08-24, correcting my own reading across ~six sweeps).

WHAT I HAD BEEN SAYING. Every stranded sweep reported the pr-audit worktree as "alive, polling on a ~40s cadence, index still 11:41, so nothing audited since 11:43". The first half is right. The second half quietly asserted that the AUDIT FUNCTION had produced nothing, and that does not follow.

WHAT THE PARENT CHAIN SHOWS.
* 10ade546c4 "audit PR #8721", 11:43:26, parent ebc7e737bd -- which IS that worktree's HEAD and its branch tip. So that commit was made from that revision, and the index write at 11:41:02, two minutes earlier, is genuine evidence of it staging. That inference was sound.
* d1c824098d "audit PR #8730", 01:22 the next morning, parent 3c9e358a0f -- a revision that worktree has NEVER been at (its branch reflog has exactly two entries: created, then one fast-forward to ebc7e737bd, and `git cherry` reads 0 ahead).

SO AUDITS KEPT HAPPENING WHILE THAT WORKTREE DID NOTHING BUT FETCH. Tonight's audit filed a bead against my own merge and pushed a commit, from a checkout at main's tip, not from there. At least two things perform this role, and the worktree I was watching is not the one that has been working.

THE CORRECTION, and it is about the shape of the claim rather than the number: an index mtime is evidence about ONE CHECKOUT. Reading it as a health signal for the capability that checkout was dispatched to provide is a category error, and it fails in the reassuring direction -- "nothing has been audited" was false every time I said it, while the audit was in fact catching my own defects.

THE DISCRIMINATOR IS THE PARENT CHAIN, not the clock: take a commit the function produced and ask whether its PARENT is a revision that checkout has actually been at. Its branch reflog answers that in one command and cannot be faked by a fetch.

STILL TRUE, and worth keeping: FETCH_HEAD movement proves that worktree is alive (measured twice, 40 seconds apart, against a mayor clock that stayed still), and it remains unreapable and unmessageable because no dispatch row records an agent id for it.

I CALLED THREE ORDINARY STALE WORKTREES "HUSKS" ALL SESSION, AND HUSK IS A TERM WITH AN OPERATIONAL CONSEQUENCE (2026-08-24).

THE METHOD DEFINES A HUSK PRECISELY: a partial removal, where the tool deregistered the worktree and deleted its metadata, then hit a lock and stopped. Its signature is four things -- it no longer appears in the worktree listing, pruning has nothing to clear, a status check inside it FAILS AND PRINTS NOTHING, and because of that a clean/dirty test reads it as CLEAN.

MY THREE FAIL ALL FOUR, and on the decisive axis they are the exact inverse: they are LISTED, their metadata directory is PRESENT, status works fine, and it reports them DIRTY (one staged file each). They are ordinary registered stale worktrees.

WHY THE WORD MATTERS RATHER THAN BEING LOOSE VOCABULARY: "husk" ROUTES TO A DIFFERENT REMEDY. The method says the ordinary removal path refuses a husk forever and that you must reach for the tool's acknowledged-husk path, which disarms links before deleting. Someone reading my sweep reports -- me, after a context roll -- would reach for that special path for trees where the ordinary path is the correct one, and would skip the ordinary path on the belief it cannot work.

THE OUTCOME HAPPENS NOT TO CHANGE, WHICH IS WHY IT SURVIVED SO LONG. They stay either way. But the REASON differs, and the reason is what a later decision keys on: they stay because they are DIRTY and carry no completion report, not because they are unremovable-by-construction. Dirty is a state waiting never clears; husk is a state retrying never clears. Different remedies, different escalations.

NO DOCUMENT DEFECT. The definition is precise, testable in one command per criterion, and I never tested it -- I inherited the word from an earlier report and repeated it perhaps twenty times. THE CHECK IS CHEAP: does the worktree listing show it, and does a status check inside it return output? Two commands separate the two states completely.

GENERAL SHAPE: a term of art in the method carries its remedy with it. Using one loosely does not stay loose -- it silently prescribes.

REQUESTED BY MIKE 2026-08-29 09:57 AUSEST, in chat, verbatim ask: "do a review of hicasso, improving test coverage and quality."

WHAT THIS IS. A review of implementation/hicasso/'s test suite against its actual surfaces, with two deliverables: (1) a findings review of where coverage is thin, weak, or low-quality relative to what the code does; (2) landed improvements for the clear cases, and follow-on beads (filed one at a time, ids appended to this bead's notes) for anything larger, riskier, or needing a ruling.

WHERE TO LOOK. Map each source module to the tests that exercise it and find the gaps — surfaces with no adversarial or negative case, behaviours only exercised through the happy path, error/complaint shapes never asserted, SSR/DOM parity holes.

QUALITY BAR, from the method and the stance. A coverage or rigour pass must add at least one adversarial or negative case per surface it strengthens — assertion-count growth alone only exercises the happy path. Quality also means the tests themselves: actionable failure output, no tautological assertions, no tests that pin incidental strings where they should pin behaviour (this repo has a measured history of hollow phrase-matcher guards — see rf2-2iaph/rf2-oflj7 for the shape; do NOT touch those files, see fences). WHAT COUNTS AS DONE. The module-to-test gap map is reported (findings doc in ai/findings/, never committed); clear test improvements merged green via PR with a ## Quality gates section; follow-on beads filed for the remainder with this bead named as owner; the delta between what this bead claims and what the tree holds at dispatch time is reported.

- implementation/hicasso/test/re_frame/bench/** and alloc_null_floor.cjs anywhere: held under rf2-t78z / rf2-oflj7 / rf2-fc7w awaiting Mike's rulings. Read them if useful; edit nothing.

POSTURE. Pre-alpha masterpiece: elegance, clarity, correctness, good practice. Trust the programmer. No over-engineering, no gold-plating, no nag-diagnostics, no test-count inflation. Reject a finding rather than action minutiae; a short list of sourced, load-bearing improvements beats a long plausible one.

title: hic: OPERATOR CALL — a prose edit under implementation/hicasso/spec/ queues three Chromium lanes; narrow the arm or accept the toll
description:
CARRIED FORWARD FROM rf2-xomo FINDING 2. rf2-xomo's finding 1 (the stale pinned premise) is fixed by PR #8664; finding 2 is a JUDGEMENT CALL and was deliberately not settled by that worker, because settling it means redesigning a classifier predicate.

*** THIS IS MIKE'S CALL. Not dispatchable as a fix until he rules. ***

THE FACT, MEASURED AT THE CLASSIFIER (paths handed to .github/scripts/report-changed-surfaces.sh directly, tip 447af7b539, both directions with a positive control):

  implementation/hicasso/spec/complaints.md  -> cljs_node_test=true, cljs_browser=true,
                                                migration_hicasso_codemod=true,
                                                hicasso_controlled=true, hicasso_hmr=true
  implementation/hicasso/src/.../core.cljs   -> the IDENTICAL set

That identity is the point: the five operative contract documents rf2-ps7ia moved into implementation/hicasso/spec/ are classified exactly as production CLJS source, because the `implementation/hicasso/*` case arm does not discriminate `.md`. A one-word typo fix in a Markdown register therefore queues cljs_browser, hicasso_controlled and hicasso_hmr -- three Chromium lanes -- plus a ~10-minute CLJS compile.

WHY IT IS A CALL AND NOT A BUG. Two standing principles point opposite ways.
  FOR keeping it: TESTING.md's standing rule is 'when in doubt, over-classify'. Over-arming is the failure mode the repo deliberately prefers, and rf2-8a6s's own comment records that this arm exists precisely because a hicasso-only diff once classified to NOTHING and merged green.
  AGAINST keeping it: the comment block above the complaint-catalogue test in implementation/scripts/_changed-surfaces.test.cjs says in terms that 'arming a ~10-minute CLJS compile for a Markdown edit is the trade TESTING.md's placement table exists to refuse'. That sentence was written about these very documents, at their old address.

THE NARROWING, IF MIKE WANTS IT. An `implementation/hicasso/spec/*.md` case placed BEFORE the `implementation/hicasso/*` arm, setting cljs_node_test only. Rationale: what these five documents actually gate is the invariants chain, which is pure Python -- check_complaint_catalogue.py, the budget-ledger reconciliation, the facade-inventory diff -- and Markdown cannot change what React puts on a page, which is the line rf2-drpa3.70 already drew for prose arms and which _changed-surfaces.test.cjs holds for every other prose arm in the file ('prose arms the JVM tier and NO browser/prod/Playwright tier').

WHAT ALREADY STANDS BEHIND THESE DOCUMENTS EITHER WAY, so the narrowing is not as exposed as it looks: all five carry UNCONDITIONAL test.yml jobs of their own -- hicasso-complaint-catalogue, hicasso-budget-ledger and hicasso-facade-inventory each carry no `needs: detect_changed_surfaces` and no `if:`, by design, precisely because a surface gate that did not cover a checker's inputs was the original defect (rf2-hic-021 / rf2-ibje). docs.yml separately arms the warm-allocation scan on implementation/hicasso/spec/budgets.md by name (rf2-ps7ia).

EXECUTION NOTE IF IT IS RULED. .github/scripts/report-changed-surfaces.sh and implementation/scripts/_changed-surfaces.test.cjs are the one-toucher pair -- the test pins the script's outputs, so this lands in ONE commit touching both, and the row PR #8664 added (implementation/hicasso/spec/complaints.md arms cljs_node_test=true) stays true under the narrowing while the three Chromium outputs would need new false rows beside it.

THE INSTANCE. PR #8674, head 527aac12f740e222f15029efa83f4946be5e12f6: ONE file, implementation/hicasso/spec/dispositions.md, THREE insertions and THREE deletions, prose only — three amendment banners. Exactly the edit this bead describes.

The narrowing as written does not refuse that trade; it keeps it and drops the browser lanes around it. The bead should not be ruled on the belief that it removes the compile.

AND THE WALL-CLOCK GAIN IS NEAR ZERO. The tests workflow took 15.4m; detect_changed_surfaces is 3.8m and node-test is 11.3m, so 3.8 + 11.3 = 15.1m — node-test IS the critical path and the three Chromium lanes finish inside its shadow. WHAT THE NARROWING STILL BUYS, stated fairly so this is not read as an argument against it: 8.4m of runner compute per prose edit is real, and the three lanes it sheds are the browser lanes — the ones this repo has repeatedly seen flake under concurrent load, where a flake costs a re-run and mayor attention rather than only minutes.

A PRECEDENT EXISTS FOR THE EXACT SHAPE. test.yml:1491 records that spec/API.md is already 'caught FIRST by an earlier arm that sets cljs_node_test only' — a prose path arming node-test alone, ahead of a broader catch-all. So the mechanism is in use and is not novel here.

THE CALL REMAINS MIKE'S. Nothing above decides it; it replaces a projected cost with a measured one and corrects what the proposed remedy actually removes.
SEVERABILITY ARGUMENT, from the worker whose PR supplied the measurement (hs11amend, PR #8674), recorded because it is a DIFFERENT kind of evidence from the minutes and it cuts where the minutes do not.

ITS POINT: no browser lane can OBSERVE a prose change inside a markdown table cell, because the file is not compiled, required or served by anything. NOT DISPATCHED — the worker explicitly did not start it, and it is part of the same operator call rather than a separate mechanical task.

STILL MIKE'S. Nothing above rules anything. What the bead now carries that it did not this morning: a measured cost, a correction to what the remedy removes, and an argument that the lanes in question cannot observe the change at all.

title: hic: tool.cljs unjoinable-intent branch (id-less trace bundle) — reachable per Spec 009, unexercised
description: From rf2-dr90's audit. tool.cljs's merge-fragments/intent-rows (~:566-577, :587) handle a ring bundle with no :dispatch-id: it keeps its own identity, sorts last, exports :unknown. notes:

REACHABILITY VERDICT (2026-08-29, hic-browser-rows cluster worker, measured at source on worker/hic-browser-rows off trunk 6eb0a2a402): NOT REACHABLE through trace-tooling/trace-buffer's bundling — closing without a test, per this bead's own terms.

THE EVIDENCE, all four legs at source:
1. read-intents' window is exactly (trace-tooling/trace-buffer fid) per frame (tool.cljs:633; explain-render's window :795 is the same door). The per-frame ring is the ONLY supplier of bundles to intent-rows.
2. The ring cannot retain an id-less event. push-to-ring! guards (when (and dispatch-id frame-id) ...) — implementation/core/src/re_frame/trace/tooling.cljc:251-259 — and its docstring names the rule: frameless emits stream live to listeners only and are never retained. That is Spec 009's B3 ruling verbatim: spec/009-Instrumentation.md:879 'frameless events SKIP the rings entirely ... NEVER retained in any ring', :881 'no shared uncorrelated bucket, no fallback slot', :965 'Frameless events bypass the ring'.
3. A bundle is minted ONLY from ring run-keys: frame-ring-event-bundles maps :run-order and event-bundle seeds :dispatch-id from that key (tooling.cljc:476-488, :414-420), so a bundle's :dispatch-id is non-nil by construction. The other trace-rings writers (set-frame-events-retained! ~:204, clear-trace-buffer! ~:563, clear-trace-rings! ~:582, the inherited-default retune ~:646) resize or empty rings and mint no run key.
4. The uncorrelated events Spec 009 SDispatch-correlation admits (registry-time emits, REPL evals — spec line 72) therefore exist on the LIVE listener stream only. The :ungrouped slot at spec :798 belongs to the flat-stream group-by-event PROJECTION, not to the ring, and read-intents does not consume it.

CONCLUSION: tool.cljs's unjoinable branch (:576-577 nil-id assoc; :581-582 sorts-last; :587 exports evidence/unknown) is defensive-in-depth against a shape the buffer provably cannot deliver. The branch STAYS — it also defends the sort/export against a hypothetical manual emit carrying a non-numeric :rf.trace/dispatch-id with a :frame tag (tooling.cljc:255-257 calls that 'extremely rare - a manual emit from outside any framework boundary'), and against any future ring-side change — but no test can honestly reach it through the public path, and fabricating a windows map to force intent-rows through it would pin nothing the runtime can produce. Grepped: ::unjoinable appears only at its definition site; zero exercise anywhere, as the audit said.
close_reason: Verified NOT reachable: the trace ring drops id-less events at push (B3 ruling, tooling.cljc:259) and bundles are minted only from run-keys, so read-intents can never see a bundle with no :dispatch-id. title: hicasso: commit basis - drop the generation term if the frame epoch already covers it (verify first)
description:
commit-basis = generation + frame-commit-epoch + registry-epoch (generation.cljs:125). bump-generation! has one caller, flush! (collector.cljs:1008); flush! is reached only via mark-dirty!, whose two callers are the cell watch (:681) and the microtask rewire (:768). The watch fires because a reaction input moved, and every frame-state install already bumps frame-commit-epoch at both write chokepoints (core/src/re_frame/frame.cljc:1734-1749, 1821, 1956, 1981) - so on the watch path the generation never moves without the frame epoch moving first. On the rewire path the affected cell exists and its own re-stamp moves the boundary snapshot; there (max (inc epoch) (commit-basis ...)) (:1031-1033) is load-bearing only through inc - max cannot add correctness to a monotone term. The rest of the machinery (disposal hook, first-registration!, registry epoch, microtask rewire, acquire-cell! re-wire guard :956) each closes a named failure and should stay.

DO: verify-first. Scenario to watch: a STAGED key across a same-id reincarnation (the basis ties there today and the generation bump partially un-ties it as a side effect). Gate: staged_read_tear, reincarnation_*, first_registration and generation_fence_coverage suites. If green with the term removed: basis = frame epoch + registry epoch, cell stamp = inc, delete !generation / bump-generation! / the reset-basis! half. If not, close with the counter-example recorded in generation.cljs. Effort: small in code, medium in verification.
notes: 2026-08-29 15:07:56 AUSEST — VERIFIED-REFUSED: the premise does not hold; the generation term is load-bearing and is KEPT. Discriminating test staged_reincarnation_basis_cljs_test (commit 049ebf2b3e, PR #8745) drives the bead's own scenario at the commit seam: a boundary renders a STAGED key, the frame is destroyed and remade under the same id with its install epoch driven to equal the predecessor's at render (the frame term ties), while ONE other cell is held on the frame; the held cell's microtask rewire flushes and bumps the generation, which the staged boundary reads through the basis at commit. WITH the term: basis@commit != basis@render, 9/9 assertions green (exit 0). WITHOUT (control plant removed @!generation from commit-basis's sum): both read 4, row red (exit 1) — the predecessor's value left on screen, the P0 class generation.cljs names. Restored, blob hash equal to HEAD. Counter-example recorded on commit-basis's docstring per the DO, including the half the term does NOT cover (a frame holding no other cell has nothing to rewire and ties either way — the :node-key axis the docstring already concedes; not this bead's to close). Negative control in the same file: with nothing in the gap the number ties and nothing re-renders. Full node-test-hicasso lane: 1355 tests / 5534 assertions / 0 failures.
close_reason: Verified-refused: the generation term is load-bearing for a staged key across a same-id reincarnation (staged_reincarnation_basis_cljs_test, 049ebf2b3e, PR #8745): with the term the snapshot moves, without it both read 4 and the row is red. Term kept; counter-example recorded on commit-basis.

title: RULING: src is 71% prose - docstring = contract plus one sentence of why; the essays move to docs/design/hicasso
description:
src/ is 17,113 lines of which ~12,000 are docstrings and comments (approx: codec.cljs 67%, collector.cljs 74%, controlled.cljs 78%, hicasso.cljc 87%, mount.cljs 76%). impl/ alone: 11,693 lines = 2,788 code + 7,207 docstring + 1,219 comment (72% prose). collector.cljs opens with a 393-line docstring before its first require; controlled.cljs is 688 doc lines for 155 of code; generation.cljs 102 doc lines for 26 of code. Docstrings cross-reference three others, so editing one mechanism means re-reading the essay on all of them, and finding flush! means scrolling ~1,000 lines. This is the shape problem underneath the rest of the review: nothing is short enough to be seen whole, which is why the dead weight survived, and it is why every rename is a multi-file multi-paragraph edit. docs/design/hicasso (146 files) already exists and is where HD-numbered rulings, measurement tables and rejected alternatives belong.

RECOMMENDATION: per file, docstring = what it is/returns, the contract, and one sentence of why (with a link to the design record for the argument); move measurement tables, rejected designs and ruling citations to docs/design/hicasso. Target roughly 1:1 prose:code. Best done per file alongside the cut tasks in this epic so the prose is trimmed once, after the code it describes has settled. This reverses the direction of PR #8736 (which polished the prose in place); that PR is not wasted - the survivors will be the timeless versions - but Mike should rule before a second prose pass starts.

WHAT THE ADDED REVIEW SAID AND HOW IT WAS WEIGHED. After filing, the dossier gained an independent second review ("Codex Recommendation"). It concurs with A and amends it in five ways. All five are adopted, one with a bound:
(1) A content rule, not a line-count regime: no 1:1 enforcement, no 40-line cap, no docstring-link checker, no migration machinery. Adopted. The bead's "roughly 1:1 prose:code" is the expected OUTCOME of applying the rule, not a threshold a reviewer applies.
(2) Move only durable design reasoning; DELETE duplicated, superseded and journey prose rather than preserving it ceremonially. Adopted, with a bound: the dossier's own sample found about half the essay material already on a design page, so moving it would write it twice; but the PR body still names each deleted essay and where its surviving copy is, so nothing goes silently.
(3) A source comment stays only where it protects nearby code from a plausible-but-wrong edit. The epoch-floor proof beside flush! and the rf2-6c12m.19 counter-example on commit-basis are such proofs and stay; module history, benchmark narrative and repeated cross-module explanation go. Adopted.
(4) A public docstring carries the smallest complete contract a caller needs (inputs, outputs, effects, ordering, failure behaviour) plus an example only where it removes real ambiguity; a private docstring says what the var does and the one non-obvious invariant behind its shape. Adopted - it is the dossier's rule with the public/private line made explicit.
(5) One small cleanup pass over untouched files when the wave is done. Adopted as the follow-up bead.
Its lexical scan read 75.8% prose against the dossier's 72%; the methods differ on ^{:doc} metadata and comment classification, both agree the shape is about three prose lines per line of code, and the ruling does not turn on which figure is right. The one material risk it names - over-trimming caller-facing facts into the unpublished design tree - is why the public-contract clause below is stated in full rather than left to taste.

THE RULE (binding on every PR that edits a docstring or comment under implementation/hicasso/src from now on):
1. A docstring carries: (a) what the var is or returns; (b) the contract - what it takes, returns and promises, its effects, ordering and failure behaviour, in full for a public var; for a private var, what it does plus the one non-obvious invariant behind its shape; (c) one sentence of why; (d) where the argument lives, as a repo-relative path into docs/design/hicasso (docs/design/hicasso/architecture.md, docs/design/hicasso/studio/<page>.md, docs/design/hicasso/decisions.md HD-NNN). An example only where it removes real ambiguity.
2. Links are repo-relative paths, NEVER [[wikilinks]]: 892 [[...]] exist across src/ and nothing resolves them (no codox config; scripts/check_doc_slugs.py scans docs/, spec/, skills/, migration/ and tools/*/spec only - DEFAULT_ROOTS line 94; PR #8736's body says "the doc link gates do not cover source docstrings"). The worker checks each retained path exists while editing and says so in the PR body.
3. A measured figure may stay in a docstring only with its page named beside it (e.g. "2.75 vs 1.42 us/read; docs/design/hicasso/studio/the-cold-read-mount-term.md").
4. A source comment stays only where it protects nearby code from a plausible-but-wrong edit (a local correctness proof). Module history, benchmark narrative, rejected alternatives, HD-ruling derivations and explanations of OTHER namespaces' mechanisms do not.
5. A content rule, not a number: no 40-line cap, no 1:1 enforcement, no docstring-link checker, no migration script.
6. Move vs delete: durable design reasoning with no home in docs/design/hicasso is MOVED there (see WHERE CUT MATERIAL GOES in the next note); prose a design page already carries, superseded prose and change-narration is DELETED. The PR body names, per essay, the path it moved to, or "deleted - duplicated at <path>" / "deleted - superseded".
7. Untouched: retained-inventory's :what strings and the rf2:builder-bypass-ok block (as #8736 left them); impl/slot.cljc until rf2-6c12m.1 retires the freeze gate (implementation/hicasso/scripts/check_freeze.py lines 57 and 799 treat a docstring as code - a changed word reds - for pinned rows, of which slot.cljc is the last).

- impl/ (18 files): 12,474 = 7,499 + 1,285 + 3,174; 73%
- impl/codec.cljs: 3,940 = 2,111 + 570 + 1,085; 71%
- impl/collector.cljs: 2,168 = 1,315 + 298 + 477; 77%
- impl/controlled.cljs: 886 = 678 + 18 + 164; 81%
- impl/mount.cljs: 639 = 436 + 53 + 127; 79%

- 451 docstrings: median 10 lines; 137 at 5 lines or fewer (the bulk already meets the rule); 91 over 30 lines; 17 over 100; 4 over 200
- the 5 longest: collector ns 392 lines, controlled ns 328, intent ns 248, server ns 211, codec ns 198; then native ns 188, overlay ns 187, boundary ns 167, defhost 156, defview 153, forms ns 135, mint-view! 129
- collector.cljs opens with the 392-line ns docstring before its first :require; rstate is at line 427 and flush! at 994
- flush! (9 lines) and with-commit (4 lines) already read as the rule asks; commit-basis (58 lines at HEAD, about 80 once PR #8745 lands) and cold-read! (59 lines) do not

WHAT THE PROSE IS (descending volume): design reasoning (why the shell is 2 hooks, why the commit basis has 3 terms, why the memo is per read); measurement (probe 2.75 vs probe-fresh 1.42 us/read, "4 ms is the SHORTEST delay measured", a Chromium epoch-tie trace inside flush!); rejected alternatives (UIx's 3-hook input wrapper, a run-shared memo, useRef in the shell); cross-references (892 [[wikilinks]], HD-numbered rulings, studio pages, test namespaces).

COSTS THAT DECIDED IT: finding a function means paging past essays; editing one mechanism means re-reading essays on three (the collector, generation and intent docstrings each explain the other two); every rename is a multi-paragraph edit (#8736 needed 27 files, +577/-565, to change vocabulary alone); worker context - codec.cljs and collector.cljs together are about 6,100 lines, roughly 75,000 tokens at 12 tokens a line, before a worker opens a test; the prose half of every diff is the half reviewers cannot check mechanically; the review behind this epic judged "nothing is short enough to be seen whole, which is why the dead weight survived".

BENEFITS, FAIRLY, AND THE AI-FIRST TENSION: the whys are real and many are measured against a named test; an AI pair reading cold-read! learns in one place why the memo is per read and what changing it would cost. No repo convention sets a docstring rule (spec/Principles.md, spec/Conventions.md, CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md); Principles.md "Low hidden context" favours discoverable reasoning, Conventions.md "annotation is not removal" says a docstring is not where a disposition lives; neither settles it. The tension with the AI-first principle is about PLACEMENT, not existence: an AI pair benefits from context it can reach by a path; it does not benefit from 1,000 lines between a function and its caller, because that is context budget spent before the caller is in view. The rule keeps the reasoning reachable - one path, one authoritative copy - and takes it out of the read path.
RULING rf2-6c12m.4, part 2 of 2 (2026-08-29 15:29:24 AUSEST) - worked examples, destinations, sequencing, acceptance.

WORKED EXAMPLES - the model for every trimming worker (copy the shape, not the words):

A) Namespace docstring - impl/collector.cljs, 392 lines. Current opening:
(ns re-frame.hicasso.impl.collector
  "HICASSO - THE COLLECTOR. The runtime's heart.
  A boundary is a real React function component minted by `defview` ...
  ## The five siblings, and why the grouping is what it is
  | module | what it owns | ...
  ## The shell, and the <=2-hook budget (HD-020)
  ... (386 more lines)
Trimmed to the rule:
(ns re-frame.hicasso.impl.collector
  "The collector: which boundaries a commit must re-run, how a body reaches
  subscription values, and the generation fence that keeps one render pass
  on one commit. React owns everything else about a boundary.

  Owns the render context, the cell table, the commit window (`with-commit`,
  `flush!`), the two read tiers, the read-set entry cache, and the shell and
  mint doors. Those form one dependency cycle, which is why they share a
  namespace; `generation`, `frames`, `roots`, `evidence` and `inventory`
  each hold a one-directional edge out of it.

  Design record: docs/design/hicasso/architecture.md (sub-read ladder,
  2-hook shell, HD-002, HD-020); measurements in docs/design/hicasso/studio/."

B) Public function - impl/generation.cljs commit-basis. 58 lines at HEAD, including a section "## Why the registry term costs the mounted case nothing"; PR #8745 (rf2-6c12m.19, verified-refused: the generation term is load-bearing and KEPT) adds "## Why the generation term stays", about 22 lines. That counter-example is a local correctness proof and SURVIVES as the one-sentence why. Trimmed:
(defn commit-basis
  "The number a staged read is judged against: this runtime's flush
  generation + the frame's install epoch (`frame/frame-commit-epoch`) +
  the registry epoch. Monotone within a frame incarnation; install-counting,
  so a value-equal install still advances it (one redundant re-render at
  worst, never a missed one). Pure; allocates nothing.

  Three terms because each sees a movement the other two cannot: the
  generation moves only through a committed cell's watch, the install
  epoch is a plain counter, and only the registry term carries a `reg-sub`
  landing in the render->commit gap. The generation term is load-bearing
  across a same-id reincarnation, where the frame term restarts and can
  tie: any other cell the frame holds is rewired by microtask and that
  flush bumps the generation (staged_reincarnation_basis_cljs_test); a
  frame holding no other cell ties either way, which is Spec 006
  invariant 5's `:node-key` axis, not this number's. Full argument:
  docs/design/hicasso/architecture.md, section The commit basis."
  [frame-kw]
  (+ @!generation (frame/frame-commit-epoch frame-kw) @!registry-epoch))
(The trimming worker WRITES that architecture.md section first - it has no home today; see below.)

C) Private function with a measurement essay - impl/collector.cljs cold-read!, 59 lines. Trimmed:
(defn- cold-read!
  "Read a key no committed cell answers for. Reuses a live sub-cache
  reaction when one exists; otherwise computes pure against one
  frame-state snapshot per body run (the probe on `rstate`), memoised per

title: RULING: defhost :callbacks roster - infer the contract from the prop position instead of declaring it
description:
defhost makes the consumer declare :callbacks {:on-close :event, :render-row :render, :x :handler} and learn a 6-row table for what one h/event means by position (docs/core/hicasso/03-events-as-data.md:113-120). But impl/intent.cljs:1200-1210 ALREADY selects the contract by position for every native tag (on* = event, else render, :ref excluded), and lower-declared-prop (intent.cljs:1283-1296) shows :handler has no positive behaviour: h/event -> identity, plain fn -> identity, vector -> refused - and a vector at an undeclared on* host prop is already refused (codec.cljs:2884). :handler appears in zero consumer-shaped code (only host_hatch and intent_cljs_test). The one consumer-shaped declaration in the repo (test/.../examples/ledger/views.cljs:14-16) declares two entries. 11 refusal ids exist solely to validate the defhost declaration map (codec.cljs:1538-2053), ~15 to police this grammar overall. The stated reason for the roster (value-first foreign callbacks) is already caught at runtime by intent-needs-the-event (intent.cljs:107,726).

RECOMMENDATION: infer on* -> event, everything else -> render, exactly as native tags do; keep :slots (genuinely uninferable - a vector is legal data). Delete :callbacks, :handler and ~8 ids (unknown-callback-contract, host-structural-callback, host-callback-slot-collision, intent-at-a-non-event-contract, host-undeclared-callback, host-unclaimed-callback, plus simpler macro-tail guards). Effort: medium. If ruled yes, dispatch with the refusal-shrink task.

RULING 2026-08-29 15:29:54 AUSEST (delegated review per Mike, 2026-08-29): Option B, 2 values - infer the callback contract from the prop position exactly as native tags already do (on* -> :event, anything else walked -> :render, :ref -> React's); keep :callbacks ONLY as an optional override taking :event or :render; delete :handler; keep :slots.
BANNER STRUCK 2026-08-29 15:29:54 AUSEST: ruled.

WHY B (decisive facts)
- The runtime already infers for every native tag: position-contract (impl/intent.cljs:1200-1210) = ref? -> :ref, event-prop? -> :event, else :render; event-prop? is one regex ^on-[a-z]|^on[A-Z] (intent.cljs:916-926). lower-declared-prop (intent.cljs:1255-1302) routes declared :event/:render to the SAME two wrappers the native walk uses (event-callback, render-callback).
- Every declaration in the repo and the guide infers identically. The only consumer-shaped one (test/re_frame/hicasso/examples/ledger/views.cljs:14-16, :137-138: {:render-row :render :on-window :event}) is exactly what inference gives. Guide declarations :on-change/:on-close/:on-pick/:on-value-change -> event and :render-row/:item-content -> render also match; the only two that do not are the two the guide invents to illustrate the roster (:on-imperative :handler, :on-render-row :render).
- :handler has no behaviour: h/event -> identity, plain fn -> identity, vector/map -> refused. A plain function already crosses untouched at every position (intent.cljs:1220-1228; codec.cljs:2865, host-prop-value's fn? arm). Zero consumer-shaped uses, tests only. Its own docstring says a plain fn is the handler contract (intent.cljs:1279-1281). It adds vocabulary, not capability.
- The stated reason for "never infer" (a value-first foreign callback such as onChange(date), where [:x ::h/value] would read date.target) is caught at runtime regardless of any declaration: event-arg! raises :rf.error/hicasso-intent-needs-the-event naming the position (intent.cljs:95-117, :710-738). The declaration never prevented the mistake; the runtime check does.
- [:>] gets inference for free: raw-element walks props through host-entry against an EMPTY declared roster (codec.cljs:3465), so today [:> X {:on-pick (h/event ...)}] is refused as unclaimed and [:> X {:on-pick [:x/y]}] as undeclared. Under B host-entry's :else arm infers, so [:>] and defhost share one classifier (the second reviewer's point).
- Both the dossier author and the second reviewer (Codex) recommend B with 2 values. The added review is a clear recommendation, not a partial opinion; I weighed it against the code and found nothing against it. It adds three implementation constraints adopted here: reuse the native classifier (no second one), apply the same default in defhost and the [:>] host walk, and a proportionate test bar (below).

WHY NOT A (infer, delete :callbacks): one paragraph smaller, but no first-class spelling for an on*-named prop whose RETURN the library consumes and which is interactive. Fluent UI DetailsList onRenderItem/onRenderCell/onRenderHeader return UI; Ant Design Table onFilter returns a boolean, onRow/onCell/onHeaderRow return props maps. The event wrapper always returns nil (intent.cljs:551-596), so an h/event there blanks the list or vetoes every row, silently. A plain function is the escape and suffices for predicates and props-returning callbacks, but a plain function gets no frame/dispatch rebinding (render-callback, intent.cljs:598-704), so an intent inside a row it returns raises :rf.error/hicasso-intent-outside-boundary at click - loud, not silent, but under A the only fix is an adapter component. Under B it is one line, {:callbacks {:on-render-item :render}}, and the render wrapper supplies the owning frame. The override costs one taught paragraph and one 2-value check that folds into .11's single bad-declaration id. The roster never prevented this hard case either: declaring such a prop :event blanks it the same way (skills/reagent-migration/SKILL.md:160 already warns).

WHY NOT C (keep as is): the consumer keeps declaring what the library already knows; the guide keeps a rule that contradicts its own native-tag behaviour; 4 ids, 1 half-id, 1 roster and ~560 lines of validation and commentary police a grammar with no consumer.

THE RULE AFTER B (position table 6 rows -> 4)
1. on*-spelled prop (native tag, defhost, [:>]) -> :event: h/event takes the event wrapper; an intent vector or key-map lowers as at a native event position; a plain fn crosses untouched.
2. Any other walked prop -> :render: h/event takes the render wrapper (frame + dispatch rebound); a vector or map crosses AS DATA via host-prop-value/clj->js exactly as at a native tag (nobody writes {:on-render-item [:x/y]} on purpose; refusing it is a guard a trusted programmer never trips). Plain fn untouched.
3. Declared :slots position -> markup (as-element); an h/event there stays refused (a function as a ReactNode renders nothing, silently) - this is the surviving half of host-unclaimed-callback.
4. :ref -> React's (check-ref!).
Override: {:callbacks {<prop> :event|:render}}, written only where inference is wrong; a declared contract outranks the spelling. Any other value is a bad declaration.

BEFORE / AFTER
;; today
(h/defhost date-picker DatePicker {:callbacks {:on-change :event}})
(h/defhost rows vendor/virtual-rows {:callbacks {:render-row :render :on-window :event}})
(h/defhost picker Widget {:callbacks {:on-pick :event :on-imperative :handler :on-render-row :render}})
;; after
(h/defhost date-picker DatePicker)
(h/defhost rows vendor/virtual-rows)
(h/defhost fluent-list FluentList {:callbacks {:on-render-item :render}})   ; the hard case: on*-named render prop
;; call sites unchanged
[date-picker {:selected (h/sub [:task/due-date]) :on-change (h/event [date _] [:task/set-due date])}]
[:> DatePicker {:on-change (h/event [date _] [:task/set-due date])}]   ; legal now too

title: RULING: refusal contract shape - drop the :recovery keyword, :where, and the runtime meta-refusal
description:
impl/error.cljc is 356 lines (~60 code). Every refusal carries id + :where (emitting fn) + :reason + :recovery keyword + coords, and check-complete! mints :rf.error/hicasso-refusal-incomplete at RUNTIME (error.cljc:265) to police the package own call sites. :recovery is a keyword such as :declare-render-or-client-only-with-an-optional-fallback - spelled once, typed by nobody, tracking API renames (complaints.md:236-295 spend 60 lines ruling on when it moves; naming-ledger row 21 shows one option rename moved three recovery keywords across runtime + witnesses + Spec 009 rows). :where duplicates the stack trace. RECOMMENDATION: (fail! id message extra) with the ambient :view/:source stamp; drop :recovery keyword and :where; delete the meta-refusal (a missing message is a code-review matter, not a runtime law). The message text still names the fix. Effort: ~2 hours + mechanical test edits (error_shape_cljs_test pins the shape). Counter-argument to weigh: a machine-readable recovery keyword could help an AI pair - but the reason string already carries the same words.

title: RULING: the native tier is a second authoring language with one consumer - shrink it to the hooks
description:
native.cljc is 1,116 lines (71% prose), 14 public names (10 surface + 4 public-by-expansion, native.cljc:161-185), 7 refusal ids, its own {:server} roster on defcomponent that duplicates defhost (native.cljc:391-401 says so), n/memo and n/lazy wrappers whose sole job is carrying a marker, a 4-production props grammar and the n/props marker. Consumer-shaped usage across examples/, tools/*/testbeds and the 8 example apps under hicasso/test/.../examples is ONE mention - the ledger docstring saying it was not needed (ledger/views.cljs:86). The guide concedes rung 4 may be a defui and that n/use-sub / n/use-frame work inside UIx (docs/core/hicasso/10-native-tier.md:260-265).

RECOMMENDATION: keep n/use-sub and n/use-frame (the only things React cannot supply) and the two facade bridges; let islands be UIx or raw React mounted through defhost / [:>]. If rung 3 (a defview returning native elements, measured 38% on one example) is judged worth keeping, keep $ alone and drop defcomponent / memo / lazy / props and their 5 grammar refusals (or collapse to 2). Effort: large. Also touches: HMR contract for native, bundle-isolation sentinel for the tier, three_way_parity suites (keep the parity FLOOR test as a perf guard regardless).

*** AWAITING MIKE - NOT DISPATCHABLE. *** Banner added 2026-08-29 14:38 AUSEST by the merge+dispatch tick (mayor session re-frame2-9a). Type is decision; the epic rf2-6c12m names it as one of five rulings that gate tasks. WHOEVER RULES STRIKES THIS BANNER IN THE SAME ACT.
